Immigration fines are authorized under several different provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act.
Broader Constitutional Challenges Beyond individual defenses, immigration advocates are challenging the expanded use of immigration fines in federal court.
And, please keep in mind that contesting an immigration fine doesn’t by itself determine a person's underlying immigration status or eligibility for immigration benefits.
Final Thoughts Civil immigration fines have become one of the federal government's most aggressive immigration enforcement tools.
text:
For years, immigration enforcement in the United States was measured largely by arrests, detention, and deportations. Today, however, another enforcement strategy has emerged—one that can have devastating financial consequences for immigrants and employers alike.

Federal immigration agencies are increasingly relying on civil monetary penalties as a powerful enforcement tool. Through Notices of Intent to Fine (NIFs) and, more recently, Notices of Violation, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) are seeking to impose significant financial penalties on individuals and businesses for alleged immigration violations.

For many recipients, these fines come as a surprise. Even more concerning, some notices seek penalties totaling more than a million dollars for an individual.

The good news is that receiving one of these notices does not mean the government automatically wins. Many fines can be challenged, reduced, or even rescinded if addressed promptly.

What Is a Notice of Intent to Fine?

A Notice of Intent to Fine (NIF) is a formal notice issued by DHS or ICE advising an individual or employer that the government intends to assess civil monetary penalties for alleged violations of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA).

Historically, these notices were relatively uncommon. Recently, the Trump Administration has begun sending them widely, part of its efforts to drive people out of the country.

More recently, ICE has also begun issuing Notices of Violation in certain cases. Unlike a Notice of Intent to Fine, which provides advance notice before a penalty is imposed, a Notice of Violation immediately assesses the civil penalty and generally provides only a limited period in which to contest it.

Who Can Receive Immigration Fines?

Immigration fines are authorized under several different provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Individuals can receive notices based on:

Failure to Depart After a Final Removal Order: Willfully failing to depart after a final removal order, with fines potentially accruing daily

Failure to Comply with Voluntary Departure failing to leave after agreeing to voluntary departure

Improper Entry entering or attempting to enter the United States at locations other than a designated port of entry

Employers are increasingly targeted through Notices of Intent to Fine following Form I-9 inspections. ICE is seeking civil penalties against businesses, and those fines can escalate quickly depending on the number of alleged violations and whether ICE believes the violations were repeated or intentional.

How Do These Fines Become So Large?

I know, the term “more than a million dollars” was thrown around earlier, which can sound shocking but this is really what people are experiencing. While some immigration fines begin at relatively modest amounts—such as civil penalties for improper entry—the most financially devastating assessments generally involve alleged failures to comply with removal orders, nearly a thousand dollars a day in certain failure-to-depart cases.

Because these penalties may accrue daily and be calculated retroactively, the total amount can increase rapidly. Using the applicable statute of limitations, the government has sought penalties approaching $1.9 million in some cases.

Adding to the concern, many recipients report that the notices provide little explanation of how the government calculated the total amount demanded, making it difficult to verify whether the assessment complies with the law.

If This Seems to Be Happening Really Fast, You’re Right

Recent regulatory changes have significantly altered how immigration fines are issued and collected. Among the most important developments are:

shorter advance notice periods before penalties become final

authorization for service of notices by regular mail rather than requiring personal service in some circumstances

expanded use of Notices of Violation that immediately impose penalties rather than merely announcing the government's intent to fine

compressed deadlines for filing administrative challenges

Because these deadlines may be very short, recipients should never ignore a notice or assume there will be additional opportunities to respond later. Acting promptly can be essential to protecting the recipient's rights and ensuring a meaningful opportunity to challenge the government's claims before significant financial penalties become final.

Don’t Panic: Legal Defenses May Be Available

Every case is different, but immigration fines are often subject to legal and factual challenges. This is where I encourage you to speak to qualified legal counsel as each case is different.

Possible defenses include challenging the alleged willfulness of failing to depart, such as if a person was detained by immigration authorities, incarcerated, hospitalized, or otherwise unable to depart, the government may be unable to establish the required element of willfulness.

Attorneys may also be able to challenge whether a voluntary departure agreement was valid, whether the individual remained eligible for relief, or whether equitable circumstances warrant reducing or eliminating the penalty.

In certain circumstances, individuals may qualify for statutory protections or exceptions, including protections available under the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA). It may also be worth looking into whether the government has complied with applicable statutes of limitation and other procedural requirements.

Broader Constitutional Challenges

Beyond individual defenses, immigration advocates are challenging the expanded use of immigration fines in federal court.

Among the issues being raised are:

Due Process: Whether notices that fail to explain how penalties were calculated violate the Fifth Amendment.

Excessive Fines: Whether penalties reaching hundreds of thousands—or even millions—of dollars violate the Eighth Amendment.

Administrative Procedure Act (APA): Whether recent procedural changes were lawfully adopted.

Institutional Fairness: Whether allowing DHS both to impose fines and adjudicate administrative appeals provides meaningful due process.

These challenges could significantly influence how immigration fines are imposed in the future.

The Importance of Acting Quickly

Perhaps the most important thing recipients should understand is this: an immigration fine is not necessarily final.

Failing to respond, however, can have serious consequences. Missing the applicable deadline may result in the assessment becoming a final order with limited or no opportunity for further administrative review.

Attorneys across the country have successfully challenged immigration fines through timely administrative responses and legal advocacy. In many cases, fines have been reduced substantially or withdrawn altogether.

And, please keep in mind that contesting an immigration fine doesn’t by itself determine a person's underlying immigration status or eligibility for immigration benefits.

Ongoing Federal Litigation

The legality of these expanded enforcement practices is currently being challenged in Maria L. v. Noem, a class action brought by the Immigrant Legal Resource Center (ILRC) and Public Justice. The lawsuit challenges both the legality of the government's civil fine program and the procedural rules governing how those penalties are imposed and reviewed. Because the litigation remains ongoing, practitioners should monitor developments that may affect pending and future cases.

Final Thoughts

Civil immigration fines have become one of the federal government's most aggressive immigration enforcement tools. Whether directed at noncitizens accused of failing to depart, individuals alleged to have entered improperly, or employers facing Form I-9 penalties, these assessments can carry enormous financial consequences.

It is vital that anyone (individual or business) receiving this type of notice recognizes that essentially these notices are legal proceedings—not simply bills. You need to respond in a timely manner or important rights could be lost.

description:
But those are just blips in the broader landscape of immigration detention.
As the Trump administration plans to pour up to $45 billion in the next few years into locking up immigrants, we’ll dive into the immigration detention ecosystem in the Bay Area and nationwide.
Alexis Madrigal: Welcome to Forum, I’m Alexis Madrigal.

Alexis Madrigal: We’re talking about the network of immigration detention facilities in the Bay Area.
text:
The federal government has been scrambling to find places to send immigrants that have been arrested at record levels – close to 50,000 in July alone. Trump’s rush to detain immigrants has led to inadequate and overcrowded facilities and out-of-state transfers. Some immigrants have been held for days in unsanitary conditions at San Francisco International Airport. Meanwhile, Gilroy residents have been fighting a proposed field office for Immigration and Customs Enforcement. But those are just blips in the broader landscape of immigration detention. As the Trump administration plans to pour up to $45 billion in the next few years into locking up immigrants, we’ll dive into the immigration detention ecosystem in the Bay Area and nationwide.

Guests:

Tyche Hendricks, senior editor covering immigration, KQED

Doug MacMillan, Reporter covering corporate accountability, The Washington Post

Sara DiNatale, reporter covering politics and the impacts of the Trump administration’s policies on the Bay Area and California, San Francisco Chronicle

This is a computer-generated transcript. While our team has reviewed it, there may be errors.

Alexis Madrigal: Welcome to Forum, I’m Alexis Madrigal. The Trump administration came into office promising to transform immigration in America, and they have endeavored to do so, arresting and deporting entirely different groups of people than previous administrations. Immigration agents arrested close to 50,000 people in July alone. So where do all those people go?

In Northern California, it’s not a simple situation. We don’t have a big ICE facility nearby. In fact, the closest one is a converted prison in California City, out in the Mojave Desert. We’re gonna talk about the network of facilities that exist now, and that may get built with the surge of money that the Trump administration is plowing into ICE.

Joining us first, we’ve got Tyche Hendricks, senior editor covering immigration here at KQED. Welcome, Tyche.

Tyche Hendricks: Glad to be here.

Alexis Madrigal: And we’ve got Sara DiNatale, who is a reporter covering politics and the impacts of the Trump administration’s policies on the Bay Area and California at the San Francisco Chronicle. Hey. So, Tyche, just kind of give us an overview here. Like, how is immigration detention supposed to work? How did it, generally speaking, work in the past, and sort of what’s different now?

Tyche Hendricks: Sure. Well, I mean, I think at the get-go we should say immigration detention is civil detention. It’s not punishment for a crime. It’s not supposed to be punitive. It is primarily aimed at people who are a flight risk or a danger, who, you know, the government feels should be held in custody until they go through their immigration court proceeding, deportation proceeding.

There are some people subject to mandatory detention, people, for example, who have certain criminal convictions. And this administration and this Republican Congress have vastly expanded, you know, who they think should be mandatorily detained, which is part of why we’re seeing this huge increase in people in detention facilities.

But, yeah, arrests are coming up to record numbers, and detention also is near a record high. And one thing we should say, even though in California there are some really high numbers, we’re the third highest in arrests after Florida, and Texas is number one. And in those places, it’s ramped up significantly.

So partly because we have these sanctuary laws that mean that when you have a traffic stop with a police officer, you’re not necessarily gonna be handed over to ICE as you would be in those other states, right?

Alexis Madrigal: Yeah. You know, what about the, you know, we’ve seen many of these arrests, either the viral ones and the many more that occur out of the public eye. Where do people actually go? Like, if you got detained — there was someone detained on Telegraph Avenue, you know, a few weeks ago or a month ago. What are the kind of pathways that someone might go through there?

Tyche Hendricks: Sure. I mean, typically, you would go to an ICE office where there are sort of short-term hold rooms in San Francisco. It’s at the ICE sort of field headquarters at 630 Sansome Street, where we’ve seen a lot of protests. And those are hold rooms meant for like a 12-hour processing, you know, short-term, not for overnight.

And then you would be taken on to a long-term detention facility. As you say, there are none currently in Northern California. So the closest are down in Southern Kern County.

But I will say that there was kind of a bottleneck with the short-term hold rooms. And people were being held there for days and days without proper medical care, medical screening, without bedding, without proper food and hygiene. And a court order has now said, that’s no good. And so ICE has sort of fallen back and tried to regroup.

Alexis Madrigal: Sara, you were reporting on what’s been happening at SFO, which seems like exactly an example of one of these situations, right? Where it’s supposed to be short-term detention, but as you discovered talking to people who were actually held there, it has not been.

Sara DiNatale: Yeah, exactly. So what’s happening at SFO, one, I mean, I think people have seen the viral videos of domestic terminal arrests. So what we’re talking about with people actually being held at the airport is happening in the international terminal.

So these are a lot less typically a lot more visible because it’s happening when an immigrant is reentering the country through customs, where they often would be — it’s not abnormal to have a secondary inspection interview. Those happen behind closed doors, you don’t have your cell phone, you’re kind of going over your particulars with a federal agent.

But what’s happening is folks, and a lot of green card holders included, are being flagged, going through that secondary inspection interview, being told like, hey, you have an old arrest on your record and we need to investigate it further. And rather than releasing them on something called parole, which essentially is like, hey, come back for a follow-up appointment, they’re holding them at the airport.

And they’re keeping them in a — they call it a lounge, to be clear. That is their language. They call it an in-transit lounge, and it is by Customs and Border Protection policy only supposed to be used for 72 hours. I would say from the people I’ve spoken to have been held there, they would say like 72 hours is still way too long.

There’s not beds. They’re mainly chairs. They renovated recently, and now they have couch-like benches, which is a step up from before, when people told me they were sleeping upright for up to eight days.

So these holds are really long. Essentially, agents are deciding what to do with them based on their arrest history and following Trump’s executive order about detaining people if they’re deemed potentially inadmissible. And eventually, after that process at the airport, they’re transferred to California City, which is that big holding facility in the Mojave Desert.

Alexis Madrigal: So talk to me, Sara, about Gilroy and what’s been happening down there. There’s this proposed facility that’s just outside the city limit, as I understand it, right? So it’s in Santa Clara County. What is that supposed to be? Is that gonna be a California City-type thing, or is it something, some intermediate kind of facility?

Sara DiNatale: Yeah, the details are not like super specific. Shout-outs to San Jose Spotlight for unearthing some of these internal documents and things that found that they had plans to house up to 150 people. So it’s kind of like not quite as large as California City, but it is still not — it would be more than something like we’re seeing at Sansome.

Alexis Madrigal: More than a lounge, private prison.

Sara DiNatale: Um, the current status right now is that construction is on hold. There’s actually a court hearing today where a judge will decide potentially what the future of that site could be.

But essentially, because it’s in Santa Clara County and not the city of Gilroy, Santa Clara County is the one that’s actually suing the federal government, arguing that the land that’s being used is zoned agriculturally and shouldn’t be used for — whether it’s a holding center or a detention facility, whatever verbiage you want to use. It would be a nice facility, and they are against that. Yeah.

Alexis Madrigal: Tyche, the one that I had heard about and saw protests around was out there in the East Bay, right? In Dublin, former women’s prison, right? What’s been going on with that?

Tyche Hendricks: Yeah, that’s been a little quiet recently. This was the, right, this former women’s prison that was closed down for, like, horrible rape abuses and sexual violence against the inmates. ICE did take a tour, I think, at one point. And the city council and a lot of elected officials really raised a hue and cry and said, no ICE facility here.

ICE told me some months ago that they were not looking at it, so it’s kind of quiet at this point. But that is a federally owned prison in the Bay Area. And, you know, Homeland Security officials have said that they’re looking for something that’s closer into San Francisco, which is a big ICE headquarters in California.

Alexis Madrigal: I mean, do we feel like detention is actually a bottleneck? Like, is the fact that we don’t, you know, if California City was actually in Dublin, Pleasanton, do you think we’d see more arrests? Like, what do we know about the relationship between those two things?

Tyche Hendricks: You — I mean, I think there is an argument that advocates are making that the more detention space there is in the area, the easier it is for people to be locked up there.

Certainly this administration — well, this Republican Congress — has been sort of throwing money at ICE and immigration enforcement more broadly. And so there is, you’re seeing around the country a vast ramp-up in detention, and people are also flown, you know, from here to there to here to there, channeled into detention facilities in Texas and other places.

Alexis Madrigal: I mean, Sara, I think this is kind of my question on this. I mean, it has seemed to many people in the Bay Area like it’s odd that we’ve had less immigration enforcement action here than in other parts of the country, given the way that the Trump administration has tended to operate and that this is like a stronghold of anti-Trump sentiment.

Do you think it’s sanctuary city policy? Do you think it’s a lack of detention centers? I mean, do you have any sense of the role that these various factors are playing?

Sara DiNatale: Yeah, I would say it’s probably somewhere in the middle. Like, there’s probably — like, both things, I think, can be true.

I know lawmakers especially have said that they think part of the reason we have had less enforcement efforts is because we don’t have a place to put people easily. It requires more coordination. That has come up in response to the center outside of Gilroy.

Now, some cities and counties in Northern California have proactively been creating ordinances that would make it more difficult for ICE to open new facilities in their areas, just by amplifying existing land-use laws and environmental impact requirements. Things that would just make it, like, more annoying to open a new facility. And they are very candid about that’s why they’re creating these new local laws.

And when you talk to those local city leaders, like the mayor of San Jose, they’re pretty explicit and like, yeah, we think that this is part of why we haven’t had as big of a nice crackdown in our community, because we don’t have that infrastructure.

So it’s definitely a belief that people carry. I mean, in my reporting, I haven’t found a definitive answer, but I think there are logical conclusions that are easy to reach between both those things.

Alexis Madrigal: We’re talking about the network of immigration detention facilities in the Bay Area. In our next segment, we’re gonna kind of take it nationwide and look at what’s happening everywhere else.

We’re joined this morning by Tyche Hendricks, a senior editor covering immigration. We also have Sara DiNatale, who you just heard, a reporter covering politics and the impacts of the Trump administration’s policies on the Bay Area and California for the San Francisco Chronicle. And, of course, we would love to hear from you.

Maybe you live near Gilroy or Dublin or another community where a detention center has been proposed. Tell us what you’ve seen on the ground. Tell us you’ve heard from your neighbors. What do you think about how your local and state leaders are responding?

And give us a call now. The number is 866-733-6786. You can email Forum at kqed.org. You can find us on Bluesky, Instagram, Discord, or KQED Forum and all those places.

I’m Alexis Madrigal. Stay tuned for more.

Bangkok, Thailand – September 08, 2026 – PRESSADVANTAGE –

Siam Legal International, a leading law firm in Thailand, is reporting that a United States federal court has struck down a policy that paused immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries, including Thailand, since January 2026. The ruling, issued August 21, 2026, by Judge Jeannette Vargas of the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York in the case CLINIC v. Rubio, directly affects Thai nationals pursuing CR-1 and IR-1 spousal visas to join American citizen spouses in the United States.

The US Department of State announced the pause in January 2026, directing consular officers to withhold approval of immigrant visa applications from nationals of the affected countries under Section 221(g) of US immigration law, citing concerns about public charge risk. Consular officers were instructed to apply this outcome regardless of whether an individual applicant had already demonstrated eligibility during the interview, according to court filings. Thailand was among roughly forty percent of countries worldwide included on the list, while nonimmigrant categories such as tourist, student, and K-1 fiancé visas remained unaffected throughout the pause.

Judge Vargas found that the policy conflicted with US immigration law by removing final decision-making authority from individual consular officers and imposing a predetermined refusal based solely on an applicant’s nationality. The court rejected the government’s reliance on a 2018 Supreme Court decision upholding an earlier travel ban, ruling that the earlier case addressed presidential authority over entry into the country rather than the government’s ability to direct officers to refuse applicants already found individually eligible. The ruling vacated the policy in its entirety rather than limiting relief to the plaintiffs, extending its effect to applicants from all 75 affected countries.

The decision differs from a separate July 2026 ruling in De Moura Gomes v. Rubio, in which a federal court in Washington also found the policy unlawful but limited relief to the family that filed the case. Under the August ruling, any CR-1 or IR-1 refusal issued on or after January 21, 2026, that relied solely on the policy is set aside, and affected cases are expected to be returned for individual review. Siam Legal International notes that this does not guarantee approval, as applicants must still satisfy standard requirements, including a public charge assessment conducted on an individual basis rather than a blanket rule.

“Thai nationals who received a hold on their spousal visa case earlier this year now have grounds to have that case reconsidered on its own facts, not as part of a blanket policy,” said Rex Baay, Senior Immigration Consultant and Operations Manager at Siam Legal International. “Applicants should not assume this ruling means automatic approval, and strengthening documentation around financial support and the sponsor’s background remains an important step while embassies work through the practical process of applying the decision.”

Applicants with a pending case may check status through the Consular Electronic Application Center to confirm whether a prior refusal has been updated since the ruling, and should confirm that medical examinations and police clearance certificates have not expired during the delay. The ruling has not resolved every claim raised in the underlying litigation, with remaining issues due before the court by September 11, 2026, and the government has not confirmed whether it intends to appeal. Siam Legal International’s US visa team continues to track the practical rollout of the decision at the US Embassy in Bangkok and other posts processing Thai applicants.

Siam Legal International first outlined the scope of the original pause and its effect on Thai applicants in a Siam Legal US from Thailand visa advisory, published earlier in 2026, and the firm continues to update its guidance as the litigation progresses. “Immigration detention has always been cruel.
But today, that cruelty has reached new heights, as the government has allowed immigration detention centers to become squalid and unsafe and record numbers of people are dying in custody.
About American Immigration Council (AIC) The American Immigration Council works to create a more welcoming and fair immigration system.
About RAICES RAICES is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, non-partisan organization headquartered in San Antonio, Texas.
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Asian Law Caucus, in partnership with the American Immigration Lawyers Association (AILA), American Immigration Council (AIC), the South Asian American Justice Collaborative (SAAJCO), Sikh Coalition, and RAICES, today filed an amicus curiae brief in the U.S. Supreme Court in Genalo v. Black, urging the Court to protect against prolonged mandatory immigration detention without a meaningful opportunity for a bond hearing.

The case asks whether the government can detain people for months or even years during their immigration proceedings without giving them a bond hearing to determine whether continued detention is necessary.

The brief explains that mandatory detention can sweep in people who pose little or no danger or flight risk, while prolonged confinement separates families, exposes people to harmful detention conditions, and makes it harder for them to obtain counsel and fairly pursue their immigration cases.

“Behind the legal arguments in our amicus brief are real people losing months and years of their lives in detention. They are parents separated from their children, family members missing the funerals of loved ones, community members ripped from their jobs and neighborhoods. They are people whose health rapidly deteriorates while waiting for care and release, like Rodrigo, who was left to cover an open wound – with shrink wrap saved from his dinner. Others endured years of needless detention only to ultimately win their cases and return home. These stories show the profound human cost of a system that forces people to remain locked and away while they fight for the right to remain with their families,” said Evelyn Wiese, Asian Law Caucus Immigrant Justice Program Director.

"Indefinite or prolonged confinement without meaningful judicial review, especially for purely civil immigration violations, directly conflicts with America’s commitment to equal justice before the law. When the government seeks to hold human beings for an extended period, fundamental fairness requires an opportunity to challenge that detention before a neutral decision-maker. The Court should reaffirm that liberty does not depend on immigration status and that due process remains a core American value,” said Jeff Joseph, President of the American Immigration Lawyers Association (AILA).

“Immigration detention has always been cruel. But today, that cruelty has reached new heights, as the government has allowed immigration detention centers to become squalid and unsafe and record numbers of people are dying in custody. The government is effectively using the prospect of months or years in these intolerable conditions to coerce immigrants into giving up their rights. In this moment, it is especially urgent that the Supreme Court recognize that the Constitution sets limits on prolonged civil immigration detention and ensure that people can get federal court review of their lengthy incarceration,” said Emma Winger, deputy legal director at the American Immigration Council.

“Indefinite detention without the opportunity to seek bond violates the Constitution, undermines the due process rights essential to our democracy, and is a severe breach of American values. The Supreme Court has previously affirmed that ‘[f]reedom from imprisonment lies at the heart of the liberty protected by the Due Process Clause.’ Nevertheless, the current administration spends billions of taxpayer dollars attempting to deprive people and families of their freedom over alleged civil infractions. RAICES calls on the Supreme Court Justices to uphold the fundamental liberty and due process rights embedded in our nation's laws.” said Faisal Al-Juburi, co-CEO of RAICES.

“A government should not be able to deprive people of their liberty for months or years without having to justify that detention. For South Asian communities, prolonged detention can bring additional harms, including barriers to religious practice, religious dietary requirements, and meaningful language access. Meaningful judicial review is a basic safeguard against unchecked government power and essential to our democracy,” said Kalpana V. Peddibhotla, Executive Director of the South Asian American Justice Collaborative (SAAJCO).

“Too many individuals across our country are suffering in long-term detention after being targeted by an overly aggressive immigration enforcement regime. When these individuals are kept from their families, their livelihoods, and their communities for long stretches of time, the suffering is compounded. We must move towards an immigration system that holds justice in a higher esteem than cruelty," said Munmeeth Soni, Legal Director, Sikh Coalition.

On October 13, 2026, the Supreme Court will consider whether detention under 8 U.S.C. § 1226(c) can become unreasonably prolonged such that due process requires a bond hearing and, if so, whether the government must justify continued detention by clear and convincing evidence.

title: Appeals Court Upholds Order Blocking IRS From Sharing Taxpayer Data with ICE
description:
The plaintiffs in the case achieved a stay last November that prevented the IRS from sharing data on millions of taxpayers with ICE.
Today’s ruling keeps the prohibition on this data sharing between IRS and ICE in place as the case continues.
“Congress has set strict parameters around the sharing of taxpayer information for a reason — that trust in the tax system depends on protection of taxpayer information.
Using confidential IRS data to advance political objectives, including immigration enforcement priorities, crosses a line that should concern Democrats and Republicans alike.
Soon after the plaintiffs challenged the new policy, a District Court issued an order stopping the unlawful data sharing, which the government appealed.
text:
Washington, D.C. – A federal appeals court has upheld an order in Center for Taxpayer Rights et al. v Internal Revenue Service et al, continuing to prevent the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) from disclosing mass amounts of sensitive personal data to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The appeals court decision is the latest milestone in the case brought by Democracy Forward on behalf of the Center for Taxpayer Rights, Main Street Alliance, Communications Workers of America, and the National Federation of Federal Employees.

The plaintiffs in the case achieved a stay last November that prevented the IRS from sharing data on millions of taxpayers with ICE. In February, after the government appealed that decision, it was revealed that the slipshod data-sharing process put in place by the Trump-Vance administration at IRS led to the illegal disclosure of confidential taxpayer information to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Today’s ruling keeps the prohibition on this data sharing between IRS and ICE in place as the case continues.

The DC Circuit found that the IRS’s new data-sharing policy is a “far cry” from the prior policy, and that the new policy “indisputably contravenes” the law. The court further said that the administration’s objections that the preliminary injunction was burdensome is “weak sauce,” and added that “the IRS is now on notice twice over regarding the legal inadequacies of its summer 2025 disclosures. The government and its personnel face steep civil and criminal consequences for willful disclosure of information.”

“Today’s order is a resounding victory for the protection of all taxpayers’ right to the confidentiality of their tax information in the hands of the IRS. It makes clear that the Treasury Department and the IRS cannot act in violation of the law just because they want to,” said Nina Olson, Executive Director of the Center for Taxpayer Rights. “Congress has set strict parameters around the sharing of taxpayer information for a reason — that trust in the tax system depends on protection of taxpayer information. By unlawfully sharing return information with ICE, the IRS violated that trust. The court’s order today is a step toward restoring it.”

“Small business owners already deal with enough uncertainty without wondering whether their tax data is being handed over for immigration enforcement. This ruling confirms what we’ve argued from the start, that the IRS broke faith with taxpayers when it agreed to share this information with ICE. Main Street Alliance will keep fighting to make sure our members’ personal information stays private and protected, as the law requires,” said Richard Trent, Executive Director of the Main Street Alliance.

“The security and confidentiality of taxpayer information are fundamental to maintaining trust between the American people and the government responsible for collecting their taxes,” said NFFE National President Randy Erwin. “When taxpayers fear that the personal information they provide to the IRS could be exploited for unrelated political or enforcement purposes, our nation’s ability to administer and collect taxes effectively is put at risk. Americans across the political spectrum value their privacy and expect the government to respect it. Using confidential IRS data to advance political objectives, including immigration enforcement priorities, crosses a line that should concern Democrats and Republicans alike. That is simply too much Big Brother for most Americans.”

In 2025, the IRS abruptly abandoned longstanding commitments to privacy and adopted a new data-access policy that unlawfully permitted the broad sharing of sensitive taxpayer data outside the agency. The IRS established a new process to share taxpayer data with ICE, including taxpayers’ last-known addresses, and the IRS processed ICE’s mass request for the last-known addresses of 1.2 million taxpayers, sharing address information for approximately 47,000 individuals. Soon after the plaintiffs challenged the new policy, a District Court issued an order stopping the unlawful data sharing, which the government appealed. That appeal failed today.

“The Trump-Vance administration’s dangerous data sharing policies have resulted in the violation of the privacy rights of millions of Americans and we are pleased the court has again acted to stop this unlawful behavior,” said Skye Perryman, President and CEO of Democracy Forward. “The privacy laws enacted in the post-Watergate era exist to prevent abuses of power just like this. The administration has already admitted to being careless and irresponsible with our sensitive, personal information, and now yet another court has held the administration in check.”

As the appeal was being considered, the IRS confirmed the Washington Post’s reporting in a court filing in which Dottie Romo, the IRS chief risk and control officer, swore in a declaration that the IRS provided confidential taxpayer information even when DHS officials could not provide sufficient data to positively identify a specific individual. The revelation came as filings made by DOJ in another case litigated by Democracy Forward have revealed that privacy protocols were violated at the Social Security Administration and that a DOGE team member at SSA signed a “voter data agreement” with an organization involved in seeking to “overturn state election results.”

The legal team at Democracy Forward on this case includes Daniel A. McGrath, Simon Brewer, Maddy Gitomer, Johanna Hickman, Robin Thurston, and Steven Bressler.

Today’s opinion can be found here.

title: CBP wants stakeholder input on supply chain visibility push
description:
Importers have the opportunity to weigh in on potential changes U.S. Customs and Border Protection is exploring to crack down on illegal imports, from collecting foreign export documentation to tapping supply chain tracing technologies.
Per the proposal, CBP is weighing whether foreign export documentation could help the agency verify import entry information and detect discrepancies that may indicate a violation of law.
Additionally, CBP is fielding responses related to supply chain traceability solutions.
The agency said it is looking to crack down on importers routing goods through a third country to cloud their true country of origin.
Questions include what technologies private sector members use for supply chain visibility and if technology could properly certify required information such as country of origin.
text:
Importers have the opportunity to weigh in on potential changes U.S. Customs and Border Protection is exploring to crack down on illegal imports, from collecting foreign export documentation to tapping supply chain tracing technologies.

A Sept. 2 rulemaking proposal from the agency is designed to support the implementation of an executive order signed in June by President Donald Trump, which features plans for new restrictions for foreign importers and higher penalty floors for noncompliance. The ultimate goal is to help CBP better detect, stop and prevent illicit imports from entering the country, according to a news release from the agency Wednesday.

“By strengthening visibility into the supply chains behind goods entering the United States, CBP can better identify high-risk shipments, stop illicit trade, and ensure that American businesses are not undercut by those who evade our customs laws,” CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott said in the release.

Per the proposal, CBP is weighing whether foreign export documentation could help the agency verify import entry information and detect discrepancies that may indicate a violation of law. The documentation could include export declarations made to the foreign customs authority, commercial invoices and packing lists verifying the contents, weight and packaging of each shipment.

CBP poses various questions for commenters related to foreign export documentation throughout its proposal, including if the importer of record should be required to submit that information for all goods entering the U.S. Additionally, CBP asks what challenges importers would face if certain import categories could be deemed a grave risk to national security and require foreign export documentation as a result.

The agency said it is also interested in proposals that would redefine or replace the manufacturer identification code, a data element derived from the name and address of the manufacturer or shipper.

“Although use of the MID is longstanding, it provides limited identifying information and does not always identify the actual party that may be of interest to CBP for enforcement purposes and is not always available to CBP early enough in the entry process to be useful,” the proposal said.

Related to potential MID changes, one of CBP’s questions asks if the agency should collect alternative information instead. Another asks if CBP should require the identification of the end recipient of the goods.

Additionally, CBP is fielding responses related to supply chain traceability solutions. The agency said it is looking to crack down on importers routing goods through a third country to cloud their true country of origin. Questions include what technologies private sector members use for supply chain visibility and if technology could properly certify required information such as country of origin.

text:
Washington — The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Tuesday to intervene in a lawsuit and allow the use of a controversial data system to review state voter rolls heading into the midterm elections.

In June, a federal judge ruled the Trump administration acted unlawfully when it created a centralized database, known as "Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements," or SAVE, that contains Americans' private information. U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan said the database was used by some states to incorrectly remove U.S. citizens from their voter rolls.

The system was part of President Trump's government-wide push to find proof of widespread instances of noncitizens voting in federal elections, which have largely been debunked and shown to be very rare.

Sooknanan said in her ruling that the "federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote," by attempting to implement the SAVE system. Sooknanan found that the administration violated three different federal laws by attempting to implement the SAVE system.

Over the weekend, the Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit denied the Trump administration's request to stay the district court's block on the SAVE database.

In a new filing Tuesday, Solicitor General D. John Sauer called Sooknanan's ruling "indefensible" and said it "threatens the integrity of upcoming elections." He also said the judge exceeded her authority and that the voting rights groups that brought the initial lawsuit did not have proper legal standing to sue. Sauer asked the justices to lift Sooknanan's stay and allow the use of the SAVE system.

"SAVE does not disqualify any voter; instead, it merely notifies the States whether the federal government can confirm citizenship," Sauer wrote. "Thus, any voter injury is caused by the States, not by the federal government, and would not be redressed by the relief the court entered against the federal government."

The new request comes after the Trump administration again asked the Supreme Court to reinstate new Postal Service rules for mail voting in the upcoming midterms.

The SAVE database was created by several federal agencies in response to an executive order signed by Mr. Trump last year that sought to impose a new proof-of-citizenship requirement for those registering to vote. The order directed the Department of Homeland Security and the Social Security Administration to create a database that would effectively allow state and local officials to verify citizenship or immigration status of individuals trying to register to vote.

The executive order drew several legal challenges, and key provisions have been blocked.

Still, the directive triggered the overhaul of the existing SAVE system. It was modified to include the records of natural-born citizens; to access records from the SSA, including Social Security numbers; and to permit bulk searches of records by entities that use the database.

title: The 75-Country Immigrant-Visa Pause Was Vacated. What Does CLINIC v. Rubio Actually Change?
description:
A federal district court vacated the State Department’s January 2026 policy categorically suspending immigrant-visa issuance to nationals of 75 countries.
It does not decide any applicant’s individual eligibility, eliminate separate visa restrictions, or resolve appointment delays attributable to other policies or operational decisions.
More fundamentally, the ruling vacated the particular State Department policy challenged in Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. v. Rubio, No.
The litigation also challenges separate State Department guidance governing how consular officers make public‑charge determinations.
The State Department attributed some disruptions to a global training initiative on public‑charge screening launched in early August.
text:
A federal district court vacated the State Department’s January 2026 policy categorically suspending immigrant-visa issuance to nationals of 75 countries. The ruling removes that policy as a basis for an automatic refusal. It does not decide any applicant’s individual eligibility, eliminate separate visa restrictions, or resolve appointment delays attributable to other policies or operational decisions.

On August 21, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York vacated a State Department directive that had suspended immigrant-visa issuance to nationals of 75 countries. In a written opinion, Judge Jeannette A. Vargas held that the policy was contrary to law and exceeded the Secretary of State’s statutory authority, including because it categorically suspended visa issuance based on nationality.

Some coverage characterized the decision as removing a major barrier for affected applicants. That is partially accurate, but the ruling’s practical effect is narrower. For immigration practitioners, and for clients depending on accurate advice, the significant distinction is between what the ruling eliminates and what it leaves untouched.

How the Pause Worked

The policy originated when the State Department announced that, effective January 21, 2026, it would suspend immigrant‑visa issuance to nationals of 75 specified countries. The Department said it was targeting nationals of countries it considered to present a higher risk of public-benefits reliance or public-charge concerns.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio implemented the policy through a cable sent to diplomatic and consular posts. The operational instructions did not necessarily stop every procedural step. Applicants could still submit applications and, in many cases, attend interviews. The policy required refusal based on nationality even where the officer had otherwise determined that the applicant satisfied the applicable eligibility requirements.

That distinction between processing and issuance was central to the policy’s practical effect. A case could continue moving through the system while the applicant remained unable to receive the immigrant-visa needed to complete the process. Officers were also instructed to use a procedural refusal under INA § 221(g) while the Department developed additional screening tools. The litigation record described additional instructions affecting some visas that had been printed but not yet delivered.

On February 2, 2026, the Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. (CLINIC) and African Communities Together filed suit in the Southern District of New York. The plaintiffs included U.S. citizens whose close family members were separated from them, as well as Colombian professionals pursuing employment‑based immigrant visas.

Clearing the Jurisdictional Hurdles

Before reaching the merits, Judge Vargas addressed three threshold arguments the government raised to keep the case out of court.

First, the court found standing. U.S. citizens kept apart from close family members and applicants who lost a concrete opportunity to receive an immigrant-visa had alleged legally cognizable injuries. The court also recognized organizational standing through affected members of African Communities Together.

Second, the court rejected the government’s reliance on consular nonreviewability. Courts generally cannot second‑guess an individual consular officer’s decision to deny a visa. But the court distinguished a challenge to an officer’s individual judgment from a challenge to a department‑wide policy that allegedly predetermined the outcome and removed the officer’s discretion. The distinction is significant: a policy challenge is not necessarily converted into an unreviewable individual visa‑denial case merely because the policy is implemented by consular officers.

Third, the court held that the policy was the final agency action subject to review under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). The government characterized the directive as temporary guidance while it conducted further review. The court focused instead on the directive’s practical operation: it took immediate effect and instructed officers to refuse visas even when applicants were otherwise qualified.

Why the Policy Failed on the Merits

Judge Vargas vacated the policy on multiple statutory grounds.

1.Nationality‑based restrictions on visa issuance

The court held that the INA did not authorize the Secretary of State to impose this categorical, nationality-based suspension through the challenged directive. The government relied in part on Trump v. Hawaii, 585 U.S. 667 (2018), which upheld presidential authority to restrict entry from certain countries. The court distinguished that precedent because the challenged policy was not an exercise of the President’s separate authority to regulate entry; it was a State Department directive governing the issuance of immigrant visas.

The distinction matters. The court did not hold that every country‑based immigration restriction is unlawful. It held that this particular State Department policy conflicted with the statutory framework governing immigrant‑visa issuance.

2.Misuse of § 221(g)

A refusal under INA § 221(g) means that the applicant has not established eligibility to the officer’s satisfaction at that stage. The case may require additional documentation or case-specific administrative processing.

The court concluded that the Department could not use that provision as a general‑purpose mechanism to refuse applicants whom the government otherwise considered qualified solely because they were nationals of one of the 75 countries.

The problem was not simply the label placed on the refusal. It was the way the Department used the procedure to implement a categorical, outcome‑determinative policy without an individualized determination under the applicable visa-eligibility standards.

3.Exceeding the Secretary’s statutory role

The court also found that the directive improperly displaced the role assigned by law to individual consular officers. Under the statutory framework at issue, the court determined that the Secretary could not use the directive to predetermine immigrant-visa refusals for an entire nationality group.

The court did not hold that public‑charge concerns are irrelevant to immigrant‑visa adjudication. The opinion did not address every possible future public-charge policy or guidance document. It held that this particular directive unlawfully imposed a categorical nationality-based refusal framework and displaced the individualized role assigned to consular officers.

What the Court Did, and Did Not, Decide

The decision is best understood as a ruling about institutional authority and procedure, not as a determination that every applicant from the 75 countries is admissible or entitled to a visa. The court did not eliminate public‑charge review, invalidate presidential entry restrictions, or require the Department to approve individual applications.

The court also rejected the plaintiffs’ separate notice-and-comment argument, concluding that the policy was not a legislative rule subject to the APA’s notice-and-comment requirement. That holding did not save the policy, however, because the court independently concluded that the policy violated the INA and exceeded the Secretary of State’s statutory authority.

Those limitations are important. They mean that the ruling should not be described as a decision eliminating public‑charge scrutiny. It is more accurately described as a decision preventing the Department from replacing individualized review with an automatic nationality‑based outcome.

Who the Ruling Actually Helps

The judgment set aside and vacated the policy and directed the Department to address refusals issued under it, subject to the precise terms of the court’s order. Applicants whose cases were refused solely under the policy may be entitled to renewed adjudication under the terms of the court’s order; they should review the refusal notice and current post instructions. That reconsideration is not an approval and the record will still be evaluated under the ordinary legal standards.

The ruling also benefits pending and future immigrant‑visa applicants from the affected countries. The Department later stated that the January pause was no longer in effect as of August 21. Absent a stay or contrary appellate action, applicants should no longer face an automatic refusal based solely on the vacated policy.

U.S. citizen petitioners and employers may see previously stalled cases return to ordinary adjudication, depending on the order, the refusal record, and the relevant consular post’s implementation. But the practical effect will depend on how quickly individual consular posts restore ordinary processing and how the Department handles cases that were refused, placed into administrative processing, or interrupted before visa delivery.

Where the Relief Runs Out

The ruling’s reach is narrower than some headlines suggest.

First, separate presidential restrictions remain relevant. The court emphasized the legal distinction between the issuance of a visa and admission to the United States. More fundamentally, the ruling vacated the particular State Department policy challenged in Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. v. Rubio, No. 1:26‑cv‑00858 (S.D.N.Y. Aug. 21, 2026). It did not invalidate separate presidential proclamations restricting visa issuance or entry. An applicant covered by both measures may no longer be subject to the vacated 75-country policy but may remain subject to applicable restrictions. Specifically, Presidential Proclamation 10998 (effective Jan. 1, 2026) restricts entry for nationals of 39 countries; applicants should check both the vacated 75‑country policy and Proclamation 10998.

Even where the 75‑country pause is no longer an obstacle, independent grounds of inadmissibility still apply. A separate inadmissibility ground, missing documentation, or case-specific administrative processing is not eliminated merely because the 75-country policy was vacated. Counsel should therefore identify the precise basis stated in the refusal record or administrative‑processing notice. A case refused solely under the vacated policy may require a different response from one involving missing documentation, a separate inadmissibility ground, an active presidential restriction, or ordinary administrative processing.

The analysis is also different for nonimmigrant visas, which were outside the challenged policy. The 75‑country pause applied specifically to immigrant‑visa applicants. It did not govern tourist, student, exchange‑visitor, or temporary‑worker visa categories, and the ruling therefore does not independently change the standards governing those nonimmigrant classifications. Separate proclamations and policies may, however, continue to restrict particular nonimmigrant‑visa categories.

Finally, other public‑charge policies remain separate from the issues resolved by the ruling. The litigation also challenges separate State Department guidance governing how consular officers make public‑charge determinations. The August 21 ruling addressed the 75‑country pause but did not resolve every public‑charge issue raised in the case. The district court entered partial final judgment on the 75‑country claims, while leaving other claims active, including challenges to separate public-charge guidance. Separately, the State Department’s worldwide interview pause is tied to updated public‑charge training. Practitioners should therefore avoid treating the decision as a wholesale rejection of the Department’s broader public‑charge or screening‑and‑vetting initiatives.

The Implementation Question

The first test of the ruling was operational. Shortly after the decision, plaintiffs reported continued interview cancellations and delays. The State Department attributed some disruptions to a global training initiative on public‑charge screening launched in early August. The Department later updated its website on August 28 to confirm that the 75‑country pause was no longer in effect as of August 21.

The episode illustrates an important practical reality: vacatur removes the legal foundation for a policy, but affected applicants may still need to monitor whether the agency has restored ordinary processing. A client may have a favorable court ruling in hand and still face delay, a stale refusal code, a canceled interview, or a consular post that has not yet implemented the change consistently. Thebroader disruption in immigrant‑visa interview scheduling underscores that implementation question.

What Happens Next

The litigation is not necessarily over. The district court entered partial final judgment on the claims concerning the 75‑country pause while leaving other claims active, including challenges to separate public‑charge policies. The government may appeal to the Second Circuit and may seek a stay pending appeal. If a stay were granted, the practical effect of the vacatur could change quickly.

The next important developments will include any appellate filing, the parties’ scheduled status submission concerning the remaining claims, and evidence of how consular posts implement the Department’s August 28 announcement. For practitioners, the most consequential question may be less whether the Department has announced that the pause is over than whether affected cases are being reopened and adjudicated without reliance on the vacated policy.

The Bottom Line

The court held that this State Department directive could not lawfully replace individualized immigrant-visa adjudication with a categorical nationality-based refusal. But the decision’s reach is specific, not sweeping.

It removes one obstacle while leaving several others in place. For practitioners, the ruling is therefore only the starting point. The next step is a case‑by‑case assessment of what caused the client’s delay or refusal, what the court’s order removes, and what barriers remain.

title: In Washington, a County Mulls Ending Sheriff Elections—and Ousting Its Right-Wing Sheriff
authors: Daniel Nichanian, Amy Sundberg, Jacob Biba, Raina Lipsitz, Piper French
description:
The Pierce County Charter Review Commission placed a charter amendment on November’s ballot that would make the Pierce County sheriff an appointed position rather than elected.
“I’m proud that I have more complaints than any other officer or sheriff in the state,” Swank said.
He traveled to D.C. alongside Adams County Sheriff Dale Wagner, another Washington sheriff who has said he thinks the Keep Washington Working Act is unconstitutional.
A few months after their trip, Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown filed a suit against Wagner for sharing information with federal immigration officials in violation of state law.
“Everybody wants to think it’s about Sheriff Swank, but this is really about a broader thought process about accountability, oversight, and transparency,” Leighton said.
text:
When Washington state voters approved new gun control rules in 2018, several sheriffs announced they would not enforce them because they believed them to be unconstitutional, prompting warnings from police reform advocates about the rogue conduct of sheriffs.

Now some sheriffs are also insisting that a state law limiting how they can partner with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is illegal, sparking further disputes over their authority while the Trump administration intensifies immigration enforcement.

As the state continues to grapple with how to exert oversight over sheriffs, voters are poised to step into these debates this fall in Pierce County, Washington’s second most populous county and home to Tacoma. The Pierce County Charter Review Commission placed a charter amendment on November’s ballot that would make the Pierce County sheriff an appointed position rather than elected.

Voters in King County (Seattle), the state’s most populous county, already approved a similar measure in 2020.

If it passes, Pierce County’s measure would take effect by January 2027, cutting short the tenure of Sheriff Keith Swank, a first-term official notorious for his rabble-rousing, inflammatory statements and social media posts, and MAGA-adjacent politics in a blue county. The county executive would appoint a new sheriff, subject to confirmation by the county council, early next year. Swank’s term would otherwise end in early 2029.

“I believe that this amendment will add increased and immediate accountability,” Charter Review Commissioner Jake Hunter, who sponsored the measure, said in a public hearing.

Hunter made the case that shifting to an appointed sheriff would allow the county to focus on candidates’ qualifications, such as how they’d manage large public entities and their budgets, rather than political popularity. “I would like to say this wouldn’t be a question if recent events had not raised serious concerns about accountability and governance for this office,” he said, adding he wanted to design a structure that “provides adequate accountability when concerns arise, regardless of who’s holding the office.”

Referring to Swank, he said, “Our responsibility is not to evaluate one individual, although a lot of us have.”

Swank is a former police captain at the Seattle Police Department, and a Seattle police report determined last year that he would have been fired from that agency over social media posts , including attacks on trans people, had he not retired first. He twice ran for Congress as a Republican, losing in 2020 and 2022, before winning the sheriff’s office in 2024.

As sheriff, he has relentlessly pressed for the authority to collaborate with ICE.

He says a state law protecting immigrants, the Keep Washington Working Act, is unconstitutional and he has appealed to the Trump administration for help. He denounced a resolution passed by the Pierce County Council that affirmed the council’s support of immigrants and its intention to follow the Keep Washington Working Act.

Swank’s fight with other county leaders escalated when he tried to hire an outside lawyer to press his case that he should be able to assist ICE. He also claimed that he should not be subject to orders issued by Ryan Mello, the Pierce County executive. Mello had said any county contract that involves federal funding would need to be reviewed and approved by his office. Swank disagreed with the legal advice provided by the county’s chief prosecutor, who warned that he had to obey Mello and that his desire to cooperate with ICE could expose the county to costly litigation, and wanted a second opinion. Swank told Bolts that the county has since allowed him to hire a strategic advisor but that this person is not allowed to be an attorney.

A June 15 meeting of the Charter Review Commission illustrated Swank’s customary confrontational style.

“I’m proud that I have more complaints than any other officer or sheriff in the state,” Swank said. A state oversight agency confirmed to Bolts that it has more open misconduct complaints filed against Swank than against any other sheriff; some of the complaints target his public statements disparaging LGBTQ+ people.

Swank went on at the meeting to urge his critics to file even more complaints. “Instead of saying transgender woman, say man,” Swank said. “Instead of saying gay, say homosexual. Instead of reality challenged, say insane, crazy, wacky. Instead of unschooled, just say stupid. Dishonest means liar. Undocumented immigrant, that’s an illegal alien. Instead of protester, say terrorist.”

Charter Review Commissioner Justin Leighton, who supported the measure at that June meeting, told Bolts in an interview that he thinks an appointment system would allow for more robust oversight over the long term. An appointed sheriff could be dismissed at the will of the county executive, whereas the only recourse for an elected sheriff’s misconduct now is meeting the high threshold of a recall.

He pointed to Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson recently asking Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes to resign. The ability to dismiss a law enforcement leader at will is not a panacea, however—three police chiefs have left the City of Seattle under a cloud of scandal since 2020.

Swank, on the other hand, believes the charter amendment would centralize too much power in the county executive’s office and raise new accountability problems.

“I think that the amendment is taking away the right of the people to vote for and elect their sheriff of their choosing,” Swank told Bolts in an interview. “It’s funny that the people who pose this amendment talk about how we have to save democracy by making the sheriff an appointed position. That’s an oxymoron there.”

The surge in immigration enforcement has added to this scrutiny over sheriffs in Washington.

Malou Chávez, executive director of the Northwest Immigrant Rights Project, told Bolts that federal enforcement is increasing due to the large amount of resources at the disposal of ICE and other federal agencies. “The arrest of community members, it’s almost normalized in many ways,” she said. “We have seen videos of community members being apprehended and people walking by, going throughout their day nonchalantly walking, not even looking to see that there’s someone being arrested.”

Swank told Bolts that he abides by the Keep Washington Working Act in order to protect his deputies from civil litigation. “I do believe we should work with ICE,” Swank said. “However, we don’t work with ICE. The Pierce County Sheriff’s Office does not work with ICE. We do not do anything related to immigration.”

But Chávez warns that living under the authority of someone like Swank who says he doesn’t want to abide by state protections still causes fear in immigrant communities. She says it makes some residents uncomfortable reaching out to law enforcement when they need help.

Swank traveled to Washington, D.C., in 2025 to meet with Trump administration officials. He later said he had reached out to the U.S. Department of Justice and ICE to ask them if they could help him “fast-track” a lawsuit against the Keep Washington Working Act to the U.S. Supreme Court.

He traveled to D.C. alongside Adams County Sheriff Dale Wagner, another Washington sheriff who has said he thinks the Keep Washington Working Act is unconstitutional.

A few months after their trip, Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown filed a suit against Wagner for sharing information with federal immigration officials in violation of state law. The lawsuit remains in court as of publication. Adams County faced a separate lawsuit alleging that deputies illegally detained someone on immigration grounds, which the county settled.

Should the November measure pass, Chávez said she doesn’t expect to see an immediate difference for the immigrant communities she works with. But over time, she thinks it could be easier for immigrant residents to press for accountability through paths they actually have access to, such as talking to a county councilmember or to the county executive’s office.

As long as the main path is to actively organize a recall, she believes community members may be afraid to speak out. “There’s that fear of retaliation or being targeted, maybe future stops,” she said, “just the potential target that someone could become in their day-to-day lives.”

Washington sheriffs have provoked scandals well before Swank. His own predecessor, Ed Troyer, followed a Black newspaper carrier, called 911, and lied to the dispatcher that the man had threatened to kill him, prompting dozens of officers to arrive on the scene, according to the attorney general’s office, which filed criminal charges against him. Troyer later admitted that he lied about being threatened.

A jury found Troyer not guilty of false reporting and lying to a public servant in 2022, but he opted not to seek reelection two years later and Swank won the contested race to succeed him.

Faced with such controversies, state officials have worked to change Washington’s oversight system for sheriffs. A new reform, signed into law in April of this year with the support of state Democrats, added new eligibility requirements for sheriffs, including a mandatory background check and five years of law enforcement experience.

The law also empowers the Washington State Criminal Justice Training Commission to remove sheriffs from office—whether they are elected or appointed—after investigating complaints against them. The commission already must certify all law enforcement officers in the state, and it has the authority to suspend or revoke their certification. But the law now provides that, if the commission decertifies a sitting sheriff or police chief, they must step down.

Reporting this summer by InvestigateWest raised serious questions about the oversight that the Criminal Justice Training Commission has actually exercised. They found that police officers accused of misconduct have frequently avoided investigations and decertification, and that the commission can take years to start an investigation.

Still, advocacy organizations such as the Washington Coalition for Police Accountability told Bolts that they strongly supported the state’s latest legislation. “The WCPA’s position is to hold these publicly elected or appointed law enforcement leaders accountable as much as we can,” Paul Benz, a member of its advisory committee, told Bolts.

According to state records shared with Bolts by the Criminal Justice Training Commission, the agency is currently reviewing open misconduct complaints against more than half of the state’s sheriffs. As of August, Swank had the highest number of such complaints filed against him at 18—an increase of eight since April.

During the bill’s initial committee hearing, several sheriffs spoke against the legislation, including Swank, whose testimony appeared to threaten severe consequences were the bill to pass.

“You want to give unelected bureaucracy the ability to decertify me and remove me from office because you don’t agree with my speech,” Swank testified. “I don’t recognize your authority to impose these controls over me, and when you try to remove me from office, thousands of Pierce County residents will surround the county city building in downtown Tacoma and will not allow that to happen.”

He added, “I hope it doesn’t come to that, but I and they are prepared. Are you prepared?”

The Washington Association of Sheriffs and Police Chiefs said after Swank’s testimony that it was considering expelling him over these comments, saying that they “devolved into what could be perceived as threatening to legislators.”

The association ultimately decided to stop short of expulsion. “WASPC issued a reprimand to the Sheriff in March 2026,” its executive director Steven Strachan told Bolts.

Swank stood by his comments in an interview with Bolts. “I went down there to tell them that it’s unconstitutional, and if they pass it, I’m not going to abide by it,” he said. “That’s just the way it is.”

A group of four sheriffs filed a lawsuit against the law after its adoption, and a local judge in April blocked the provisions that pertain to sheriffs. “It appears that the Legislature does not trust the people of the state of Washington to have good judgment,” Thurston County Superior Court Christine Schaller said while issuing her ruling.

The state is appealing the decision but, for now, sheriffs in Washington would remain in office even if they are decertified.

Swank casts Pierce County’s November ballot measure in similar terms—as a bid to get rid of him. “This is a way to remove me from office without having to go through the recall process,” he told Bolts.

Mello, the county executive who would nominate a new sheriff if the charter amendment passes, is a Democrat, as is a narrow majority of the county council, which would have to approve the choice. Swank is a Republican, though the sheriff election he won in 2024 was nonpartisan, as were the elections the county held in 2025 to form the Charter Review Commission.

Leighton, the commissioner who proposed the amendment that set the measure’s effective date to January 2027, instead of 2029, says this had nothing to do with the length of Swank’s term.

“I feel very strongly that I don’t want something kind of just lingering for two years,” Leighton told Bolts. “In my mind, it has nothing to do with the person or the term. It is, ‘the voters have decided, let’s move forward with what the voters wanted right then and there.’”

Leighton pointed out that the commission only convenes every 10 years to review possible changes to the county charter, and the community was already talking about this issue before Swank’s election. The county revised its charter back in 1980 to make sheriffs an appointed position, before switching back to holding sheriff elections in 2006.

“Everybody wants to think it’s about Sheriff Swank, but this is really about a broader thought process about accountability, oversight, and transparency,” Leighton said. “It’s about what really we need as a community.”

text:
A federal appeals court on Tuesday upheld a lower court ruling blocking information sharing between the IRS and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after the immigration agency requested the last known address of millions of people.

The three-judge panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit found ICE’s sweeping request for addresses of 1.28 million people who may be unlawfully present in the U.S. violated laws established in the wake of the Watergate scandal that bars the IRS from sharing information with other agencies unless it meets “stringent conditions.”

The ruling finds plaintiffs were likely to prevail in the matter and agreed the policy was reviewable under the Administrative Procedures Act, upholding a ruling from November that blocked the IRS from aiding with deportations.

The IRS can share information with other agencies to help prosecute certain crimes, but those agencies must also list a specific point of contact.

“The IRS failed to require ICE to provide a ‘specific reason’ why the requested return information ‘is or may be relevant to [a qualifying] proceeding or investigation,’ as the statute demands,” wrote Judge Cornelia Pillard, an appointee of former President Obama, for the panel.

“It entirely fails to ensure that ICE lists a federal employee, let alone one ‘personally and directly engaged’ in a qualifying investigation of a particular taxpayer. That failure has serious consequences. When ICE requested information on 1.28 million taxpayers in the summer of 2025, ICE identified the same person as the point of contact for every single request.”

The panel also found information sharing would violate privacy laws.

“The Data-Exchange Procedure reduces noncitizens’ privacy rights in their tax returns. By providing a distinct, automated pathway for ICE to request noncitizens’ information, the Data-Exchange Procedure deprives noncitizens of the protections that section 6103 guarantees to all taxpayers,” the panel found.

The ruling is another blow to ICE, which hoped to use the data to help locate migrants it is trying to support.

The Trump administration has pushed to link a number of government databases in the hopes of locating those who may not be lawfully present in the country.
