text:
Francisco, a 52-year-old window installer, couldn’t sleep. He burst into tears during family dinners. The sight of an unfamiliar black Suburban parked near his longtime apartment in Oakland, California, sent him rushing to lock the doors and hide.

His employer threatened to report him to federal immigration authorities this spring, Francisco said, to discourage him from collaborating with state labor officials investigating a co-worker’s complaint against the business. KQED is not using Francisco’s full name or naming their employer because he lacks legal immigration status and fears retaliation.

“I was afraid,” Francisco said. “I tried to not show it to my family so they wouldn’t get nervous or upset. But inside, I was afraid. It’s traumatic.”

Supervisors threatening immigration consequences is nothing new in industries with a large noncitizen workforce and lower-wage jobs, such as construction, hospitality and in-home care. But as President Donald Trump’s administration ramps up immigration arrests to levels not seen in years, bad-faith employers are taking advantage of the political climate to exploit vulnerable workers, who are now more fearful of deportation, according to state officials and employment attorneys.

It’s hard to estimate the extent of this kind of workplace intimidation, which is generally unlawful, because relatively few people report it to labor regulators. Still, state figures point to a spike in immigration-related threats during both the first and current Trump administration.

“I do believe that this is the tip of the iceberg and that there are many, many more of these immigration-related threats,” said Ruth Silver Taube, supervising attorney at the Santa Clara and San Mateo County Legal Advice Line. “These threats are designed to deter workers from coming forward. And I think they’re successful.”

Francisco, who has worked in California for 25 years, mostly in construction, said he had never before faced an Immigration and Customs Enforcement-related threat. Francisco worried his wife and two older children, who also don’t have legal status, could be detained and separated from a younger son, a U.S. citizen by birth.

The father of three became so anxious, imagining that he was being watched or followed, that his wife took him to see a psychiatrist. Francisco eventually found a different job and is seeking legal aid to figure out next steps. A spokesperson for the California Labor Commissioner’s Office, which investigates retaliation complaints, identified two open investigations against Francisco’s former employer.

Francisco knows of other construction workers getting similar threats.

“It makes me angry,” he said, adding that more construction workers he knows are facing similar rhetoric. “Unfortunately, it is the price we pay — those of us who are undocumented here.”

Trujillo’s team has documented dozens of reports of veiled or explicit threats this year, though most workers decline to pursue the cases or seek redress, she said.

Silver Taube believes just one of dozens of clients has been arrested and deported after reporting immigration threats and wage theft to state regulators during the first Trump term. The Labor Commissioner’s Office recovered unpaid wages for the man and ensured he received them in Mexico, she said.

The state agency also intervenes to stop retaliation from happening or continuing by promptly informing employers that they could be on the hook for up to $10,000 in penalties per violation if the allegations of immigration threats against them are corroborated.

“Worksite enforcement remains a cornerstone of our efforts to protect public safety, national security and economic stability while rescuing individuals who may be victims of labor trafficking or exploitation,” the DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “These operations target illegal employment networks that undermine American workers, destabilize labor markets, and threaten American communities.”

Employing noncitizens without work authorization also incentivizes “dangerous and illegal practices, including social security fraud,” the spokesperson said, because those immigrants often use stolen, fabricated or expired social security numbers to get jobs.

The U.S. Department of Labor did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Under federal and state laws, employees have a right to minimum wage, overtime, a safe workplace and other protections, regardless of their immigration status. Punishing a worker for trying to exercise those rights is unlawful.

California lawmakers approved a bill last week that would clarify the law to explicitly say that all immigration-related threats, including preemptive ones to dissuade employees from exercising their rights, are illegal. Gov. Gavin Newsom has until Sept. 30 to sign or veto the measure.

Yet, managers may ignore the rules. Threats can be made in the heat of the moment, and not as a well-thought-out management tool, said Paul DeCamp, who represents employers with the firm Epstein, Becker & Green in Washington, D.C.

“If a supervisor gets annoyed, perhaps because the workers are talking about unionizing or they’re complaining about working conditions, the supervisor, in an attempt to try to take control of the situation, may make a threat like this, which of course is illegal,” said DeCamp, a former administrator of the wage and hour division at the U.S. Department of Labor. “But the supervisor may not understand that or may think that the workers would be afraid to do anything about the threat.”

California Labor Commissioner Lilia Garcia-Brower said her agency anticipated that Trump’s efforts to deport millions of immigrants would have a chilling effect on undocumented and other noncitizen workers. The labor commissioner has expanded its education and outreach efforts, including by partnering closely with advocacy organizations and community leaders who have workers’ trust. An estimated 1.5 million undocumented immigrants make up less than 10% of the state’s workforce.

“We do not collaborate with the federal government. We do not ask about immigration status. We don’t ask for Social Security numbers. And it is safe for them to proceed in cooperating with us,” Garcia-Brower said. “I don’t need a statistic to reiterate that there is a significant amount of fear in the community. What I want to make sure that I am continuously communicating: worker protections.”

Edith, a fast food worker in the San José area, said she decided to come forward with a complaint because she is desperate for relief. Her manager has discriminated against her and other older employees, unfairly cutting their work hours, she said. Edith said that when she asked the manager about it last summer, they replied that anyone complaining about their schedule would be reported to ICE.

Edith stopped asking questions, even after her work hours were slashed again. KQED is not using Edith’s full name or naming her employer because she fears losing her job.

“We didn’t know that was illegal — what she told us. I was afraid of going to work. But I have to work because I need to,” the 56-year-old said in Spanish. “It has been, and still is, a huge deal. It is something very difficult.”

She had never been threatened with deportation in the 35 years she’s worked in the state cleaning homes and in restaurants, she said. Eventually, Edith and co-workers sought advice from the California Fast Food Workers Union.

By then, the manager had also told employees that they should “hide in the garbage” or “jump out of the window” if ICE agents came to the workplace, according to two age-discrimination complaints against the business with the California Civil Rights Department that were reviewed by KQED. The department also investigates immigration threats.

“You have to do something,” said Edith, referring to her complaint, which she hopes will lead the restaurant owners to ensure employees are treated fairly. “We do have rights, and we shouldn’t be treated this way.”

text:
PORT ANGELES — A Port Angeles man with legal refugee status was detained by U.S. Border Patrol agents last week.

Noune Phompor, 47, was arrested by the U.S. Border Patrol Blaine Sector on Sept. 1.

“Border Patrol Agents apprehended a Laos citizen illegally present in the U.S. near Port Angeles,” the agency posted to social media on Wednesday. “The subject has an extensive criminal history including burglary, vehicle theft and weapons/drug offenses. He is now awaiting removal proceedings.”

Phompor is being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center, 1623 E. J St., Suite 2, in Tacoma, according to locator.ice.gov.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

The Border Patrol’s social media post is not entirely truthful, Phompor’s family and friends have said.

Phompor has had indefinite refugee status since he and his family came to the United States in 1981, according to documents provided by lifelong friend Travis Pace.

For decades, Laos did not have a formal repatriation treaty or Memorandum of Understanding with the United States, according to the Asian Law Caucus, which is why Phompor’s refugee status was indefinite.

Although friends and family admit Phompor committed crimes in his 20s while addicted to methamphetamine, Phompor served his time, and from 2010-14, he checked in monthly as part his orders of supervision. He has not committed a crime, or even been pulled over for a speeding ticket, since at least 2014, his family said.

“He committed crimes 20 years ago,” Pace’s wife Chelsea Littlejohn said. “He’s a product of what America made. He actually is a story of success. He turned his life around and to send him back (to Laos) is unjust.”

Phompor was arrested during his lunch break at Chipotle, where he’s worked since May 2025. Phompor has been the sole provider for his family, partner Joanna Mabrey and 1-year-old son Kyden, Littlejohn said.

As an indefinite refugee, Phompor was issued a Social Security number and has been working legally.

Family of refugees

Phompor’s parents and three oldest siblings fled Laos during the Laotian Civil War (1959-75). The family stayed in a refugee camp in Thailand for four to five years where Phompor’s older sister, Khoune Phompor, was born in 1977 and Noune Phompor was born in 1979.

“My mom and dad and three siblings, probably all under the age of 10 at the time, they pretty much walked from Laos, crossing the border into Thailand,” Khoune Phompor said. “My mom remembers having to walk through the jungles, and they could hear bombs.”

During the Laotian Civil War, the Kingdom of Laos “was a covert theater during the Vietnam War with both sides receiving heavy external support in a proxy war between the global Cold War superpowers,” according to Wikipedia. “The fighting also involved the North Vietnamese, South Vietnamese, American and Thai armies, both directly and through irregular proxies. The war is known as the ‘Secret War’ among the American CIA Special Activities Center and Hmong and Mien veterans of the conflict.”

Through a deal with American forces, in exchange for fighting against the communists, Laotians would be rescued and brought to the United States, Littlejohn said.

Instead, the Phompor family waited years in the Thai refugee camp until the Bangkok American Embassy’s U.S. Refugee Program declared on Feb. 6, 1981, that “The United States Immigration Service has accepted these persons (the Phompors) for resettlement in the United States and has asked the Ministry of Interior to transfer them to Bangkok,” according to a document Pace provided to the PDN.

From Bangkok, the family traveled to Stockton, Calif. From there, they settled in Fresno, Calif.

Life in California

Phompor grew up in Fresno, where he met Pace, and the two became best friends.

“He is one of the best people I’ve ever known in my life,” Pace said. “He’s always been encouraging, so overcoming, so full of life and happy and ready to help. He’s always been a great person.”

The two made mistakes in their youth, Pace said while crediting Phompor with keeping him alive.

“We got into some hairy stuff when we were young living in the hood in California, and if it wasn’t for him, I wouldn’t have made it out of it,” Pace said.

Phompor was addicted to meth for “a short-lived” time, Pace said, noting that many people who grew up in that area also struggled with addiction and crime.

When Phompor was arrested in his 20s, he was told to sign a form agreeing to be deported if Laos ever agreed to accept deportees, Littlejohn said. At the time, Phompor was told that would never happen, she said.

Phompor moved to Port Angeles six years ago.

Governmental changes

In 2018, the U.S. government labeled Laos a “recalcitrant country” and placed sanctions on Lao officials and citizens to force a change in their policy not to accept deportees, according to the Center for Immigration Studies.

“In June 2025, the U.S. placed a partial travel ban on Laos and cut off visas for certain Lao individuals citing visa overstays and failure to cooperate with U.S. deportation policy,” according to the Asian Law Caucus. “The Lao government has been issuing travel documents in response to pressures from the U.S. There are over 4,800 people considered by ICE to be nationals of Laos who have removal orders and are living in the United States.”

Phompor, however, was never given a removal order or informed that his immigration status had changed, Littlejohn said.

She has been the driving force in keeping track of where Phompor is being held, informing friends and family of what is happening and trying to get him a lawyer.

She is working with the Seattle Clemency Project to try to get a lawyer for Phompor, who has been given a deportation date of Oct. 20.

“(Sunday night), I was given some unfortunate information,” Littlejohn said. “Even though some of these detainees are given these dates that are weeks out, apparently they’re getting shipped out out of nowhere so he might be shipped out before that Oct. 20 date. That’s really scary because I had a lot of hope we could get some stuff done by Oct. 20.”

Port Angeles Mayor Kate Dexter has reached out, Littlejohn said.

“(Dexter’s) looking into it, and she’s also trying to get some senators and representatives involved,” Littlejohn said.

Pace and Littlejohn have been able to speak to Phompor since he’s been detained.

“He’s terrified he’s never going to see his kid again, or his family,” Pace said. “He’s terrified of going to a country where he doesn’t know anyone. He is absolutely horrified at what’s going to happen next.”

text:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) asked the Supreme Court Tuesday to lift a lower court order and allow the Trump administration to use a flawed federal immigration database to initiate voter registration purges.

The petition marks the department’s latest rushed attempt to leapfrog an appellate court and get the Supreme Court’s conservative-appointed majority to stay a lower ruling blocking President Donald Trump’s attempt to increase the executive branch’s control over elections.

The DOJ filed the request just days after the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals denied the administration’s motion to pause U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan’s June order blocking its use of the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) modified Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) system.

Originally designed to help states check the citizenship status of people applying for government benefits, the Trump administration has tried to turn the SAVE program into a new system to monitor state voter registration lists.

In her order, Sooknanan found that the endeavor violated several federal laws, “haphazardly” threatened “the sacred right to vote” and “trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens.”

In his filing to the Supreme Court, Solicitor General D. John Sauer called Sooknanan’s order “indefensible” while claiming it “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections by vacating the federal government’s authority to internally use Social Security data when fulfilling its duty to respond to requests by States to verify the citizenship of individuals for voting and other purposes.”

Though Sauer claimed DHS was using SAVE in response to requests from states, the department’s leadership has tried to force states to use the program or lose out on emergency and disaster grants.

Voting groups and privacy groups have repeatedly warned that the SAVE program was never designed to check voter eligibility and, when used in this manner, would likely erroneously disqualify eligible voters.

In fact, in states where the database has been used, eligible voters were routinely flagged as noncitizens.

Before Sooknanan’s block, the Trump administration used SAVE to check the citizenship status of more than 67 million registered voters. Those checks flagged thousands of people as potential noncitizens, but further investigations found that most were actually eligible voters.

Though the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals kept Sooknanan’s order in place, it did order that the Trump administration’s underlying appeal be expedited.

Now, the DOJ has gone directly to the Supreme Court before the appeals court has officially weighed in on the matter.

This is a breaking news story. Please check back for additional details.

text:
The Trump administration urged the Supreme Court on Tuesday to restore the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) overhauled immigration verification system in time for the midterm elections.

“The district court has issued an indefensible order that threatens the integrity of upcoming elections,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote.

DHS’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) is used to determine eligibility for certain federal programs. DHS made significant updates to the system after President Trump directed it to ensure election officials had appropriate access to verify their voters’ citizenship.

The changes connect SAVE to Social Security records and allow bulk queries. Sauer said the modified system had been processing more than a million requests each day and was making voter registration eligibility checks more efficient.

The administration brought the case to the justices after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit voted 2-1 on Friday to uphold a block on the overhaul. A judge had found it violated the Social Security Act and a federal privacy law.

It’s the latest election-related dispute to land on the Supreme Court’s emergency docket as the midterms approach. As the clock continues to tick down to November’s contests, the justices also are mulling efforts to restore a GOP-favored congressional map in Missouri and Trump’s mail-in voting restrictions.

Sauer argued the database overhaul is legal and the lower courts wrongly concluded the administration had forfeited its arguments. He also asserted the plaintiffs — organizations focused on voting and privacy issues — had no legal right to challenge the overhaul.

“The federal government, the States, and the public face irreparable harm from the court’s sudden upending of the updated system and from being required to return to an older, more cumbersome, and less reliable version of the system,” Sauer wrote in the filing.

The request heads to Chief Justice John Roberts, who by default handles emergency matters arising from the nation’s capital. He could also refer the case to the full court for a vote.

text:
A federal judge has dismissed the libel lawsuit Newark Mayor Ras Baraka filed last year against Alina Habba, the former top federal prosecutor in New Jersey, over comments she made on social media and TV about his botched arrest outside Delaney Hall.

In a decision released Friday, U.S. District Judge Brian R. Martinotti said Habba was acting within her scope as acting U.S. attorney for New Jersey when she accused Baraka on social media and during a Fox News interview of illegal trespass and “grandstanding” during the May 9, 2025, visit to the federal migrant jail in Newark during which he was arrested.

“Making a public statement about potential criminal activity within a prosecutor’s jurisdiction falls within the ambit of a prosecutor’s employment,” Martinotti wrote. “Habba’s use of social media and her participation in media interviews to address criminal activity in New Jersey falls within the spatial limits of her employment as the interim United States Attorney for District of New Jersey.”

Baraka also failed to seek relief first from the Department of Justice, which the Federal Tort Claims Act requires, before filing his lawsuit, wrote Martinotti, an Obama appointee.

But the judge also said he wasn’t ruling on the merits of Baraka’s libel claims. He left the door open for the mayor to renew his claims, dismissing the case without prejudice. That means Baraka can amend and refile his complaint if he addresses the judge’s concerns, and Martinotti gave him 21 days to do so.

It’s unclear if he will. His attorney and city spokespeople did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

New videos capture tense moments surrounding arrest of Newark mayor

Baraka sued Habba and Ricky Patel, the special agent in charge of the Newark Division of Homeland Security Investigations, for false arrest and malicious prosecution in June 2025, a few weeks after Patel ordered armed, masked immigration agents to “take him down” during a tense visit Baraka made to Delaney Hall.

Three Democratic members of Congress — Reps. LaMonica McIver, Rob Menendez, and Bonnie Watson Coleman — also were there that day to inspect the prison, and McIver had asked Baraka to attend their post-inspection news conference.

After he arrived, a prison guard invited Baraka onto prison grounds past the fenced perimeter, where protesters had gathered. He waited there until Patel directed him to leave the fenced area about 45 minutes later, and even though he complied, the agents arrested him five minutes later, charged him with trespass, and held him in federal custody for five hours.

Ten days later, prosecutors dropped the charge and a federal judge scolded them for the “hasty arrest” and “embarrassing retraction” of the charge.

Baraka, a Democrat who was running for governor at the time of his arrest, accused Habba and Patel of political motivations. When Habba announced she was dropping the trespassing charge against Baraka, she filed criminal charges against McIver, accusing her of assaulting federal agents as they arrested Baraka. The U.S. 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals last month rejected McIver’s bid to avoid trial on two of the three charges she faces.

text:
California is at risk of losing nearly $12 billion in federal funding for public assistance programs after the Trump administration threatened to cut off grants to states unless they report every known unauthorized immigrant to immigration authorities.

The threat came in the form of a new legal opinion this month reinterpreting a 1990s welfare-reform law to mean that all agencies in states receiving welfare funding — which is every state in the nation — must report all “individuals known to be not lawfully present” to the federal government or risk losing grants that aid low-income people.

That’s a dramatic reversal from the Clinton-era interpretation of the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, which said that only state agencies administering the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) programs needed to provide information to federal immigration authorities.

Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office was defiant in its opposition to the threat.

“This is nothing new — Trump has always tried to play cruel games with states that protect working families,” Newsom spokesperson Diana Crofts-Pelayo said. “The courts have repeatedly rejected the Trump administration’s politically motivated attacks on blue states — should the Trump administration move forward, we expect the same here.”

TANF — known in California as CalWORKS — is short-term cash assistance for people in poverty, including nearly 900,000 Californians as of 2024. SSI provides cash benefits to elderly, blind or disabled people with low incomes, including 1.1 million Californians as of 2025. That’s roughly 2 million Californians benefitted from the two programs.

California receives a $3.7 billion annual block grant for TANF and roughly $8 billion a year in SSI funding, according to Ryan Woolsey, a policy analyst at the state Legislative Analyst’s Office.

More than a million unauthorized immigrants have California driver’s licenses, thanks to a 2013 law known as AB 60 that allows residents to obtain a license regardless of their immigration status. And more than 100,000 students without status are enrolled in California public universities, where they qualify for in-state tuition and some state financial aid under AB 540, passed by the Legislature in 2001.

Sen. Alex Padilla, who helped spearhead AB 60 when he was a state lawmaker, called the administration’s move an effort to vilify immigrants by holding hostage aid to seniors, people with disabilities and struggling families.

“Instead of doing anything to make life more affordable, this administration is choosing to distract from their disastrous policies by sowing chaos and fear,” Padilla told KQED in a statement. “Kids and working families will pay an even greater price because of their cruelty, and I won’t stop fighting for the justice they deserve.”

Johnson called the Department of Justice’s new opinion unusual from a legal standpoint, and he said he expects it to be challenged in court by states such as California on the grounds that it is arbitrary and capricious and doesn’t consider the interests of those who’ve relied on the Clinton-era understanding of the law.

“It’s very rare to reinterpret an interpretation that was put into place a quarter-century ago and has never been questioned or undermined by legislation or a court decision in any way,” he said.

But Johnson cautioned that the opinion was carefully written and could be challenging to overturn.

A spokesperson for California Attorney General Rob Bonta said the office is reviewing it.

“The Trump administration is continuing to try to coerce states into its hateful agenda, this time by attempting to rewrite decades-old law,” spokesperson Nina Sheridan said. “We’re evaluating the Office of Legal Counsel’s opinion.”

text:
VENICE — Oscar-winning filmmaker Laura Poitras said on Monday she ​hopes a new documentary about U.S. immigration raids will help “denormalize” violence under President Donald Trump’s ‌mass deportation campaign.

Premiering at the Venice Film Festival, the 25-minute documentary “They’re Here”, co-directed by Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller, follows volunteers in Minneapolis as they track the movements of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents conducting deportation operations earlier this year.

“The reality is a ​nightmare. The entire country is under attack and immigrants are living in fear throughout the ​United States right now,” Poitras said ahead of the screening.

Confronting protesters in the snow

Trump ⁠launched his deportation drive immediately after taking office in January 2025. He has defended ICE’s tactics and ​argued that people who entered the U.S. illegally must be sent home.

The Minneapolis sweep drew weeks of demonstrations ​and confrontations between protesters and ICE agents in which immigration officers shot dead two U.S. citizens.

“In the mainstream media, this kind of violence is being normalized. We believe very strongly in the power of cinema to denormalize this violence and to ​show what’s happening,” Poitras told a news conference.

Poitras, whose full-length documentary “All the Beauty and the Bloodshed,” won Venice’s ​top Golden Lion prize in 2022, said she and Mueller decided to make a much shorter film because they felt ‌it ⁠was urgent to show immediately what was happening.

Shot largely from the perspective of local residents tracking the movements of ICE teams, “They’re Here” cuts between volunteer dispatch networks and the story of a Mexican man hiding from immigration authorities with the help of his son.

The documentary shows locals plotting the routes of unmarked ICE cars, ​masked agents confronting protesters on ​snow-covered streets and handcuffed ⁠detainees boarding deportation flights.

Community Response

The Minneapolis crackdown became one of the flashpoints in the broader deportation campaign and the U.S. administration eventually scaled back the operation after ​months of unrest.

Mueller said the filmmakers wanted to document both the scope of ​the anti-migrant sweep ⁠and the community response it provoked across the city.

“The resistance remained one of documentation more than anything else, precisely because it was about keeping people safe rather than fighting ICE,” she said. “These are our neighbors, and we ⁠don’t want ​them stolen from us.”

She said the eventual drawdown on ICE ​operatives showed that the community action had worked.

“ICE removed 80% of its agents. So there was a real response to this kind of ​resistance, which I think we can all take hope from,” she said.

text:
DHS and USCIS have issued an interim final rule allowing certain children born in the U.S. to foreign government employees to voluntarily register as lawful permanent residents (green card holders), expanding a process that previously applied primarily to children of foreign diplomats.

Proposed Rule for New Registration Process for Certain U.S.-Born Children of Foreign Government Employees

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) have published an interim final rule expanding eligibility for lawful permanent resident (LPR) registration to certain children born in the U.S. to foreign government employees who are not U.S. citizens. The rule broadens an existing framework that previously applied primarily to children born to foreign diplomatic officers.

The rule is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on September 9, 2026, and applies prospectively to eligible children born on or after the rule’s effective date. Children born before the effective date will continue to be treated under the regulations in effect at the time of their birth.

Expanded Definition of “Foreign Government Employee”

Under the new rule, the term “foreign government employee” includes:

Foreign diplomatic officers accredited to the U.S.

Foreign embassy or consular employees who are nationals of the sending country

Individuals employed by a foreign government in an official capacity

Employees of international organizations that possess international organization immunity in the U.S.

The rule also clarifies several categories that are not considered foreign government employees for these purposes, including certain contractors, third-country nationals employed by embassies, personal staff and employees of state-owned enterprises who are outside qualifying visa classifications.

Lawful Permanent Residence Registration

Voluntary Green Card Registration Available

Eligible individuals can voluntarily register for lawful permanent residence by filing Form I-485. If USCIS approves the application, it will recognize the individual’s permanent resident status as effective from their date of birth.

USCIS will revise the instructions for Form I-485 and related forms to reflect the expanded eligibility category for children born to foreign government employees.

Alternative Registration Requirement

The rule notes that individuals who do not register as lawful permanent residents may still be subject to federal alien registration requirements and may need to file Form G-325R, Biographic Information (Registration), unless otherwise exempt.

Applicability and Timing

The rule takes effect upon publication in the Federal Register.

The provisions apply only to children born on or after the rule’s effective date.

Children born before the effective date are not covered by the new requirements.

Ongoing Litigation

DHS noted that a preliminary injunction in Casa Inc. v. Trump may limit implementation of the rule. Unless the court modifies or lifts the injunction, DHS will not implement any provisions that conflict with the court’s order.

text:
A U.S. District Court judge upheld a New Jersey executive order limiting federal immigration officials’ access to nonpublic parts of state property, ruling the federal government had failed to prove its discrimination claim.

Friday’s decision by Judge Georgette Castner keeps in place a February executive order issued by Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) that, absent judicial warrants, bars immigration officials from private parts of state land and broadly bans them from using state property as staging areas for immigration operations.

“ICE is not making New Jersey’s communities any safer. That’s why I signed an Executive Order restricting access to nonpublic state property by its untrained agents. Once again, Trump tried to stop us, and once again we won,” the governor said in a statement.

The Trump administration sued in February, arguing the executive order was preempted by federal law, impermissibly discriminated against federal immigration authorities, and unlawfully sought to regulate the federal government.

The federal statutes the Trump administration cited do not conflict with the executive order, the judge ruled, because they impose no duty to cooperate on state officials.

She added that the order does not prevent immigration enforcement, but instead bars New Jersey resources from assisting those efforts in most cases. Federal law mandating New Jersey offer its resources to aid immigration enforcement would violate the anticommandeering doctrine, which broadly says the federal government cannot dictate the content of state legislation or order state officials to enforce federal law, the judge said.

“Congress contemplated state assistance in federal immigration enforcement, but it contemplated that assistance on a voluntary basis,” wrote Castner, a Biden appointee. “The fact that New Jersey has decided not to volunteer — in the limited context of EO12 — is in accordance, not in conflict, with Congress’s design.”

Ruling the New Jersey order was preempted would improperly shift some costs for immigration enforcement onto the state, the judge ruled.

The executive order does not impermissibly regulate the federal government because it applies to state property, a distinction the judge said made New Jersey a proprietor rather than a regulator.

Even if that wasn’t the case, the order would survive because it does not “substantially interfere” with immigration enforcement as would, for example, a ban on private detention facilities that ICE uses — near exclusively — for immigrant detention, the judge said.

“The United States does not allege facts suggesting that immigration officers ‘almost exclusively’ rely on private state-owned property to effectuate immigration enforcement or that it has to ‘entirely transform’ its approach to immigration enforcement as a result” of the executive order, the judge wrote.

The judge found the order does not discriminate against the federal government because allegations of discrimination require a showing that a policy applied unequally to similarly situated individuals or groups. Because only the federal government is tasked with civil immigration enforcement, the order does not treat federal law enforcement worse than state or local law enforcement, the judge ruled.

Spokespeople for the U.S. Department of Justice did not immediately return a request for comment. It’s unclear whether the federal government will seek to appeal the decision.

text:
New York, NY—On August 21, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York ruled in favor of the Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. (CLINIC), in their federal lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s indefinite suspension of immigrant visa processing for nationals of 75 countries.

CLINIC’s legal case was provoked by the U.S. Department of State (DOS) and Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s policy pausing all immigrant visa issuance to 75 countries, disproportionately affecting countries with majority nonwhite or ethnic minority populations, including many in Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Middle East and Eastern Europe. The Trump administration cited concerns about these immigrants becoming “public charge” risks, and expanded its definition of “public charge” to include any public benefit used, even though most visa applicants are not eligible for cash welfare and remain ineligible for years. The plaintiffs argued that this is a nationality-based ban that replaces the law’s requirement for individualized consular review with a blanket rule, which they say exceeds the agency’s statutory authority.

Murad Awawdeh, President and CEO, New York Immigration Coalition:

“The New York Immigration Coalition applauds the court’s decision. By siding with the plaintiffs, the court restores the long-standing immigration process that ensures visas are issued on a case-by-case basis, not decided by nationality. The court called the administration’s actions what they were: illegal. Maintaining objectivity in immigration matters means ensuring that decisions, evaluations, and representations are neutral, evidence-based, and free from personal bias or politics, so they serve the integrity of the legal process and the best interests of the parties involved. This ruling means that a mother in Brooklyn can go back to planning for being reunited with a daughter that she has been waiting years to hold.”

text:
[Episcopal News Service] Two Vermont Episcopalians were among seven clergy members arrested Sept. 4 during a protest at a Department of Homeland Security building in Williston used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.

The Ven. Susan McMillan and the Rev. Earl Kooperkamp of the Diocese of Vermont had joined in blockading the doors of the facility for about an hour, until they were arrested by local police and state troopers, according to WCAX-TV. Vermont State Police later released booking photos of the clergy members, including McMillan and Kooperkamp, standing in front of a concrete block wall.

Vermont Bishop Shannon MacVean-Brown, in a message to the diocese, said that McMillan and Kooperkamp were released shortly after being booked on charges of unlawful trespass. She added that civil disobedience has “a long history in our country and The Episcopal Church.”

“Archdeacon McMillan and Rev. Kooperkamp joined a smaller group who chose to enter the offices, aiming to disrupt the work of ICE. This was planned as a nonviolent action by a broad grassroots coalition of Vermont faith leaders,” MacVean-Brown said. “As Christians, we are called not only to bear witness to injustice but to act. When Jesus tells us to love our neighbor, that is not a passive action. It is constant, immediate, and proactive.”

MacVean-Brown also shared a statement from McMillan about the protest.

“Our national leaders, claiming to be Christian, authorize heinous and immoral policies, and the implementation of those policies starts right here,” the archdeacon said. “Every day, from this building, ICE surveils, determining which man, woman or child should be targeted. And then that person, or someone mistaken for that person, or a brown-skinned person who happens to be nearby, is kidnapped, incarcerated without due process, and their life destroyed.

“If Jesus were here in the U.S. today, he could easily be caught in this trap and deported. This is not Christianity and I have to fight this cruelty in every way I can.”

text:
BOSTON — Governor Maura Healey today released new guidance and resources to implement the PROTECT Act, providing state government actors, health care providers, law enforcement agencies, and employers with clear direction as additional protections for residents under the law take effect.

The new guidance addresses protections for nonpublic areas of state property and in health care facilities, limits state and local law enforcement participation in civil immigration enforcement, and a new state law requirement for employers to notify workers in writing if ICE is going to inspect employee records.

“We passed the PROTECT Act to keep people safe from the dangerous tactics we are seeing from ICE here in Massachusetts and across the country,” said Governor Maura Healey. “This guidance makes clear what officials across state government, health care providers, law enforcement agencies, and employers need to know and do if they come across ICE. The PROTECT Act is about keeping our communities safe, protecting people’s rights and preserving the trust that allows people to seek care, report crimes and access the services they rely on.”

“The PROTECT Act gives communities across Massachusetts important protections, and this guidance helps turn those protections into practice,” said Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll. “Our employers, health care providers, law enforcement officers and state employees are on the front lines serving people every day. We want to make sure they have the clarity and support they need to do their jobs, keep people safe and continue providing the services that families and communities depend on.”

Governor Healey signed the PROTECT Act on August 5, establishing some of the strongest protections in the nation against abuses by federal immigration authorities. The law limits civil arrests in courthouses, schools, child care programs, nursing homes and nonpublic areas of health care facilities; restricts the use of state property for civil law enforcement; strictly limits state and local participation in civil immigration enforcement; strengthens protections for workers and families; and creates a state civil rights remedy for constitutional violations.

The guidance released today includes:

State Property

Governor Healey and the Executive Office for Administration and Finance (A&F) issued statewide guidelines limiting civil law enforcement activity in nonpublic areas of state property.

Under the guidelines, civil law enforcement activities, including civil arrests, are prohibited in designated nonpublic areas of state buildings and other property, unless they are required by state or federal law or to administer a state or federally supported program, authorized by a valid judicial warrant or judicial order, or necessary to address a specific and immediate health or safety threat.

The Act applies broadly to any property owned, leased, occupied, controlled by or used for business by the Commonwealth, except courthouses. The guidelines instruct state agencies and other Commonwealth offices to review their property portfolio and designate areas as “nonpublic,” with the goal of preserving access to essential public service and the ability to conduct business with the state, without fear or intimidation.

“We, as an administration, take the health and safety of residents of Massachusetts seriously,” said Administration and Finance Secretary Matthew J. Gorzkowicz. “No one should be afraid to access state buildings or the government services to which they are entitled. These guidelines will ensure people feel safe and protected by their state government.”

Health Care Facilities

The Executive Office of Health and Human Services (EOHHS), Department of Public Health (DPH), Department of Mental Health (DMH), Department of Developmental Services (DDS) and MassHealth developed guidance and a model policy to help health care providers implement new protections for nonpublic areas of their service sites. The law requires covered providers to establish policies for interactions with law enforcement engaged in civil law enforcement, including federal immigration enforcement, within 30 days of today.

“No one should have to weigh their health and safety against the fear of immigration enforcement,” said Health and Human Services Secretary Kiame Mahaniah, MD, MBA. “The PROTECT Act will help residents maintain access to services they need, and ensure that places where people go for care will remain a trusted resource.”

The requirements apply to a broad range of providers, including hospitals, community health centers, clinics, mobile clinics, nursing and rest homes, emergency medical services, adult day health centers, substance use disorder treatment programs, certain physician and advanced practice nursing practices, providers serving people with intellectual or developmental disabilities, and certain MassHealth day habilitation providers.

Under the Act, certain covered providers must designate a point of contact for interactions with civil law enforcement, identify nonpublic areas where people receive care or discuss protected health information, or that are otherwise not open to the public, and establish procedures so staff, volunteers, and administrators know how to respond to requests from civil law enforcement. Civil arrests are not allowed in those designated nonpublic areas without a judicial warrant, except as otherwise required by law or to administer a state or federally supported program. Covered providers required to adopt a policy under the Act must do so by October 4. Today’s release of guidance and a model policy by the Healey-Driscoll Administrations is designed to assist in those efforts.

Law Enforcement and Civil Immigration Enforcement

The Executive Office of Public Safety and Security (EOPSS), Municipal Police Training Committee (MPTC) and Massachusetts Chiefs of Police Association (MCOPA) developed new roll call training materials to help police officers, dispatchers, records staff and other law enforcement personnel understand the PROTECT Act’s requirements and how they apply to day-to-day public safety work.

Beginning today, the law limits when state and local law enforcement may inquire about, record, share or act on a person’s immigration or citizenship status. It also restricts the use of state and local personnel, facilities, equipment and other public resources to conduct or participate in federal civil immigration enforcement and prohibits holding someone past the time they are otherwise eligible for release based solely on an immigration detainer.

The guidance makes equally clear what the PROTECT Act does not change. Massachusetts law enforcement can continue investigating and enforcing criminal laws, making lawful arrests with a judicial warrant, conducting booking procedures, keeping the peace, responding to emergencies and working with federal, state and local partners on criminal investigations.

If a crime or breach of the peace occurs during a federal civil immigration operation, officers may respond to address the public safety issue while remaining separate from the civil immigration enforcement activity itself.

Notice to Employees of I-9 Inspections

The Executive Office of Labor and Workforce Development (LWD), Office for Refugees and Immigrants (ORI) and Attorney General’s Office issued guidance to help Massachusetts employers comply with a new state law requirement to notify employees of upcoming inspections of I-9 employment eligibility records by ICE.

Under the PROTECT Act, Massachusetts employers must provide employees with written notice within 48 hours of receiving a Notice of Inspection from ICE for I-9 forms or other employment records, except where otherwise required by federal law.

The Administration is also providing employers with a sample notice that can be used or modified to comply with the law. Notice must be provided individually to employees and should be provided in the employee’s primary language; posting a notice at the workplace alone does not satisfy the requirement.

“This guidance gives employers clear steps to follow while ensuring workers receive timely and accurate information,” said Secretary of Labor and Workforce Development Lauren Jones. “By making sure employers and employees are informed, we are strengthening workplace protections and helping employers across the state understand and meet their responsibilities under the PROTECT Act.”

Today’s guidance builds on guidance released by Governor Healey last month to help K-12 schools and child care programs implement the PROTECT Act. Those resources provided model policies and procedures for responding to civil law enforcement, reviewing requests for access, protecting confidential information and communicating with students and families.

Earlier this year, Governor Healey also signed Executive Order 650 to protect access to essential state services and issued statewide guidance to schools, child care providers, colleges and universities, health care facilities and places of worship on interacting with federal immigration enforcement.

The Healey-Driscoll Administration will continue working with state agencies, employers, health care providers, law enforcement and communities across Massachusetts to fully implement the PROTECT Act and ensure its protections are carried out effectively statewide.

text:
A protest in a Frederick neighborhood turned violent Friday night as Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers clashed with demonstrators, leaving some injured and prompting calls for an investigation.

Protesters gathered near Stoneybrook Court after ICE vehicles were spotted in the area on Thursday. By Friday, more than 100 community members had joined the demonstration, chanting and linking arms in opposition to the federal immigration enforcement activity.

“We were attacked. Our community was physically attacked by federal law enforcement officers,” Frederick City Council President Cesar Diaz said. “In the past, we’ve seen them come in, they do something, they kidnap someone and then they leave. This time, they stuck around.”

Witnesses said ICE officers appeared to be targeting a specific house and began driving SUVs onto sidewalks, ordering protesters to move.

“He started to really come at me and so I moved off. There was another woman there with me, and then, there was another protester sort of in front, like caddy-corner to me. He actually plowed into that person and started pushing them with his car,” said Soolah Kemp, a protester.

Kemp also described how a group of protesters later linked arms in front of the home.

“They were just standing there. It wasn’t like they were fighting. They weren’t. They just linked arms,” Kemp said.

Video from the scene captured the moment officers physically engaged with protesters.

“(They were) beating people with batons, kicking them, punching them, throwing people on the ground, just to attempt to get into the front door of this home,” said Tatiana Santos, who is with Indivisible Frederick Forward.

Protesters suffered cuts and bruises, with some requiring hospitalization. Frederick police eventually arrived to deescalate the situation. Witnesses said ICE officers broke into the home and later spoke with the family inside.

“We were asked to be quiet so that they could have a conversation with ICE and then ICE left,” Santos said.

Witnesses said it did not appear that ICE made any arrests during the incident.

Diaz expressed concern about the implications of the encounter.

“This is the first time that’s happened in Frederick. I think that level of action is the first time that’s happened anywhere in Maryland, and now, people are concerned. Is this the new normal? Is this an escalation?” Diaz said.

Diaz also noted that he had not seen a warrant for ICE’s activity. Community members are now calling on the Maryland attorney general to investigate the incident.

Baltimore City Councilwoman Odette Ramos, D-District 14, criticized the officers’ actions, writing: “Shame on ICE for their violent, unconstitutional behavior.”

Requests for comment from the governor’s office, Frederick police, and ICE have not yet been answered.

text:
STOCKHOLM, Sweden (AP) — A far-right Belgian party was likely not entitled to use IKEA’s trademarks to promote an anti-immigration campaign and may have caused “significant detriment” to the furniture giant’s reputation, the European Union’s highest court ruled on Tuesday.

In 2022, the Belgian far-right and Flemish separatist party Vlaams Belang unveiled what it called the “IKEA Plan – Immigration Really Can Be Different” at a press conference, using IKEA-style logos, signs and imagery to present proposals aimed at tightening immigration rules in Belgium.

IKEA brought an infringement action before a Belgian court, arguing its trademarks were used illegally. In response, the Vrijheidsfonds association, which was in charge of the campaign on the party’s behalf, argued that its use of the company’s trademarks without permission was protected by freedom of expression.

The Belgian court referred the case to the European Court of Justice (ECJ), which found that “the use of those IKEA trade marks may cause significant detriment to the repute of those trade marks and to the interests of their proprietor.”

The court said invoking freedom of expression in such cases requires the trademarks to be used in good faith or in the public interest, conditions that did not appear to be met. It added that it did not appear that using IKEA’s reputation to disseminate a political message took precedence over IKEA’s rights and interests.

While the Belgian court will make the final decision, it is expected to take the ECJ’s guidance into account when issuing its ruling.

“Inter IKEA fully believes in – and deeply respects – freedom of expression,” the company said in a statement welcoming the ruling. “At the same time, it cannot accept the use of the IKEA trademarks in ways that damage their reputation or distinctive character, particularly when such use serves no other purpose than to free-ride on the reputation of the IKEA brand.”

text:
Mr President,

In Syria, we welcome the steps taken by the government on its political transition, including convening a new parliament, addressing Assad-era legacies, and engaging the international community. But the situation remains delicate. We urge the government to proceed in an inclusive and representative way, protecting the rights of all Syrians.

In South Sudan, the human rights situation remains fragile, while developments cast doubt on prospects for peaceful, inclusive and credible elections. We remain concerned by violence against civilians, restrictions on political space and continued impunity, including conflict-related sexual violence. All parties must demonstrate restraint, engage in dialogue and ensure accountability.

China has yet to implement the recommendations of the Office of the High Commissioner’s Xinjiang Assessment. Evidence of violations in Xinjiang and Tibet persists, freedom of religion or belief is being further restricted, and the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress risks undermining the rights of individuals belonging to minorities. We welcome the High Commissioner’s continued engagement on these issues.

Finally, five years into Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the human cost continues to grow. As Russia continues its assault on Ukraine’s sovereignty, the international community must not look away. We remain steadfast in our support for Ukraine and in efforts to hold Russia to account.

Thank you.

text:
An analysis by a Kentucky policy center shows the number of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests in the commonwealth continues to grow as the number of local agencies helping ICE has exploded over the past year.

The Kentucky Center for Economic Policy, using data from the Deportation Data Project, showed the number of ICE arrests in Kentucky is at close to 5,000 since President Donald Trump took office in 2025.

An increasing number of those ICE-related arrests are a result of the growing number of Kentucky law enforcement agencies with agreements with ICE to enforce immigration policy, the data showed.

In January 2025 the number of ICE arrests in Kentucky was 114. By July 2026, the number of monthly ICE arrests grew to 443. About 15.8% of those arrests were credited to local law enforcement agreements, the Kentucky Center for Economic Policy analysis showed. In November 2025, only one ICE arrest was credited to local law enforcement.

The Trump administration has pushed an aggressive agenda to deport people who have entered the country illegally.

As part of that crackdown, the administration has pushed local agencies to sign agreements with ICE to augment those enforcement efforts, commonly referred to as 287 (g) agreements.

Data from ICE show a five-fold increase in the number of Kentucky jails, police and county sheriffs who have signed those agreements from July 2025 to August 2026.

In July 2025, a Lexington Herald-Leader review of those agreements showed 11 agencies with formal agreements with ICE. In August 2026, that number had jumped to 55 agencies.

There are financial incentives for local law enforcement to participate. As part of a July 2025 federal budget and spending bill, local law enforcement can now receive up to $7,500 per ICE trained employee, $100,000 to buy vehicles and other equipment and money to cover some overtime and retirement benefits, according to ICE’s website.

The above benefits are for police agencies that sign task force model agreements. The task force model allows officers trained by ICE to enforce immigration law during routine police activity, like traffic stops. This model was once discontinued over concerns about racial profiling, but it was revived by the Trump administration in January 2025.

The other agreements include the jail enforcement model, which allows jail officials to interrogate those who are arrested and detained about their immigration status. The warrant service officer model allows a designated jail employee to serve ICE warrants on people in custody.

The vast majority of Kentucky law enforcement agencies, 52, with agreements with ICE have task force model agreements. Counties can have multiple agreements. For example, Grayson County agencies have signed agreements for all three models.

title: DHS Should Provide Options for Voluntary Vetting of Facility Personnel for Terrorist Ties | U.S. GAO
description:
This Q&A discusses chemical facility security, including staff vetting.
A Department of Homeland Security program had facilities vet their staff for links to terrorism.
Chemical Facility Operations Chemical facility with pipes and two workers in blue jumpsuits and yellow hard hats.
In 2007, DHS established a regulatory program to mitigate security risks for high-risk chemical facilities.
As part of this program, CISA required facilities to vet their personnel and certain unescorted visitors for terrorist ties against the U.S. government’s terrorist watchlist.
text:
In 2025, 89 million people lived or worked near a U.S. facility with high-risk chemicals. In terrorists' hands, these chemicals could inflict mass damage, including impacts equal to a nuclear explosion.

This Q&A discusses chemical facility security, including staff vetting. A Department of Homeland Security program had facilities vet their staff for links to terrorism. But the program ended in 2023 and facilities can't access the watchlist on their own.

Without federal options to vet staff for this purpose, these facilities are vulnerable to insider terrorist attacks.

We recommended DHS implement options to vet staff for terrorist ties.

Chemical Facility Operations

Chemical facility with pipes and two workers in blue jumpsuits and yellow hard hats.

What GAO Found

The Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is the sector risk management agency (SRMA) for the U.S. chemical sector, responsible for implementing programs to assist facility owners and operators in identifying and mitigating security risks. In 2007, DHS established a regulatory program to mitigate security risks for high-risk chemical facilities. As part of this program, CISA required facilities to vet their personnel and certain unescorted visitors for terrorist ties against the U.S. government’s terrorist watchlist. Vetting against the U.S. terrorist watchlist is an inherently governmental function that the private sector cannot perform on its own; therefore, CISA set up a process with options facilities could use for such vetting. Authorization for the regulatory program lapsed in July 2023. The program, including personnel vetting, was discontinued. High-risk chemical facilities are now responsible for identifying and mitigating their own security risks.

According to CISA officials and selected private sector stakeholders GAO interviewed, losing access to the terrorist vetting process is the most significant challenge high-risk facility owners and operators have faced since the discontinuation of CISA’s regulatory program and it has left a gap in chemical facility security that poses substantial risks. The statutory authority that establishes SRMA responsibilities specifies that SRMAs are to implement security programs to assist stakeholders in identifying and mitigating risks to their assets and systems. As of May 2026, CISA said it was exploring whether the agency’s SRMA authority could be used to set up a vetting process. Without federal options for the terrorist vetting of personnel, facility owners and operators lack a critical tool to protect their facilities from an insider terrorist attack and from potential disruptions to critical national supply chains.

From fiscal years 2024 to 2025, the number of CISA active personnel dedicated to chemical sector activities declined from 214 (96 percent of authorized positions) to 52 (25 percent of authorized positions). The active personnel did not include full-time personnel scheduled to separate from CISA by the end of calendar year 2025 through deferred resignations programs. CISA said the reductions have necessitated reducing or eliminating services, such as most on-site facility assessments, but also said the agency continues to offer other services, such as security training and cybersecurity guidance. Selected private sector stakeholders told GAO that CISA’s personnel reductions and the loss of experienced staff have reduced their contact with CISA regarding facility security vulnerabilities.

Chemical Facility Warehouse and Operations

Why GAO Did This Study

According to DHS, as of 2025, more than 89 million people lived or worked within 2 miles of a U.S. facility using high-risk chemicals. DHS estimates that should high-risk chemicals be weaponized, it could cause significant harm to surrounding populations, from fatalities within the facility to the equivalent impact of a nuclear explosion.

GAO was asked to examine DHS’s efforts to mitigate security risks to the U.S. chemical sector. This report addresses, among other issues, CISA and sector stakeholder assessments of sector security following the discontinuation of a facility regulatory program, effects of the lack of a federal terrorist vetting process for chemical facility personnel, and effects of fiscal year 2025 reductions in CISA personnel on sector support services.

GAO reviewed relevant statutes, CISA guidelines and procedures, and CISA data on full-time authorized positions and active agency personnel for fiscal years 2024 and 2025. GAO interviewed CISA officials; conducted site visits to five chemical facilities; and interviewed private sector stakeholders, including representatives from the private sector coordinating council, three industry associations, and six chemical companies.

title: The Alachua County Commission signed an anti-ICE resolution. What's next?
description:
After four months of debate and concerns about risks to state funding, the Alachua County Commission passed a resolution Aug. 11 opposing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations in the county.
The resolution also highlights concerns about the expansion of immigration enforcement in Alachua County.
The GINI proposal Gainesville Immigrant Neighbor Inclusion Initiative’s five-point petition was first presented to the Alachua County Commission April 28 during public comment.
Alachua County Attorney Sylvia E. Torres said the state hasn’t pushed back against Orange County’s resolution, but the Florida Attorney General’s office could issue a warning to it or Alachua County for passing a resolution conflicting with state law like the 287(g) agreement.
The Alachua County Sheriff’s Office signed the agreement, while the Gainesville Police Department hasn’t.
text:
After four months of debate and concerns about risks to state funding, the Alachua County Commission passed a resolution Aug. 11 opposing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations in the county.

Drafted by the Gainesville Immigrant Neighbor Inclusion Initiative, the three-page resolution expresses a commitment to ensuring all residents, regardless of immigration status, feel safe interacting with law enforcement and seeking social services. It warns against discriminatory actions by law enforcement, but does not mention ICE specifically.

The resolution also highlights concerns about the expansion of immigration enforcement in Alachua County. It urges federal immigration officers to clearly identify themselves and inform residents about the purposes of law enforcement activities.

The board voted 4-0 to sign the resolution, with Commissioner Mary Alford absent. In an Aug. 12 Facebook post, Alford wrote that she was absent from the meeting and agreed with the resolution, but believed it could bring “unwanted attention” to Alachua County.

In June, Jacob Torner, the vice president for programs at the TaskForce for Ending Homelessness, wrote to city and county officials that passing an anti-ICE resolution could cause the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development to view Gainesville and Alachua County "less favorably" when awarding federal funds for local services.

The GINI proposal

Gainesville Immigrant Neighbor Inclusion Initiative’s five-point petition was first presented to the Alachua County Commission April 28 during public comment. The resolution didn’t make it to the agenda until June 23, when the commission unanimously voted to delay the decision so it could discuss it with the county attorney.

The petition was also brought to the attention of city commissioners during the public comment portion of a June 18 meeting.

During a July 16 meeting, the Gainesville City Commission voted to postpone the decision on the resolution despite over a dozen public commenters encouraging the commissioners to support it. It’s unclear when the city commission will revisit the decision.

The county’s meeting

County commissioners and staff discussed the resolution for over two hours Aug. 11, weighing potential risks to state funding, such as grants given to the city and county by the state.

Ahead of the vote, commissioners considered actions by other counties, like Orange County, which passed a similar resolution opposing current ICE operations in March to oppose a rumored ICE detention facility in east Orlando.

Alachua County Attorney Sylvia E. Torres said the state hasn’t pushed back against Orange County’s resolution, but the Florida Attorney General’s office could issue a warning to it or Alachua County for passing a resolution conflicting with state law like the 287(g) agreement.

The 287(g) agreement allows state and local law enforcement agencies to carry out immigration operations. The Alachua County Sheriff’s Office signed the agreement, while the Gainesville Police Department hasn’t.

“There’s a history of the attorney general sending out letters that say, ‘What you’ve done is not within your authority’ or that it is ‘malfeasance or misfeasance in office,’ ordering you to basically repeal the action or threatening removal from office,’” Torres said in the meeting.

However, the GPD issued a general order Aug. 27 requiring officers to report anyone they suspect is in the country illegally. The move was made to comply with state requirements, which is mandated by the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA).

During public comment at the county’s Aug. 11 meeting, more than 10 residents and activists took to the podium to encourage commissioners to support the resolution.

Before the vote, Commission Chair Ken Cornell said he didn’t plan to support the resolution. However, after hearing public comment and support from fellow commissioners, Cornell voted in its favor. He said the non-binding resolution, which has no legal weight, would help build public trust.

Is the resolution purely symbolic?

Although the county passed a resolution publicly opposing current ICE operations, the decision doesn’t guarantee or require an end to local law enforcement cooperation with ICE.

Andrea Jacoski, a University of Miami law professor and associate director of the university’s immigration clinic, said the resolution seems to be a symbolic gesture acknowledging community concerns. It can’t supersede state and federal ICE operations in the county, she added.

“I don't actually know that passing a resolution will pull away from their obligation to actually continue to share information or effectuate ICE detainers,” Jacoski said.

ICE detainers, or immigration holds, are written notices sent by ICE to local or state law enforcement asking them to hold a person so ICE can take them into custody.

While the county’s resolution may not prevent ICE operations entirely, Jacoski said, it can build public trust and demonstrate solidarity with its immigrant communities.

“It's important, and it's good that people are recognizing that it is very harmful for our immigrant neighbors and the large immigrant population across Florida,” she said.

Community reactions

After months of discourse, Alachua County Commissioner Marihelen Wheeler said the resolution upholds the county’s responsibility to care for its residents by encouraging ICE officers to treat them fairly.

“It has very nice words put together to ask that folks here don’t wear masks and that they treat people well and that they don't profile anybody,” Wheeler said. “But again, it’s not binding, and so, more than anything, it’s an acknowledgment that there are communities being jeopardized by the tactics coming out of Washington and now out of Tallahassee.”

Wheeler added she’s done far more for immigrants than support a non-binding resolution.

In an attempt to promote binding change, Wheeler said she’s addressed community concerns like GINI’s with U.S. Rep. Kat Cammack and her team, who represent Alachua County and the surrounding area in the U.S. House of Representatives.

“[Cammack] knows that this is a topic that I'm most concerned about,” she said. “So we sat down together … and we were trying to come up with some ideas that we might be able to address the concerns of the community in a more face-to-face and direct way.”

Her relationship with Cammack began when Wheeler ran against former U.S. Rep. Ted Yoho in 2014. Cammack was his campaign manager at the time.

Wheeler looks back at her 2014 campaign for House and her platform on immigration as evidence of her decadelong support for immigrants.

She suspects the Gainesville City Commission has been waiting for the county commission’s decision to make its own about the resolution, she added.

While waiting on the city commission’s vote, she said, she’s been gathering a group of volunteers to talk with Cammack.

“What I’m trying to do is set up a meeting with those folks who were willing to go to have this discussion about what is happening,” she said, “and what we can expect in the future and how we might be helpful in trying to get some kind of immigration reform policy going.”

Having achieved the county’s approval, GINI representative Ethan Maia de Needell said the organization is now focusing its efforts on the city.

He said future work with the county will aim to make the county’s social services more accessible to the immigrant community. GINI hopes to help facilitate those efforts and hold the county accountable, he added.

“The demands in the resolution are not extreme,” he said. “They are simply a gesture of what the city prioritizes, which we hope are the constitutional rights of its residents.”

title: ICE dragged him from his doorstep in January. His elderly partner fears he'll die in detention
description:
