text:
BENNER TOWNSHIP — Penn State’s airport has seen a dramatic surge in flights chartered by ICE to move people between detention centers in the United States.

While ICE has said such transfers are necessary for operational reasons such as bed space, immigration experts claim the practice is intended to cut detainees off from loved ones, wear them down, and make it harder to pursue legal challenges.

The State College Regional Airport is a roughly 40-minute drive from the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, the largest immigration detention facility in the Northeast. Since the beginning of the Trump administration, the facility’s average daily population has increased. Detainees and their advocates allege poor-quality food, inadequate healthcare, and inhumane conditions.

As part of its work to fulfill President Donald Trump’s campaign promise to “carry out the largest domestic deportation operation in American history,” ICE has dramatically expanded its Air network by growing its fleet of planes, strengthening partnerships with charter airlines, and widening its network of airports.

In 2025, the State College Regional Airport serviced just two ICE flights. Through July of this year, that number rose dramatically to 107, according to data from advocacy group Human Rights First.

Stay informed

Sign up for Talk of the Town, an update of the news that matters to your community — from the PA Wilds to Happy Valley.

Email address

Penn State owns both the State College Regional Airport and the Penn State Aviation Center. The former serves commercial flights, and the terminal is owned and operated by the Centre County Airport Authority. The latter is a fixed-base operator run by the university that serves private flights with fueling, hangar storage, and aircraft maintenance.

“There are no contracts between the airport and DHS/ICE. We do not have specific details about charter flights as we are limited by what the commercial charter company operating flights communicates to the airport,” said Wyatt DuBois, senior director of university public relations. “However, it appears there has been an increase in charter flights associated with DHS/ICE.”

ICE flights are handled like any chartered or corporate aircraft arriving at the airport, he told Spotlight PA in an email. Charter companies or brokers typically provide aircraft information and an estimated arrival time but not the name of the individual or entity arranging, or on board, the flight.

Like all airports that receive federal funding, the State College airport is required to comply with Federal Aviation Administration guidelines on accepting flights, DuBois told Spotlight PA in an email.

Aviation experts agreed with Penn State, telling Spotlight PA the airport can legally refuse flights only over indiscriminate safety concerns.

“If they have federal funding, they don’t have much of a leg to stand on legally to stop the flights from coming in,” said Frank Turney, a law professor at the University of Maryland and a solo aviation law practitioner for over 30 years.

When airports accept grants from the FAA, they are required by federal law to ensure “the airport will be available for public use on reasonable conditions and without unjust discrimination.” The only exception is if they’re unable to safely accept an aircraft.

Should an airport refuse ICE flights, the FAA can pursue several types of punishment, Turney said, ranging from fines to the freezing of federal funds in the pipeline. King County, Washington, was ordered by a federal court to accept deportation flights after it attempted to block them.

The FAA didn’t respond to several requests to comment for this story. ICE didn’t respond to multiple requests and then directed Spotlight PA to the Department of Homeland Security, which didn’t respond to questions by the newsroom’s deadline.

Meanwhile, Penn State has taken steps in recent months to get out of the airport business.

On Feb. 26, the university’s Board of Trustees unanimously voted to advance the transfer of the airport’s operating assets to the county authority. “Our fundamental mission as an institution of higher education is to provide a world-class education to our students,” Sara Thorndike, Penn State’s chief financial officer, said in a statement at the time. “Operation of the airport, while vital to the continued success of the university, does not directly support that core educational mission.”

Considering the current speed of negotiations, that transfer could take one to two years, a Centre County Airport Authority official said at a recent meeting.

At that same Aug. 27 meeting, about a dozen concerned residents gathered to oppose the flights.

One resident told the board during public comment that he was shocked to learn the airport had become a hub for ICE flights: “I would hope that you stop this, and I, just in good conscience, can’t be a resident here and let this happen.”

Authority Chair Chris Groshel told attendees that the airport authority is responsible only for the main terminal building and the parking lot.

“We don’t even know what’s going on,” Groshel said of ICE flights at the airport. “It’s not our area of control.”

‘ICE Air’ continues to grow

The number of people detained and deported under Trump has soared compared to his predecessor, with many arrests targeting people who do not have criminal convictions. DHS claims to have deported 675,000 people during Trump’s first year back in office.

ICE’s purse has also grown dramatically under the Trump administration. As of the end of June 2026, ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection had $152 billion in available funding. Some of that money is being used to expand ICE’s network of detention centers, though efforts to convert warehouses in Pennsylvania were later abandoned.

A pivotal part of the agency’s deportation infrastructure is ICE Air, which the agency says “facilitates the transfer and removal of aliens via commercial airlines and chartered flights.”

In July, ICE conducted 2,159 enforcement flights, including a record 329 removal flights to 37 countries, up 14% from the previous month and 59% from July 2025.

However, the vast majority of flights are domestic transfers or so-called “shuffle flights,” which move people to and between detention centers and deportation staging facilities across the United States. These shuffle flights reached a monthly record of 1,363 in July, a 75% year-over-year change, according to data from Human Rights First.

State College Regional Airport has been receiving ICE flights since at least 2025, Human Rights First’s data dashboard shows, but the number has dramatically risen. During the first seven months of this year, 107 ICE flights have flown into and out of State College — the 18th most flights of the 147 airports used for ICE enforcement, according to the nonprofit.

Routine ICE flights arrive at and depart from the airport three to four times a week. Most of those flights go to Alexandria, Louisiana, a main deportation staging facility.

Savi Arvey, director of policy, refugee, and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, said that the increase in domestic shuffle flights can be attributed to parallels in ICE arrests.

“Flights have just continued to increase month by month, and with the amount of funding — with the blank check that this administration has worked with Congress to give ICE the authority to carry out flights and other operations — I think we’re going to only see them increase,” Arvey said.

ICE has said these shuffle flights create bed space at crowded facilities and transport people with removal orders to deportation hubs, but immigration experts say the transfers are just another tool to isolate people who are detained and discourage them from fighting for release.

People detained by ICE can file petitions for habeas corpus, which require the government to justify why someone is being held. In most cases, those petitions must be filed in the federal district where the detainee is physically confined. Every transfer changes where that petition must be filed.

For those who can afford lawyers, no-notice shuffle flights give them little opportunity to contact their attorney. This, along with barriers to phone access while detained, makes it next to impossible for people to fight their cases, said Nancy Hiemstra, a professor at Stony Brook University who researches U.S. immigration enforcement policies.

“It is totally by design to deport people quickly,” Hiemstra said. “It means that a lot of mistakes will be made, but that is intentional. The Trump administration just wants to get people out.”

Fetaine Seddighzadeh, a special projects consultant at Human Rights First, echoed that argument. Being transported back and forth from facilities, and separated from legal representatives and support networks, discourages people who are detained, Seddighzadeh said.

People are given little to no notice when they’re selected to board a flight, Hiemstra said, calling this typical of the detention experience. For morning flights, they’re usually woken in the middle of the night, moved to a holding room with others, and kept in shackles. They are often crowded for hours in places with nowhere to lie down, sit, or use the bathroom.

“Often, the run-up to getting on to a flight is pretty awful,” Hiemstra said.

It’s common for people on flights to experience a range of abuses, such as not being given food or water for long periods of time, not being allowed to go to the bathroom, or being shackled at length, she added.

Depending on the destination of the flight, people can be in shackles for several hours, including while at the detention facility before boarding a bus to the airport, during the shuttle ride from the detention center to the airport, and the shuttle to their destination.

Spotlight PA previously spoke to a Berks County man detained by ICE for 45 days, who was flown from State College to Louisiana, then back again, with no information on where he was being taken. He was twice woken in the middle of the night and driven to the airport, fearing he would be deported to Mexico.

“They put a chain around us and tied it to our handcuffed hands, and they also handcuffed our feet throughout the whole transport process. Sometimes, when you stop and think about it, it feels inhumane,” Erasmo Zavala, who later won his release through the courts, said. “They treat you as if you really were some kind of criminal. But what kind of criminal dedicates himself to his family and mostly goes from work to home?”

Spotlight PA’s A.J. Rao contributed reporting.

text:
Matrix, the Bonavero Institute of Human Rights and the Refugee Studies Centre (University of Oxford), and the Sutherland School of Law (University College Dublin) are co-hosting a series of webinars to explore the contested relationship between the rule of law, human rights and migration governance.

Commencing on 7 October 2026, the series will bring together experts from legal practice, advocacy, and academia to share expert insights into contemporary contestations across a range of fields – clarifying how and why political actors distort and undermine human rights commitments, and exploring whether current systems differentiating refugees, victims of trafficking and other migrants are fit for purpose. Are universalist commitments part of the problem or the solution in the face of anti-migrant politics and xenophobic policy reflexes? Can human rights survive the current onslaught? Or do the rule of law and human rights provide vital bulwarks to humanise, or even potentially reimagine migration governance?

Episode 1: After Chișinău and the EU Pact on Asylum and Migration: human rights, the ECHR and migration

Date: Wednesday 7 October 2026

Time: 17:00-18:00

Register here

In the context of growing political pressure to restrict the already very limited rights of refugees and migrants, this webinar will examine the Council of Europe’s May 2016 Chișinău Declaration and the EU Pact on Asylum and Migration of June 2016. Our speakers will consider these recent legal developments and whether existing legal safeguards embedded in international and domestic law remain capable of protecting the rights of refugees and migrants in a challenging political climate.

Chair:

Professor Philip Leach, Middlesex University & Matrix

Speakers:

Professor Başak Çalı, Bonavero Institute of Human Rights

Professor Alice Donald, Middlesex University

Professor Andrew Forde, Dublin City University, Chairperson, Irish Refugee Council, Member, Irish Human Rights & Equality Commission

Episode 2:The Refugee Convention at 75 – Fatally limited or vitally focused?

Date: Wednesday 28 October 2026

Time: 17:00-18:00

Register here

The 1951 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees was drafted 75 years ago. It has evolved through formal additions (the 1967 Protocol), expansion (regional instruments in Africa and Latin America), and human rights driven evolutive interpretation. This webinar explores whether it is fit for purpose – does it meet the challenge to protect those fleeing war and conflict and climate crises? What additional sources of international protection are available or needed? What are the implications of current containment practices and the erosion of international protection?

Chair:

Eleanor Mitchell, Matrix

Speakers:

Professor Cathryn Costello, UCD & Matrix

Professor Catherine Briddick, Refugee Studies Centre, University of Oxford

Randhir Gayan Wanigasekara, UNHCR London

Episode 3: Is the international/domestic framework for trafficking effective?

Date: Wednesday 4 November 2026

Time: 17:00-18:00

Register here

International, regional and domestic laws on trafficking aim to prevent trafficking, protect victims and ensure prosecution of perpetrators. This webinar explores whether the current regime meets its stated purposes, and whether anti-trafficking measures work when confronted with increasingly oppressive migration controls.

Chair:

Samantha Knights KC, Matrix

Speakers:

Ahmed Aydeed, Deighton Pierce Glynn

Professor Siobhán Mullally, Established Professor of Human Rights Law; Director, Irish Centre for Human Rights, University of Galway; former United Nations Special Rapporteur on Trafficking in Persons.

Dr Maayan Niezna, University of Liverpool

Episode 4: Migration for work and education – myths and realities

Date: Wednesday 18 November 2026

Time: 17:00-18:00

Register here

Migration for work and study are the most significant forms of migration in terms of numbers, including to the UK and Ireland. This webinar will explore the myths and realities surrounding the law and policy in these fields, examining the trade-offs in immigration policy, including the implications of temporariness for the right to work and human rights of migrants. Are temporariness and selectivity desirable or necessary features in this field, or a mask for precarity and discrimination? What would a human-rights based immigration policy look like?

Chair:

Professor Cathryn Costello, UCD & Matrix

Speakers:

Professor Diamond Ashiagbor, University of Birmingham & Matrix

Madeleine Sumption, Director, Migration Observatory, University of Oxford

Professor Martin Ruhs, Migration Policy Centre, European University Institute

Episode 5: The Rule of Law in Reimagining Immigration Law & Enforcement

Date: Wednesday 2 December 2026

Time: 17:00-18:00

Register here

The ideal of the rule of law is poorly institutionalised in immigration law and enforcement. In this final seminar, we invite speakers to reflect on how the rule of law could be used to reimagine immigration law and enforcement, by taking state violations more seriously, tempering the coercive power of the state, enabling migrants to legalise their status, or even questioning the conception of sovereignty underpinning contemporary borders.

Chair:

Professor Cathryn Costello, UCD & Matrix

title: Supreme Court to consider unresolved proportionality question in EU deportation appeals
description:
Does national law preclude EU law protections having a role?
The Upper Tribunal (write-up here) initially held that while substantive EU rights are not imported into national law for post-Brexit conduct, some procedural protections still are.
Losing, or not exercising, the right of appeal under the regulations risks undermining the person’s position if the human rights appeal is successful.
EU proportionality The Court of Appeal had to grapple with what the correct reading of Articles 20 and 21 of the Withdrawal Agreement was.
The appellants argued that this meant following national legislation, but subject to an EU proportionality assessment.
text:
The Supreme Court has granted the appellants permission to appeal the Court of Appeal’s decision in Vargova and Molnar v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2026] EWCA Civ 31. The case will determine how to apply the Withdrawal Agreement to people with status under the EU Settlement Scheme who face deportation following criminal offences committed after 31 December 2020. Does national law preclude EU law protections having a role?

The Upper Tribunal (write-up here) initially held that while substantive EU rights are not imported into national law for post-Brexit conduct, some procedural protections still are. This included the right to be notified of a decision, to an effective remedy, and to a fair hearing, but not the EU principle of proportionality.

The Court of Appeal (write-up here) agreed that proportionality does not apply, but it did not go on to resolve the broader question of whether national law now applies exclusively.

The right of appeal

The decisions under appeal in these cases were ‘stage 1’ notices, not refusals of human rights claims. These attract a right of appeal under regulation 6 of the Immigration (Citizens’ Rights Appeals) (EU Exit) Regulations 2020, which allows a person with leave under the EU Settlement Scheme to appeal a decision to deport them.

On 25 June 2025, before the Court of Appeal hearing, the Home Secretary added regulation 6(1A), which defined a deportation decision as one made only after the person has been invited to make representations against deportation. So, not the first notice sent out. In practice, the Home Office now tends to attach the right of appeal to the refusal of the human rights claim itself (the ‘stage 2’ decision).

Anyone advising an EU national with status under the EU Settlement Scheme who has received a stage 2 decision should check they have been given, and have exercised, a right of appeal under regulation 6, whether granted at stage 1 or stage 2. The Court of Appeal held that a stage 1 decision does restrict a person’s residence rights under the Withdrawal Agreement, and so the appeal under regulation 6 should not be ignored.

If the Home Secretary has failed to consider important information already available to her (such as a trafficking decision or the correct position on the EU application) in issuing the decision it is possible to mount an effective challenge. It is vital to confirm, from the original indictment if possible, the dates of all offences relied on by the Home Secretary. This is an area prone to error. Sentences are not always passed chronologically so a later sentence could be for pre-31 December 2020 conduct. If the Home Secretary relies on such conduct, a person’s case must be considered under the public policy grounds set out in Chapter VI of the Citizens’ Rights Directive.

If a stage 2 decision, headed as a refusal of a human rights claim, also contains a right of appeal under regulation 6, this should be exercised, even if late, to ensure that the person has a remedy under the Withdrawal Agreement. At the very least this will confirm that the person is covered by the Withdrawal Agreement, however the protections come to be interpreted in practice. Losing, or not exercising, the right of appeal under the regulations risks undermining the person’s position if the human rights appeal is successful.

EU proportionality

The Court of Appeal had to grapple with what the correct reading of Articles 20 and 21 of the Withdrawal Agreement was. Article 20(2) allows residence to be restricted for post-Brexit conduct ‘in accordance with national legislation’, while Article 21 imports certain safeguards from the Citizens’ Rights Directive for decisions falling within the scope of the Withdrawal Agreement. The appellants argued that this meant following national legislation, but subject to an EU proportionality assessment.

The Court of Appeal disagreed. Mixing the two regimes risked inconsistent interpretations across member states. It also rejected the idea that proportionality counts as a ‘procedural safeguard’ capable of being imported under Article 21, as Article 21 does not confer an independent right to a proportionality assessment. The Supreme Court will have to look at how the safeguards in Article 21 should be applied.

Staying cases already in the tribunals

After the Court of Appeal’s judgment, the Upper Tribunal was reluctant to stay cases pending the outcome of the application to appeal to the Supreme Court. Now that permission has been granted, the tribunal appears more willing to stay cases where an appellant’s pre-Brexit residence, and the scope of any surviving EU law protections, form a substantial part of their case.

What difference might a positive outcome for the appellants make?

Some may be tempted to wonder what might change if the Supreme Court finds that decisions to deport EU nationals for post-Brexit conduct must comply with the EU principle of proportionality after all. The answer depends on whether the parties to the Withdrawal Agreement envisaged removing all consideration of a person’s historical integration in the UK under free movement law, and whether such integration is capable of reducing or outweighing the public interest in deportation.

The Supreme Court will now look at these arguments afresh in January 2027.

This article was co-authored by Julian Stern and William Shelley. Julian Stern represents Ms Vargova and Mr Molnar. William Shelley is a solicitor at Turpin Miller LLP. He is a member of the public law team and has been closely involved in the cases of Vargova and Molnar.

title: 'US is shooting itself in the foot': Expert on Trump's H-1B crackdown - Firstpost
description:
Talking to Firstpost, Prof. Yale-Loehr explained how the Trump administration is shrinking the H-1B visa programme, rather than bringing any monumental reforms.
So does the president actually have the legal authority to impose a $100,000 payment on H-1B visa holders and on H-1B visa employers without congressional approval?
The plaintiffs opposing the H-1B visa fee argue that only Congress can impose that kind of tax and that the president cannot do it unilaterally.
"Well, I think the H-1B visa fee increases have already been struck down by one court, and we'll see what happens.
But I think that the lower courts tend to be sympathetic to challenges to these immigration restrictions," he said.
text:
In the span of one and a half years, US President Donald Trump's administration introduced a major crackdown on immigration. Trump had promised to weed out illegal immigrants during his 2024 presidential campaign.

But what was concerning for many, as Stephen Yale-Loehr, who retired as the professor of immigration law practice at Cornell Law School, points out, was his attack on legal immigrants — more specifically those holding H-1B visas. From proposing a whopping $100,000 renewal fee to removing the 60-day grace period, the Trump administration's new visa regulations made many question the programme's future.

Talking to Firstpost, Prof. Yale-Loehr explained how the Trump administration is shrinking the H-1B visa programme, rather than bringing any monumental reforms. The retired immigration law professor also highlighted how some of the proposals are legally vulnerable and can be easily challenged in court.

What's the difference this time?

The fundamental difference between the Trump administration's current immigration policy and the one he introduced during his first term, Yale-Loehr said Trump is attacking "all aspects of immigration" this time.

"Trump's first administration primarily focused on tougher enforcement and going after people who are illegally in the United States. This administration is doing that, but also trying to restrict all immigration, legal and illegal. This administration is doing that, but also trying to restrict all immigration, legal and illegal," he told Firstpost.

"When it comes to business-related immigration, you see it from the very beginning to the very end. So, for example, if a student from India wants to get an F-1 visa to study in the United States, it's taking a lot longer, and there are more background checks, social media vetting, etc. So the denial rates for getting into the United States are higher."

"And if you're not from India, but from one of 75 other countries, they imposed visa bans for those countries, although recently a federal court struck that down as illegal," he said.

New challenges for students and professionals

The immigration law expert pointed out how, this time, there have been restrictions on "curricular practical training." "So maybe you're studying at Cornell in computer science, and you're offered an internship at Google for part-time. In the past, you could do that through curricular practical training. Now, however, the immigration agency is saying that they're only going to allow curricular practical training where the training is required for the major, not just that it's optional," he said.

Prof. Yale-Loehr also pointed out how, in recent times, there is a limit on how long a person can stay in the United States as well. "Previously, F-1 students got what's known as duration of status, meaning they could stay here as long as it took to get their degree. So if a degree took five years instead of four years, that was not a problem," he said.

"Now, the administration is saying that the duration-of-status concept is terminated and people are here only for fixed amounts of time. That too is being litigated, and we should get a decision on that by September 14th," he said. If the student manages to get through all the restrictions, he or she would face new challenges while acquiring H-1B visas.

"Visa fee increases, stricter vetting, taking longer to get H-1Bs. So it's harder to get an H-1B. And if you do that and your company sponsors you for a green card, the backlogs at immigration are longer than ever, with more background checks. I think I read something that the employment-based immigration backlog currently exceeds 1.2 million people," he said.

The situation before Trump returned to the White House

During the 2024 presidential race, the border crisis was a major issue among voters, with the then-Biden administration facing backlash over its handling of the situation. When asked whether Trump's immigration policies are coming as a solution to the problem or creating new issues.

Prof. Yale-Loehr admitted that under the Trump administration, there are fewer people trying to cross the border illegally. However, he maintained that "this is not going to solve the enforcement issue." "It's like a balloon. If people can't come in illegally one way, they'll try to come in illegally or legally another way," he said.

"Really, we need to have more work visas in the United States so that people can come in temporarily to work and then send money home to their relatives in Mexico or wherever. In addition, this administration has gone way beyond tackling illegal immigration and is restricting legal immigration in all different kinds of ways," he averred.

Citing a website that has been tracking all of the immigration restrictions, Prof. Yale-Loehr noted that "this administration has come up with over 760 immigration restrictions".

"So it's not just an attack on illegal immigration; it's an attack on all immigration," he remarked.

What is surprising this time?

From the very beginning, Trump has pledged to be hard on immigration. When asked why these actions are coming off as surprising even to his core supporters, Yale-Loehr reiterated how Trump initially pledged to go after illegal immigrants but is now being harsh on legal immigrants as well.

"Well, he was always saying and trying to go after illegal immigration, but he didn't really say anything about legal immigration, number one. And he had made some comments about, you know, wanting to keep people who are very bright in the United States, so people thought maybe he would not touch legal immigration or at least some aspects of legal immigration," he told Firstpost.

The second aspect, Yale-Loehr pointed out, is how his enforcement actions have gone too far in the eyes of many Americans. "Instead of going after the worst of the worst, meaning criminals, you know, there are regular people who have applied for asylum and not committed any crimes who have been picked up when they go to their immigration court hearings," he said.

"So people are upset that the enforcement efforts have gone too far. You may have read, for example, that even some US citizens have been killed protesting those immigration enforcement actions. So I think that he's gone too far, and we'll see what happens in the midterm elections," he added.

H-1B visas: Trying to reform the system or shrink the programme

When asked if Trump's policies are shrinking the H-1B programme or trying to bring reforms, Yale-Loehr said: "I think they're trying to shrink the programme. They claim that they're doing it to fight fraud, etc, but the way they're going after it with these proposed visa fee increases and the increased scrutiny makes it harder for everyone to get an H-1B visa, even if you're a perfectly valid employee and working for a Fortune 500 company."

On why the H-1B is being scrutinised more than other visas, Yale-Loehr noted that there has been more publicity surrounding the programme. "I think that there's been more publicity in the past about supposed H-1B abuses than, say, the L-1 intracompany transferee visa category, but it's also a very heavily used temporary work visa category," he explained.

"I think for both of those reasons, the focus has been on H-1Bs, but even people trying to come in temporarily on B visas are having a harder time. And recently, the administration said that someone who comes in on a B visa but overstays could be picked up and deported."

So does the president actually have the legal authority to impose a $100,000 payment on H-1B visa holders and on H-1B visa employers without congressional approval? The immigration law professor noted that there are two arguments on the issue.

"Well, that's the whole argument in the litigation. The plaintiffs opposing the H-1B visa fee argue that only Congress can impose that kind of tax and that the president cannot do it unilaterally. And so, so far, the courts have received and seemed receptive to that argument and said that the visa fee is not appropriate. But we'll see if the administration tries another way to impose a fee without calling it a fee," he remarked.

"One other thing I did not mention is that the immigration has recently proposed stopping spouses of H-1B workers from getting their own work permits. And that's a real hardship for people. You know, many spouses from India and other countries want to work in the United States, and they've been able to work, but the immigration agency wants to take that ability away," he asserted.

The legal saga

When asked which of the proposals are more vulnerable to legal challenges, the immigration law expert pointed to the H-1B visa fee increases. "Well, I think the H-1B visa fee increases have already been struck down by one court, and we'll see what happens. But I think that the lower courts tend to be sympathetic to challenges to these immigration restrictions," he said.

"But when cases get up to the US Supreme Court, the highest court in America, the US Supreme Court seems more sympathetic toward President Trump being able to do what he wants. So we have to see what happens at the US Supreme Court level."

With the US Congress failing to bring instrumental reforms in the country's immigration policies, one question that emerges is whether the judiciary has become the de facto policymaker. Professor Yale-Loehr agreed with the sentiment.

"The agencies are de facto immigration policymakers. Also, the courts are, because they are interpreting whether the agency actions are lawful or not. Congress has failed to reform our immigration system for over 30 years. And the world has changed significantly since then," he said.

"But our immigration system has not. So Congress should hold hearings and propose legislation to reform our immigration system. But the whole concept of immigration is very controversial. And therefore, Congress has been unwilling to tackle that complex and politically difficult issue," he told Firstpost.

'The US is shooting itself in the foot'

For years, Indians have been one of the major beneficiaries of H-1B visas. With Trump's latest restrictions, experts have warned that Indians and other bright minds could end up opting for other countries, affecting the American economy.

In response to this assertion, Prof. Yale-Loehr admitted that in this way the "United States is shooting itself in the foot by not allowing the best and the brightest to be able to come here to study or to work after they finish their studies."

"We're educating them at the best universities in the world, but then we're forcing them to go back home to start up their own companies there rather than in the United States. I think I recall one study that said that 40 per cent of all startups in the United States are founded by either immigrants or sons or daughters of immigrants," he explained.

"If we're forcing all those people to go back home to India or elsewhere, those startups are going to be in those countries, not in the US. So my final question to you is: putting border restrictions and being hard on immigration was one of the policies Trump stood up for during the campaign," he said.

Long-term ramifications

When asked if he sees long-term ramifications of Trump's stringent immigration policies, the immigration law expert noted that these restrictions would be hard to undo. "Trump had many immigration restrictions in his first administration, and it took all four years of the Biden administration to be able to undo most, but not all of those. And there's no way that a Democratic president in 2028 is going to be able to undo everything that Trump has put into place," he said.

"So this has a long-term effect on the US economy, on US culture, and on the status of the United States," he maintained, citing historical instances to support his assertion.

"The closest analogy I can think of is that back in 1924, the US Congress imposed major restrictions on immigration to the United States, and it took us over 20 years to sort of climb out of those restrictions and start to have a sensible immigration policy again," he said.

The Terms of CSC's Enforcement Scope Under the House Settlement The House settlement created an enforcement system to review certain NIL arrangements and ensure they comply with the settlement's rules.

text:
The legal architecture governing college sports' name, image, and likeness (NIL) economy continues to take shape. On August 4, a federal court issued a decision about who can be investigated under the enforcement system created by the House settlement and who gets to oversee those investigations.1 Judge Claudia Wilken of the US District Court for the Northern District of California ruled that certain companies that work with colleges and athletes cannot automatically be exempted from scrutiny under the settlement's NIL rules. In doing so, the court declined to overturn a special master's earlier decision refusing to categorically exclude multimedia rights companies and third-party brand sponsors from the definition of "Associated Entities or Individuals" under the House settlement's injunctive relief framework. At the same time, however, the court opened the door to further scrutiny of how the College Sports Commission (CSC) investigates those entities and affirmed class counsel's right to obtain information necessary to monitor compliance with the settlement.

The ruling does not decide whether any particular company violated the NIL rules. Instead, it addresses who may fall within the CSC enforcement framework and how challenges to that framework will be handled going forward. Specifically, the court made clear that the enforcement process itself remains subject to judicial oversight under the terms of the House settlement.

While the court's order does not resolve questions about the scope of CSC authority, it underscores a larger point: the next phase of NIL litigation may be less about whether CSC enforcement power exists and more about how CSC exercises that power.

The Terms of CSC's Enforcement Scope Under the House Settlement

The House settlement created an enforcement system to review certain NIL arrangements and ensure they comply with the settlement's rules. The College Sports Commission (CSC) is responsible for administering that system.

The settlement also discusses "Associated Entities or Individuals," which it defines as follows:

a. An entity that is or was known (or should have been known) to the athletics department staff of a Member Institution, to exist, in significant part, for the purpose of (1) promoting or supporting a particular Member Institution's intercollegiate athletics program or student-athletes; and/or (2) creating or identifying NIL opportunities solely for a particular Member Institution's student-athletes;

b. An individual who is or was a member, employee, director, officer, owner, or agent of an entity described in …(a) above;

c. An individual who directly or indirectly (including contributions by an affiliated entity or family member) has contributed more than $50,000 over their lifetime to a particular Member Institution or to an entity described in …(a) above;

d. An individual or entity that (1) has been directed or requested by a Member Institution's athletics department staff to assist in the recruitment or retention of prospective or current student-athletes, or (2) otherwise has assisted in the recruitment or retention of prospective or current student-athletes; or,

e. Any entity owned, controlled, or operated by, or otherwise affiliated with, the individuals or entities described in …(a)-(d) above other than a publicly traded corporation.

In the In re NIL Litigation decision, the dispute centered on two types of organizations:

Multimedia rights companies (MMRs): Companies that often manage a university's media, sponsorship, advertising, and related commercial rights.

Third-party brand sponsors: Businesses that enter into endorsement, marketing, sponsorship, or similar commercial deals involving college athletes.

The Special Master's Challenged Decision

The issue of whether all MMRs and third-party brand sponsors qualify as "Associated Entities or Individuals" gained prominence after CSC's recent scrutiny of certain NIL arrangements involving a university and its multimedia rights partner. The plaintiffs argued that MMRs and third-party sponsors should generally be treated as independent businesses rather than as entities associated with a university and therefore should not be subject to CSC review solely because of those relationships.

On June 25, the special master rejected the plaintiffs' request for a blanket ruling declaring that all MMRs and third-party brand sponsors are not "Associated Entities or Individuals." The Special Master concluded that neither MMRs nor brand sponsors could be universally excluded because the definition depends on the specific facts, including the nature of a company's relationship with a particular institution and its involvement in NIL activities.

The plaintiffs then filed objections to that ruling and requested that Judge Wilken: (1) reverse the special master's order; (2) order the CCS to stop investigating and regulating third-party NIL agreements with MMRs and third-party brand sponsors "absent a specific basis to do so"; and (3) order defendants2 to produce the documents and information concerning the CSC's investigations or, alternatively, remand to the special master.

Judge Wilken's Ruling

The court declined to reverse the special master's decision in any respect, effectively holding that there is no one-size-fits-all answer to whether an MMR or third-party sponsor qualifies as an associated entity under the settlement. Some third parties may fall within the definition and others may not, depending on their relationships, conduct, facts, and circumstances.

That finding is important because it rejects a bright-line rule that would have automatically excluded entire categories of companies from the settlement's enforcement framework. Instead, the court preserved a case-by-case analysis.

Notwithstanding the denial of the requested relief, the court did leave the door open for judicial review of this question in future cases by rejecting the defendants' argument that disputes regarding CSC investigations should be resolved in arbitration, rather holding that it has authority to hear challenges involving the interpretation and enforcement of the settlement itself.

The court did not decide whether any particular CSC investigative practice violates the settlement; because that issue had not first been presented to the Special Master, the court referred it back to the Special Master for further consideration.

The order also contains an important ruling on access to information. The court found that plaintiffs are entitled under the House settlement to request documents and information relating to CSC investigations when necessary to monitor and enforce compliance with the settlement's injunctive-relief provisions. Questions regarding the scope of those requests were likewise referred back to the special master.

Why the Decision Matters

Viewed narrowly, the ruling rejects any categorical line-drawing in construing whether a third-party falls within the definition of "Associated Entities or Individuals" and offers no guidance as to where the boundaries of that definition lie. Viewed more broadly, however, the ruling highlights a central challenge in the post-House era: determining if a purportedly independent NIL arrangement is truly independent.

The House settlement was designed to prevent third-party NIL deals from being used to circumvent compensation limits and recruiting restrictions on colleges that have opted into the settlement while still preserving legitimate third-party NIL opportunities. As Judge Wilken's refusal to adopt any categorical rule recognizes, drawing that line is often difficult.

MMRs illustrate the issue particularly well. Many MMRs maintain longstanding commercial relationships with universities, manage sponsorship assets, and help facilitate opportunities involving student-athletes. Because they may operate both as business partners of institutions and as participants in the NIL marketplace, their status under the House settlement is not always clear.

A narrow interpretation of "Associated Entities" could leave open opportunities to move compensation outside established regulatory controls. A broader interpretation could subject independent businesses to increased oversight and review. By declining to adopt a categorical rule, the court left those questions to be resolved through future fact-specific disputes.

The decision also signals two broader trends.

First, regulators are likely to focus on the substance of NIL relationships rather than the labels attached to them. Organizations with significant institutional connections may face scrutiny even if they characterize transactions as independent commercial arrangements. As a result, universities, MMRs, sponsors, and other participants in the college sports ecosystem may wish to periodically review NIL-related practices, governance structures, and institutional relationships with counsel to assess potential regulatory risk.

Second, the ruling suggests that the conduct of regulators will itself remain subject to judicial oversight. By allowing plaintiffs to challenge investigative practices and seek information about enforcement activities, the court indicated that the operation of the enforcement system may be reviewed alongside the transactions being investigated.

The practical consequence may be a dual layer of scrutiny: closer review of NIL transactions by regulators and closer review of those regulators' decisions by the courts.

For universities, conferences, MMRs, sponsors, and athletes, the immediate takeaway is that uncertainty persists. The order preserves the CSC's authority to investigate potential issues while also permitting continued challenges as to how that authority is exercised. It is another sign that the future of college sports governance will depend not only on the rules themselves, but also on how those rules are interpreted, enforced, and reviewed.

As the House settlement moves from theory to implementation, that distinction is likely to shape the next chapter of the NIL era.

As colleges, conferences, multimedia rights companies, sponsors, and other stakeholders navigate the evolving NIL landscape, proactive legal guidance is increasingly important. Steptoe's Sports Integrity Team closely monitors developments involving the House settlement, CSC enforcement activity, athlete compensation, and related litigation. We help clients assess NIL structures, evaluate institutional relationships, respond to regulatory inquiries and investigations, and develop compliance strategies that account for a rapidly changing legal environment. As courts, regulators, and industry participants continue to define the contours of NIL governance, Steptoe is positioned to help clients anticipate risk, adapt to new requirements, and pursue their business and athletic objectives with confidence.

text:
An immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation officer pleaded not guilty to six counts of making false statements to FBI investigators, according to the Department of Justice. A newly unsealed federal indictment alleged that Christian Castro lied about how events unfolded during an immigration operation that ended with a non-fatal shooting. The shooting took place during Homeland Security’s big immigration sweep in the Twin Cities area, dubbed Operation Metro Surge, earlier this year. Two other officer-involved shootings during that time resulted in the deaths of suspects.

According to the recent indictment, Castro attempted to stop a vehicle driven by a Venezuelan man who was in a vehicle. The pursuit led to Castro, age 52, tackling the much-younger suspect in the front yard of a duplex where the suspect lived. The two men wrestled on the ground while another duplex resident, Julio Sosa-Celis, came outside to help the Venezuelan wrestle free from Castro, the DOJ said. Sosa-Celis and the suspect then ran inside the duplex and were closing the door when Castro fired a shot that hit Sosa-Celis in the leg, according to the recent indictment.

What does the DOJ think he lied about? Castro earlier said that the two men assaulted him with a broom and a snow shovel, which prompted him to fire at the pair. The officer reported that a man came out of the duplex and began hitting him with a red broom while he tried to handcuff the suspect on the ground, according to the DOJ. Officer Castro also said that a third person exited the duplex and also began hitting Castro with a snow shovel from the front porch.

Castro at first said that he was on his back, taking a beating from three men, when he reached for his gun, according to federal authorities. He claimed to have sat up and fired one round in the men’s general direction as the two of them began running, according to the DOJ. Castro described a three-minute physical struggle with the men.

Federal officials initially charged Sosa-Celis and another individual with assault, but dropped the charges after video evidence called into question the accuracy of Castro’s account. No person struck Castro with a broom or shovel as alleged, and the entire physical altercation between the officer and the residents lasted about 11 seconds, according to the federal grand jury indictment.

authors: Eugene Volokh, Jacob Sullum, Naif Alrogi, J.D. Tuccille, Elizabeth Nolan Brown, Katarina Hall
description:
Upon seeing Moorman enter the parking lot, the ICE officers, who had just exited their vehicles, immediately re-entered their vehicles.
As Moorman proceeded to exit the parking lot, the ICE officers "looped around and followed [him]."
With the ICE officers following him, Moorman circled around the Cracker Barrel, another adjacent parking lot, and an adjacent dead-end road.
After a few minutes, Moorman and the ICE officers returned to the Cracker Barrel parking lot.
The ICE officers led Moorman toward a rural area on the outskirts of Springfield where Moorman and his wife live.
text:
The next morning, on August 21, 2026, Moorman stood on the side of a main road in Springfield alongside a reporter wearing a press badge, and recorded ICE officers conducting an arrest. An ICE officer wearing a yellow vest, identified as Defendant John Doe No. 1, approached Moorman and the reporter, put his phone in their faces as if to scan or take a picture, and then continued walking.

Later that day, Moorman entered the parking lot of a Cracker Barrel restaurant in Springfield to observe and photograph ICE officers after identifying [other] known ICE vehicles…. Upon seeing Moorman enter the parking lot, the ICE officers, who had just exited their vehicles, immediately re-entered their vehicles. Moorman observed Defendant John Doe No. 1 looking at him with binoculars.

The ICE officers then pulled out of their parking spots. As Moorman proceeded to exit the parking lot, the ICE officers "looped around and followed [him]." With the ICE officers following him, Moorman circled around the Cracker Barrel, another adjacent parking lot, and an adjacent dead-end road.

After a few minutes, Moorman and the ICE officers returned to the Cracker Barrel parking lot. Each time Moorman pulled into a parking spot, the ICE officers would pull in front of and block Moorman's vehicle and prevent him from moving out of his spot. The ICE officers would each block Moorman's vehicle for ten seconds at a time, sometimes taking photos of his license plate, before allowing him to move to another location in the parking lot. This happened for the next ten to fifteen minutes. Throughout this encounter, Moorman put his vehicle into park each time the ICE officers were in front of him and kept his hands on the steering wheel so that the officers could see them.

Moorman eventually was able to exit the Cracker Barrel parking lot but ended up on a dead-end road nearby. At that point, Moorman was approached by the Nissan Pathfinder driven by Defendant John Doe No. 3, who was masked and wearing large sunglasses. The officer waved at Moorman, apparently signaling Moorman to follow him; Moorman complied with the officer's direction.

As Moorman followed the Nissan Pathfinder, a Hyundai Sante Fe driven by Defendant John Doe No. 1, followed behind Moorman. The ICE officers led Moorman toward a rural area on the outskirts of Springfield where Moorman and his wife live. During oral argument, the AUSA offered no explanation for the ICE officers' leading Moorman back to his residence.

Upon realizing this, Moorman called other volunteer ICE watchers to warn them about the situation. He also called his wife, who was home alone with their pets, and told her that ICE officers were heading toward their home, and to lock the doors and stay inside. Moorman's wife cowered in the house holding a baseball bat out of fear.

The Nissan Pathfinder then pulled up to the end of Moorman's driveway and slowed. Defendant John Doe No. 3 put his arm out of the vehicle's window and pointed at Moorman's house. He took pictures of Moorman and his wife's vehicles. After this encounter, Moorman and his wife installed a security camera at their home and now keep their doors locked at all times.

ICE officers continued to engage with Moorman throughout the next several days. [Further details omitted for space reasons. -EV] …

The Court takes notice that national incidents similar to those described herein have devolved into circumstances leading to serious injury or loss of life to officers and members of the community alike….

Moorman seeks a TRO enjoining Defendants, and those acting in concert with them, from "taking further threatening, intimidating, and retaliatory action against [him] in response to his exercise of his First Amendment rights … without a legitimate law enforcement purpose." According to Moorman, such actions include, but are not limited to, pursuing his vehicle, attempting to box in his vehicle, approaching him, traveling to his home, or shouting at him to intimidate him, without a legitimate law enforcement purpose. While these events considered seriatim would be less concerning, when considering the allegations together, they amount to a substantial and troubling violation of Moorman's First Amendment rights….

First, Moorman engaged, and continues to engage, in protected conduct. Eight circuits have expressly held that filming government agents performing official duties in public is protected under the First Amendment. Other courts in this district have also recognized this right….

While some courts have imposed reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions on an individual's right to record law enforcement, the record shows that Moorman conducts his ICE watching activities in a safe and lawful manner; he records ICE activity only while in public spaces, takes precautions to make sure he is not threatening officers' safety such as keeping his hands visible, follows applicable traffic laws, and does not interfere with ICE's enforcement operations. Moorman has also participated in specific training for individuals who wish to monitor law enforcement activity in a safe, lawful, and peaceful manner.

Second, Moorman has suffered adverse action(s). An adverse action is one that "would deter a person of ordinary firmness from continuing to engage in" protected conduct under the First Amendment….

While some retaliatory acts are so de minimis that "they do not rise to the level of being constitutional violations," Defendants' actions in this case surpass that threshold…. Moorman asserts that Defendants, over the course of several days, nearly swerved into his vehicle; scouted Moorman's home for no legitimate purpose (on multiple occasions) causing Moorman's wife to fear for her safety; continuously stalked Moorman around Springfield; and cut off and trapped Moorman's vehicle in a parking lot. At minimum, ICE officers seized Moorman in the Cracker Barrel parking lot on August 21, 2026, see U.S. v. See (6th Cir. 2009) (noting that blocking a person's car with a patrol car was a warrantless seizure), thus constituting adverse action. See Wood v. Eubanks (6th Cir. 2022) (holding that a Fourth Amendment seizure amounts to an adverse action for the purpose of a First Amendment retaliation claim).

Finally, Moorman has demonstrated a causal connection between his protected conduct and the adverse actions allegedly perpetrated by Defendants…. Defendants remain free at a later stage to show that they would have taken the same action regardless of Moorman's protected conduct. However, at this time, nothing in the record supports that showing, and Moorman need only demonstrate a likelihood of success, not a certainty.

Here, Defendants cannot identify a single, legitimate basis for continuing to harass and intimidate Moorman for exercising his First Amendment rights. Defendants, and others acting in concert with them, including all other ICE officers stationed in Springfield, Ohio, will suffer no cognizable harm from a TRO that does no more than require them to comply with the Constitution they are already bound, and have sworn, to follow. Moreover, it is always in the public interest to enjoin unconstitutional conduct.

Moorman's proposed TRO is limited in scope; it requests that Defendants refrain from harassing and committing retaliatory acts—including pursuing his vehicle, approaching him, photographing him in a threatening manner, traveling to his home, or shouting at him for the purposes of intimidation—without a legitimate law enforcement purpose.

To that end, two items merit mention. First, the Court is not telling ICE— part of the executive branch—how to do its job.

Second, the Court is not entering into the political fray to suggest whether or not ICE should be engaging in deportation activities in Springfield, Ohio.

What the Court is holding is that, when government actors engage in such conduct, the Constitution requires that it be undertaken without hazing, retaliation, or harassment, particularly with regard to an individual who does not interfere with ICE's enforcement function or police power. As Justice [Gorsuch] aptly said, the "Government is not free to disregard the First Amendment in times of crisis." Roman Catholic v. Diocese of Brooklyn v. Cuomo (2020) (Gorsuch, J.) (concurring) ….

title: A young immigrant's death compounds Springfield group's grief and resolve amid ICE enforcement
description:
For months, Springfield Neighbors United has hosted a monthly vigil to show support for the city’s Haitian immigrants.
Since the end of July, ICE has been sending letters to many of Springfield’s Haitian immigrants, requiring them to report to either their Westerville or Blue Ash offices.
They are urging national politicians to end the GPS ankle monitor program.
During Friday’s vigil, attendees sang, repeated the names of Haitian immigrants who have been removed by ICE agents , lit candles and prayed.
At the same time, Joseph believes ankle monitors are not reflective of the ideals that attract immigrants to the United States.
text:
The tail end of a late summer storm rumbled across Springfield. Gusty winds quieted into an easy breeze, fewer rain drops fall and temperamental dark clouds lumber across the early evening sky, giving way to sunshine.

As if on cue, a medley of people gathered in Fountain Square across from the Marriott Hotel on Sept. 4. Quickly they filled the tiny space and spilled onto the grass leading to it.

For months, Springfield Neighbors United has hosted a monthly vigil to show support for the city’s Haitian immigrants.

"We do this in solidarity with people who are being deported and detained and disappeared by ice across the country," said the Rev. Michelle Boomgaard, a member of Springfield Neighbors United.

She said Friday’s vigil took on a more poignant feeling as many in attendance held handmade signs featuring a large red heart. Underneath, the name Pierre Damas Bel was spelled out. He’s a 20-year-old Haitian immigrant who died in a suspected suicide on Aug. 31, soon after ICE agents required Bel to wear a GPS ankle monitor in lieu of being detained. In a released statement, the Department of Homeland Security said it is not responsible for his death.

Susan Harrison was at the vigil and defiantly waved her sign.

"They're having to wear ankle monitors, which is tracking them for mass deportation and the fact somebody felt so distraught by it that they committed suicide by walking into the freeway,” Harrison said. “I think it's really important that we all stand together. These people have been part of the community, brought back vibrancy to Springfield."

Since the end of July, ICE has been sending letters to many of Springfield’s Haitian immigrants, requiring them to report to either their Westerville or Blue Ash offices. There they are interviewed, their immigration papers are reviewed and they can choose between wearing a GPS monitor or being immediately detained.

Many are comparing them to the shackles used during slavery. Because of this sentiment, local faith and community leaders are promoting a new campaign "‘Unshackle Springfield." They are urging national politicians to end the GPS ankle monitor program.

Marc Joseph, a Haitian community activist, said more and more of his clients are complaining about the monitors. He said one woman is in her 60s, has the monitor on her left leg, and he said a doctor’s report found she’s developed edema and psoriasis.

"Seeing an old woman like that in pain, she couldn't even walk that day. I felt destroyed inside of me when I saw her," Joseph said.

Joseph said the woman's physician recommended the monitor be removed and they gave the paperwork to ICE agents in Blue Ash, but he said ICE would not remove it.

During Friday’s vigil, attendees sang, repeated the names of Haitian immigrants who have been removed by ICE agents , lit candles and prayed.

Pastor Bernadette Dominique said the public support sends an encouraging message to her people and gives them hope.

"It means we are not alone,” Dominique said.

The evening sun bathed Fountain Square in a warm glow. Participants hugged, laughed and gradually dispersed.

Joseph said he and his countrymen are holding fast to their faith, they believe God will provide a pathway to safety despite the current actions by the Department of Homeland Security. At the same time, Joseph believes ankle monitors are not reflective of the ideals that attract immigrants to the United States.

Headlines Monday, September 7, 2026

Students walk out of school to protest ICE

Boulder Valley high school students joined students from more than 200 Colorado schools in a demonstration against federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, or ICE.

The students walked out of classrooms on Friday, in order to send a message of opposition to ICE tactics, which they characterized as needlessly brutal.

The walkout was organized by several student groups, including the Colorado Youth Coalition.

In Boulder County, students from Boulder High, New Vista, Centaurus, and Monarch high schools joined the “ICE Out” demonstrations. Students in Denver and St. Vrain Valley also took part in demonstrations around the metro area.

In a letter to parents, a BVSD spokesperson said that while the district encourages students to stay in school, they also support their right to demonstrate.

One of the student gatherings was near the band shell in Boulder Creek Park. Students told KGNU that everyone has a right to be safe in Boulder, regardless of their immigration status.

“ I’m here to stand up for the people who can’t stand up for themselves. There are people who are being harmed and there are horrible things happening with ICE and it needs to stop,” said one student. “I don’t care if people are undocumented. I care that people are safe,” said another.

ICE agents arrested more than three thousand people in Colorado alone during 2025, according to the Deportation Data Project.

READ MORE

READ MORE

Federal wildfire aid approved

President Trump approved federal aid for Colorado counties damaged from the Gold Mountain and Aspen Acres wildfires.

The fires burned hundreds of homes and over 140,000 total acres.

A statement from Governor Polis celebrated federal funds being used for debris removal and to rebuild communities – calling back to the Marshall fire.

“Removing debris from homes and buildings destroyed is the most important step to begin rebuilding, and now, that work can occur promptly and at no cost to homeowners, just as it did after the Marshall Fire.”

The request from Governor Polis for federal funds was first made August 23.

While these funds from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) have been cleared, two more state requests for disaster assistance are under review.

KGNU has previously reported that these funds were not guaranteed; the Trump administration denied FEMA funding last year after the Elk and Lee fires destroyed Western areas of the state.

READ MORE

READ MORE

Adams school district may close six schools

Adams 12 Five Star Schools recommend the district board of education close six schools to save $5 million annually. The plan was announced this past Thursday and will be voted on by the district October 7.

The schools recommended for closure are: North Mor Elementary, Rocky Mountain Elementary, Centennial Elementary, Cherry Drive Elementary, The Studio School, and Shadow Ridge Middle School.

If the district votes to approve the closures, the schools would close at the end of the 2026-27 academic year. In a press release, Adams 12 said they’ll work to retain their staff despite the recommendation.

For a list of where students would attend if the school they attend now were to close, visit adams12.org/newsroom.

READ MORE

Trussell family wants independent investigation after CBI affirms county response

Colorado’s Bureau of Investigations decided that Boulder County’s initial response to investigating the death of CU Student Megan Trussell was QUOTE, “reasonable, substantial and supported by the available evidence.”

A 40-person review team of CBI-appointed investigators affirmed Boulder County’s assessment of Trussell’s death.

Trussell was last seen February 9 of last year. She was found in rough terrain in Boulder Canyon. Boulder County said her cause of death was a suicide due to the toxic effects of amphetamines and hypothermia.

CBI also affirmed Boulder’s response and investigation were sound. Trussell’s family was not convinced of the CBI investigation’s legitimacy. A statement from the family says CBI did not know basic facts about the case when the bureau approached the family with news of their review.

CBI started their review of the case in January after Trussell’s parents requested the review under a 2022 law that requires the state to review certain types of cases involving Indigenous people.

Trussell’s family says they’re still trying to receive a complete autopsy report and photographs.

They’re also trying to get an independent review from an entity who is not connected to entities that have already reached conclusions about their daughter’s case.

ICE has signed a $16.7 million contract with a Kentucky company for thousands of them. They cost $2,495 apiece and can deliver up to 380 volts through direct contact with a person's skin. DHS said Cornelio Estrada-Gonzalez got out of the car Osman was driving and ran from officers before he was caught following a brief foot chase.

Cox walked through the city, stopping at two locations that have recently experienced criminal activity. Cox used the visit to highlight what he described as Gov. Wes Moore’s failure to address Baltimore’s challenges. “Baltimore City was left behind – and Wes Moore, where is he?” Cox said. Cassidie Stevens/WBFF-News.

BALTIMORE COULD END YEAR WITH LOWEST HOMICIDE RATE IN 50 YEARS: Baltimore is on pace to record fewer homicides this year than it did during its record-low 2025 — and could finish 2026 with its lowest homicide rate in nearly five decades, according to a Baltimore Sun analysis of census and police department data. Adam Bednar/The Baltimore Sun.

WHAT THIRD PARTY CANDIDATES MADE IT ON THE BALLOT? Sam Husseini’s name will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot as a Green Party candidate for Maryland’s 4th District seat in Congress, after state election officials certified his candidacy this week. It wasn’t easy. Like the handful of other third-party candidates whose candidacies were accepted Monday, Husseini had to overcome a “huge hurdle” to get on the general election ballot, that candidates in the two major parties don’t have to deal with. And he will continue to deal with challenges that include limited campaign funds, lack of exposure and scant party support. Pera Onal/Maryland Matters.

CROWD SUPPORTS BETHESDA OLYMPIAN IN REFLECTING POOL INCIDENT: Chants of “Trumped up charges!” and “Free Davey Hearn!” filled the air outside a courthouse in Washington, D.C., on Friday afternoon, where dozens of people gathered to support the Bethesda resident and former U.S. Olympic canoeist who the federal government accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. The rally was in advance of a hearing that day in which Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman listened to arguments about whether Hearn’s charges should be dismissed with or without prejudice. Ceoli Jacoby/Bethesda Today.

BA CO CROWD TO PLANNERS: NIX LARGE DATA CENTERS: An overflow crowd sent the Baltimore County Planning Board a clear message Thursday night: They don’t want large data centers in the county. The board is considering a proposed plan on how the county should regulate data centers. Before the hearing about three dozen protesters gathered outside the board’s office. John Lee/WYPR-FM.

STATE ORDERS CHANGE TO HISTORIC SITE SUBLEASING POLICY: The nonprofit preserving Maryland’s oldest mill village and the Maryland Department of Natural Resources have maintained a unique stewardship agreement over the property for decades. Now, the DNR says The Friends of Jerusalem Mill must stop subleasing state-owned housing to private, unvetted residents, in keeping with an updated state policy that enforces stricter controls for who can live in publicly owned properties. Luke Kaiser/The Baltimore Sun.

Over the past 40 years, the volunteer-run nonprofit has restored the miller’s house, the mansion, the general store, the blacksmith shop and one of Maryland’s last operational covered bridges. On weekend afternoons year-round, the organization’s volunteers dress in period attire and demonstrate to visitors what life was like during that early industrial era. Olivia Bensimon/The Baltimore Banner.

FREDERICK CITY CRIME DOWN 17%: Crime within the city of Frederick is down 17% in July when compared to the same time last year. That’s according to Mayor Michael O’Connor, who announced it during his state of the city address Wednesday. Nathanael Miller/WYPR-FM.

title: Far-right AfD win signals shift in Germany, raises alarm in Europe | PBS News
authors: Liz Landers, Dan Sagalyn, Sonia Kopelev
description:
Liz Landers: In Germany, a dawn of a more divisive era of domestic politics.
Liz Landers: Germany's political system is positioned that each state is largely autonomous, much more reliant on the state's Parliament than the federal level in Berlin.
Liz Landers: Meanwhile, in the United States, President Donald Trump shared the news of the AfD's victory in a social media post.
Liz Landers: This news, of course, over the weekend, I think has shocked some people around the world.
Liz Landers: Liana Fix, thank you for your expertise.
text:
Amna Nawaz:

Germany's far right AfD, or Alternative for Germany party, yesterday won a major parliamentary election victory in the Eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

The blow -- the win, rather, is a blow to chancellor Friedrich Merz, mired with record low approval ratings. And it marks a growing divide in German politics. The AfD party is anti-immigration. It's been labeled as xenophobic and as extremist by German intelligence.

Liz Landers reports.

Liz Landers:

In Germany, a dawn of a more divisive era of domestic politics. Germany's far right Alternative for Germany Party, or AfD, won 44 percent of seats yesterday, just three seats short of a majority in the Eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

The party has vowed to crack down on immigration and broaden its power to the national level.

Alice Weidel, Leader, AfD Party (through interpreter):

And if we assume responsibility for government in Germany at the national level, we will close the borders, and only those who have a legal right to reside in Germany will be allowed to come here. We will deport those who commit crimes here and those who are residing in this country illegally.

Liz Landers:

And if it is able to successfully form a parliamentary coalition with other parties in order to govern, it would have extensive control over the state's domestic immigration, education, and other policies.

AfD's anti-immigration stance has bled into its leaders' statements, which have been accused of being Islamophobic, antisemitic, and antidemocratic. Last year, the German intelligence agency labeled AfD extremist.

AfD's win in the state is a turn in the state's politics. Saxony-Anhalt, once part of East Germany prior to reunification, voted for the ruling Christian Democratic Union, or CDU, in its last parliamentary election.

Yesterday's win also a reflection of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's plunging approval ratings, with an 87 percent disapproval rating in Saxony-Anhalt and just 16 percent approval nationwide as of July. He faces stiff competition. Today, he acknowledged his party's loss.

Friedrich Merz, German Chancellor (through interpreter):

We are all deeply shocked. We did not expect this to happen in this way. Yesterday marked a turning point, not only in Saxony-Anhalt, but throughout Germany. I must admit, this is the most serious election defeat that the CDU has had for years, for decades.

Liz Landers:

Germany's political system is positioned that each state is largely autonomous, much more reliant on the state's Parliament than the federal level in Berlin. The far right party's win also renewed concerns internationally.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez today decried the win as an indicator of Europe's destabilization.

Pedro Sanchez, Spanish Prime Minister (through interpreter):

What we saw yesterday in Saxony is a warning and also a confirmation, a warning that the far right threat, thanks in large part to the surrender of the traditional right, is gaining ground in Europe and in the world.

Liz Landers:

Meanwhile, in the United States, President Donald Trump shared the news of the AfD's victory in a social media post. Last year, Vice President J.D. Vance shocked many when he appeared alongside AfD's leadership and chastised the German government's decades-old position of refusing to work with parties labeled extremist.

For perspective on the outcome of the election in Germany, we turn to Liana Fix, senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and author of "Germany Rearmed: The Return of War and the End of Illusions."

Liana, thank you for joining the "News Hour."

Liana Fix, Council on Foreign Relations: Absolutely. Thank you for the invitation.

Liz Landers:

How do you explain why the AfD did so well in the election?

Liana Fix:

So one popular explanation is that in East Germany and East Germans, in particular since unification, have felt economically deprived, that they are not on the same living standards as their West German compatriots.

But that explanation really only goes so far. It is primarily about the self-perception, about the feeling of being left behind, because East Germany really has caught up in the economic situation.

And at the same time, it is mixed with a profound sense that immigration policies have gone too far in Germany, and a general shock about all the change that is happening in Germany these days, both the Russia shock, also the A.I. shock, the China shock to Germany's industry.

It's a challenging time to be a chancellor of Germany.

Liz Landers:

What are some of the policies that AfD advocates for?

Liana Fix:

So, the federal level, the AfD in general is very anti-immigration. They want to deport both refugees, but also asylum seekers from other parts of Europe and the world. They are very much in favor of a very strict rule of law, but they also, especially in education, for example, in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD has proposed to focus more on the centuries before the Nazi era, and not to place too much emphasis on the Nazi era.

They also have some ideas about kicking out public broadcasters from Saxony-Anhalt. Overall, it is a very disruptive agenda. And, at foreign policy, they do want closer ties with Russia and China.

Liz Landers:

This news, of course, over the weekend, I think has shocked some people around the world. But how likely is it that the AfD will actually come to power?

Liana Fix:

So this is Saxony-Anhalt. It is a small East German state, but it is relevant because, for the first time, the firewall the German parties have built against the AfD, no one should work or enter into a coalition with the AfD, is really crumbling, because in this case you would need all the other five parties, from conservatives to very left-wing parties, to build a coalition only to prevent the AfD getting into power.

So that's why this election is so powerful. It's such a danger to Chancellor Friedrich Merz, because it is about the future direction of the Conservative Party in Europe and partly also about his own future.

On the federal level, this -- the AfD is polling as the strongest party ahead of Friedrich Merz's Conservative Party, and quite comfortably ahead. But it's very unlikely that this would translate in the next election into a government responsibility for the AfD. However, 10 years down the road, that picture might look different.

Liz Landers:

Speaking of 10 years down the road, is this election seen as a bellwether and signal for how future elections are likely to go in Germany?

Liana Fix:

It absolutely is.

And the next elections are already coming up at the end of September in two weeks' time. There will be two more elections in the state of Berlin, but also in another East German region. They are not as dramatic as in Saxony-Anhalt. So the AfD is not as far ahead as it has been in this election.

But, still, further setbacks for Friedrich Merz, for Chancellor Friedrich Merz, in these elections might actually raise the leadership question in Germany, and that at a time when Russian hybrid warfare campaigns are escalating against Germany. So it is really very much a twin threat that Chancellor Merz is facing here.

Liz Landers:

The AfD is pro-Russian. Will this election result have an impact on Germany's support for Ukraine and its efforts to shield itself from these Russian hybrid attacks?

Liana Fix:

No, they will not directly, because foreign policy, security policy are obviously a federal issue that cannot be disrupted by Saxony-Anhalt.

But there are some concerns, for example, that, if the AfD gets into power, Saxony-Anhalt should not be included in sensitive intelligence sharing anymore because of the concern that intelligence might be leaked to extremists or to Russia. There are also concerns that, what if the AfD gets in power on Saxony-Anhalt and tries to prevent any mobilization efforts of the German army, of the Bundeswehr in that country?

So these are actual considerations. And then, of course, Germany's European neighbors, from Poland to France, are very concerned. They welcome Germany's rearmament, Germany's historic rearmament, that it is going through now.

But, as I argue in my book, of course, they don't want to see that military power in the hands of the AfD. Even if that is only a possibility like 10 years or 15 years down the line, it is still a very scary thought for Germany's neighbors.

Liz Landers:

Liana Fix, thank you for your expertise.

Liana Fix:

Thank you.
