The Trump administration is ratcheting up its fight to get more crude flowing through California and reverse the state’s efforts to move away from fossil fuels.

Its latest salvo is a federal review of California’s coastal management program, which is run largely by a state commission that has had a powerful role for decades in shaping development along the coast. Environmental advocates fear federal officials could use the review to strip the California Coastal Commission of its ability to have a say in projects involving federal agencies that affect the state’s rugged coastal bluffs, pristine beaches and world-class surfing spots.

The administration, citing a need for energy security and job creation, has already announced plans for new offshore oil leases in California as well as Florida, where the federal government has not allowed drilling since 1995 because of concerns about oil spills in the Gulf of Mexico.

Trump officials also helped a Texas firm jump-start an old pipeline system that had been idled since its 2015 rupture caused one of California’s worst oil spills, blackening beaches for 150 miles (240 kilometers) from Santa Barbara to Los Angeles and polluting habitat for endangered whales and sea turtles. Federal officials also recently took a step toward authorizing fracking on an old oil platform 9 miles (14 kilometers) off Ventura County — a move opposed by the state’s coastal commission.

“It’s just part of that overall belief that they have, that they’re going to get rid of renewables and go back to good old-fashioned fossil fuels, and what better place to start than California?” said Deborah A. Sivas, a professor of environmental law at Stanford Law School. “We’re the feds — we’re going to tell the state what to do.”

California has some working offshore rigs, but there has been no new oil leasing in federal waters since the mid-1980s and no new state leasing for even longer. The state barred new offshore oil leases after a catastrophic spill in 1969 spewed between 3.5 million and 4.2 million gallons of crude into the Santa Barbara Channel. The disaster killed thousands of seabirds and helped give rise to the modern environmental movement.

California now uses so much solar and wind energy that nearly half the state’s electricity came from renewable resources in 2024, according to the state’s energy commission. That’s also the source of a fight with the Trump administration. Last week, state officials sued the federal government over its buyback of an offshore wind lease aimed at discouraging the expansion of wind energy in favor of fossil fuels.

California has also tried to wean residents off gas-powered cars — another push opposed by the Trump administration.

California’s coastal commission is the latest target

California’s coastal commission, an independent agency with appointed members, was formed in 1972. It has often been in the spotlight for taking up high-profile projects on the state’s tourism-dependent coast. The panel voted against but later approved a U2 guitarist’s plan for mansions on seaside bluffs, though the building proposal was eventually nixed by a court. It also rejected a proposed desalination plant to create drinking water in Huntington Beach.

The commission also has a say in federal projects along California’s coast, in line with a 1972 federal coastal management law. More than 30 states have similar programs to protect their coastal resources and all are subject to periodic federal evaluation.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announced the unexpected review of California’s program in May while denouncing the commission’s opposition to an expanded launch schedule for SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rockets from Vandenberg Space Force Base. Commissioners cited concerns that more launches could harm sensitive species and limit public access to the coast.

“Obstructionist policies that delay critical national infrastructure in the name of environmental extremism are unacceptable,” Lutnick said. He said the review will examine how California has addressed federal priorities on spaceport infrastructure, offshore oil production, pipeline maintenance and desalination projects.

Targeting California raises a fight that could reverberate nationwide, experts say. Until now, no state with a coastal program has been stripped of its authority to review federal projects. Many Californians who spoke at an hourslong public hearing in Santa Monica in August said they don’t want their state to be the first.

“This isn’t about performance. This is about power,” said Maureen Ellenberger, a Santa Barbara resident who is upset about the decision to let Houston-based Sable Offshore Corp. resume pumping through the old pipeline. “It’s about whether the Trump administration can strip California’s authority because they don’t like the answers the coastal commission gave to oil companies.”

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is carrying out the review. It isn’t known when it will be completed.

The commission isn’t new to controversy

In the past, California’s coastal commission has clashed with elected officials from both political parties. Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom rushed to the commission’s defense this year, but in 2025 suspended its permitting requirements for home rebuilding following the devastating Los Angeles area wildfires.

Trump’s battles with the commission began before his first term when he put up a 70-foot (21-meter) flagpole on his golf club in Rancho Palos Verdes. The commission ultimately allowed for it after a lengthy battle.

Last month, the commission unanimously voted to oppose the plan for fracking on a 45-year-old platform in federal waters off Ventura County after a lengthy public hearing. The federal Bureau of Ocean Energy Management released an environmental analysis for the proposal, which energy company DCOR said would more than triple daily oil output in 16 wells from 1,100 barrels to 4,000 barrels.

“This is just simply one of those cases where the juice isn’t worth the squeeze,” Coastal Commissioner Ray Jackson said during a hearing on DCOR LLC’s plan. “It creates far too many opportunities for something to go wrong. When something does go wrong it is our ocean, beaches, wildlife and coastal economy that pay the price.”

The company said it’s evaluating whether to appeal to the commerce secretary.

(NewsNation) — A major illegal gambling and drug investigation in Memphis recently ended with 121 immigration arrests, but authorities had a specific target.

Court records show the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation contacted U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement back in May for help identifying Marco Sabillon-Urbina — a Honduran national suspected of criminal activity at the El Corralon nightclub.

Sabillon-Urbina was among those arrested when ICE carried out “Operation Corral Light” in Memphis on Aug. 30 and is now in U.S. Marshals custody.

State and federal authorities executed warrants at El Corralon as part of an investigation into suspected illegal gambling and drug activity. TBI said agents seized narcotics and evidence of illegal gambling.

The Department of Homeland Security says Sabillon-Urbina had previously been ordered removed from the U.S., was deported in 2024 and later re-entered the country illegally.

A DHS spokesperson said Sabillon-Urbina had been convicted of three counts of firearm possession and charged with unlawful use of a controlled substance and a traffic offense.

But ICE’s involvement went well beyond one man, with agents arresting 121 people in all during the operation. DHS said those arrested were in the country illegally and highlighted several who had criminal histories.

DHS has publicly identified five of those arrested with criminal histories, including larceny, drug possession, domestic violence, DWI, assault, child endangerment and prostitution.

“It’s really interesting that the Department of Homeland Security has decided to release the names of five people who have criminal backgrounds, but no criminal charges for anything that actually happened that night,” said Maria Oceja, co-founder of Vecindarios 901, a Memphis rapid response network that monitors ICE activity. She called the agency’s framing “misleading.”

Authorities have not said all 121 arrested were involved in the alleged gambling or drug activity.

Memphis Mayor Paul Young says city police did not plan or carry out the operation and were only called in to help with traffic and crowd control.

“The people impacted by what happened this morning are our neighbors,” Young said. “They are part of our Memphis community, and they deserve to be treated with dignity.”

The criminal investigation into the nightclub is ongoing.

Sabillon-Urbina was well known to federal authorities. He first came to the U.S. from Honduras in the 1990s and the New York Times reports that he was later granted Temporary Protected Status.

But court records show that status eventually lapsed.

text:
UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, reiterates its concerns regarding continued restrictions on access to asylum in Hungary while welcoming the Government's commitment to review the country's asylum framework and related legislation.

The Agency notes the recent decision of the Government of Hungary to extend, until the end of 2026, the decree authorizing the police to automatically and summarily remove people intercepted for irregular entry or stay, including those who apply for international protection.

UNHCR recognizes States' legitimate interest in ensuring effective border management and addressing irregular movements. However, the Agency remains seriously concerned that the current framework continues to prevent many people who may be in need of international protection from accessing asylum procedures in Hungary. UNHCR has consistently raised concerns about these measures since the introduction of the decree on the "crisis situation caused by mass immigration" a decade ago, in 2016.

Of particular concern is the continued use of measures allowing the summary removal of people intercepted for irregular entry or stay, as well as the requirement for asylum-seekers to initiate the asylum process through Hungarian Embassies in Serbia or Ukraine. UNHCR considers that these measures significantly limit access to asylum and the right to seek asylum. They are also inconsistent with the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning anyone to a place where they would face danger due to conflict, persecution, or serious violations of human rights.

At the same time, UNHCR appreciates Hungary's continued solidarity with refugees fleeing the war in Ukraine and encourages the application of the same principles of protection and access to asylum to all persons seeking safety, irrespective of their country of origin.

UNHCR welcomes the Government's commitment to review the relevant legislation in the coming weeks. The Agency urges the Government of Hungary to establish a sustainable framework, through a transparent and consultative process, that balances effective border management with access to asylum and is fully aligned with Hungary's obligations under international and European law.

UNHCR looks forward to engaging constructively with the Government of Hungary and stands ready, in line with its mandate and expertise, to provide technical support throughout the legislative review process and in efforts to ensure access to asylum procedures in line with international refugee and human rights law.

text:
ICE agents and protestors clashed over the weekend in Frederick where federal officers were staking out a neighborhood.

Witnesses say the agents tried to run people over with an SUV, putting protestors in danger.

The protestors gathered at a neighborhood near the Golden Mile Friday evening after ICE agents had been spotted in the area for nearly two days.

According to witnesses, protestors were there to collect evidence and observe the agents.

Ceasar Diaz, president of the Frederick City Council was at the gathering.

“They actually drove their car onto the sidewalk and started driving their vehicles towards the peaceful observers, literally using their SUV to clear the sidewalk,” Diaz said. “To me, that's attempted murder. That is not how law enforcement is supposed to work in this country.”

Tatiana Santos is a member of Indivisible Frederick Forward, an ICE watchdog group.

“They just wanted peaceful observers out there who were able to document and witness what was happening,” Santos said. Some folks were beaten with objects, batons and punched.”

ICE started becoming aggressive around 9:30 p.m. when ICE agents started moving toward protestors sitting in front of a home and entered it.

No arrests were made.

The incident comes as ICE has been increasing enforcement in the area through “Operation Community Safe.” More than 1,300 people in Maryland and Virginia were arrested over the first two weeks of August. Few had a criminal history.

The Frederick Police were called to de-escalate the situation, and ICE eventually left the scene.

WYPR reached out to ICE for comment, but the agency was unable to attribute any comments to an actual person who worked there.

title: An Afghan man helped the U.S. fight the Taliban. ICE took him on terrorism allegations - STLPR
description:
An Afghan man spent years helping the U.S. military fight the Taliban, then made a new life legally in St. Louis County.
The Afghan man, who holds a green card, has been in the United States legally since 2014.
“Due to allegations of terrorist activity and seeking admission by fraud, [the Afghan man] has been placed in removal proceedings and will remain in ICE custody.
When asked about the warrant, the Afghan man told STLPR he wasn’t familiar with the allegations.
The Afghan man told STLPR he believes his arrest may be tied to his attendance at a 2016 anti-Trump protest in downtown St. Louis.
text:
An Afghan man spent years helping the U.S. military fight the Taliban, then made a new life legally in St. Louis County. Now, he’s in custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and facing deportation proceedings on allegations he aided a terrorist organization.

St. Louis Public Radio is not using the man’s name because he said he fears the Taliban would kill him and family still in Afghanistan for working against the group, notably for assisting the U.S. military during Operation Enduring Freedom — a global counterterrorism operation launched after the Sept. 11 attacks that took place 25 years ago this week. The man, now in his 30s, was a child when the towers fell.

The Afghan man, who holds a green card, has been in the United States legally since 2014. He entered through the State Department’s now-sunsetting Special Immigrant Visa program — an effort to bring Afghans employed under U.S. contracts to the United States.

Since then he’s built a life in the St. Louis area, marrying and having children — the youngest born just weeks ago — and earning several degrees. He works as a scientist and was hoping to one day become a medical doctor. The U.S. government appears to have been building a case against him since at least 2021, according to a federal search warrant issued for a hard drive. The warrant includes allegations linking him to a group associated with al-Qaida.

He maintains his innocence, telling St. Louis Public Radio from the Ste. Genevieve County Detention Center that his rights as a permanent resident are being violated.

“The burden of proof is on them. They should prove it beyond a reasonable doubt and give me a fair chance — the constitutionally guaranteed right to a jury trial,” he said when reached by phone on Monday. “They have unconstitutionally imprisoned me and took that right away from me.”

ICE arrests across the country have surged over the summer, setting a record high of nearly 50,000 arrests in July, according to data provided by ICE to the Deportation Data Project at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA. The wave of arrests follows Congress approving billions in immigration enforcement funding in June. In Missouri alone, federal data shows, deportations have nearly tripled.

ICE contends the man provided “material support to a terrorist organization” and “willfully misrepresented a fact” on his May 2019 naturalization application, according to a Sept. 2 statement to STLPR. The immigration agency, as well as the FBI, did not respond to STLPR’s follow-up questions about the specific accusations.

“Due to allegations of terrorist activity and seeking admission by fraud, [the Afghan man] has been placed in removal proceedings and will remain in ICE custody. He will receive due process,” the ICE statement continued. “Possessing a green card is a privilege, not a right. Under our nation’s laws, our government has the authority to revoke a green card if our laws are broken and abused.”

Cata Estrada, the Afghan man’s 36-year-old wife — who gave permission for her name to be used — said the government gave her husband more than 100 pages of allegations on Sept. 1 related to a 2018 trip to Afghanistan. The man contends in a 2023 federal lawsuit that he traveled there to visit family. The man and Estrada deny ICE’s claims and said that, for years, the federal government has treated him as a terrorist without clearly explaining why or charging him in criminal court.

The Afghan man is one of more than a dozen plaintiffs in the 2023 federal lawsuit arguing the U.S. government violated their constitutional rights by putting them on terrorist watchlists for unfounded reasons. He asserts that stalled his naturalization application pending since 2019, subjected him to unfounded scrutiny when traveling and impacted his ability to send money to his family back in Afghanistan.

STLPR has not obtained or reviewed the full trove of documents. Estrada told STLPR that officials at the Ste. Genevieve County Detention Center, where her husband is being held, told her they “don’t do handoffs” when she tried to obtain the documents in person.

The former U.S. military translator’s immigration court hearing is scheduled for Sept. 14 in Kansas City Immigration Court.

Working with U.S. forces

The man’s family provided STLPR with a collection of U.S. military and government records documenting his work as a linguist, interpreter and cultural adviser to American and Afghan forces fighting the Taliban.

The documents, spanning 2012 to 2023, cover a time when the U.S. military trusted him with sensitive work, allowed him to fight in combat alongside American troops and helped him seek refuge in the country whose government is now attempting to deport him. The records include recommendations from Army and Marine Corps officers, military intelligence advisers and direct supervisors who vouched for his loyalty and trust, while urging the federal government to grant him a Special Immigrant Visa.

Two officials said at the time that they did not consider him a threat to U.S. national security, one of them retired Army Col. Robert Benjamin.

Benjamin told STLPR by phone last week that he at one time oversaw roughly 9,000 interpreters across Southwest Asia and Africa. He authenticated a recommendation letter he wrote and said the man worked with him daily as his personal cultural adviser, as well as a linguist and interpreter, both on base and in the battlefield. The retired officer said that the stakes were high and that if the Taliban had found the man working with U.S. troops, “they would absolutely have killed him and probably tortured him before it happened.”

Benjamin initially told STLPR that he stood behind his recommendation. The next day, he recanted his support.

He told STLPR that he received a phone call from a government agency informing him that ICE had detained the Afghan man he vouched for more than a decade ago, detailing some of the accusations.

Benjamin wouldn’t discuss the government's allegations but appeared shocked to learn of them and emphasized he could no longer back his former employee.

Allegations

A 2021 FBI search warrant for an encrypted hard drive tied to the man illuminates some of the government’s allegations against him. The warrant was under seal and only made public in March 2025.

The government says the man had numerous ties to a global terrorist organization, regularly used Facebook to communicate with its members and stored large amounts of encrypted information on the hard drive, in a way that could have been done “to conceal it from law enforcement.”

Federal investigators wrote they believe the hard drive contained evidence that he supported terrorist organizations and their members, saying that violated part of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, a federal law that carries penalties of up to 20 years in prison and a $1 million fine.

The FBI’s warrant confirms the man served as a U.S. military interpreter in Gardez, Afghanistan, from approximately October 2010 to April 2014. But after his service, the government claims, the man communicated with members of Jama’at ul Dawa al-Qu’ran (JDQ). The State Department designated the Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan-based group as a foreign terrorist organization in 2016.

In the warrant, the government asserts that some consider the group to be part of the Taliban because in 2010, JDQ swore allegiance to then-Taliban leader Mullah Omar. The group also has long-standing ties to al-Qaida and Lashkar e-Tayyiba, a separate Pakistan-based militant and extremist group founded in 1989. JDQ was behind the 2010 kidnapping and death of British aid worker Linda Norgrove.

The Afghan man regularly communicated with JDQ senior leaders online and in person, the FBI asserts, contending that his social media messages show he knew that JDQ was designated as a global terrorist organization by the U.S. government.. During one conversation with a JDQ member, the man allegedly acknowledged JDQ has been blacklisted and stated the reasoning was because there are “some dogs in congress here [in the USA] who are anti-Islam.”

Just weeks after arriving in the United States, the man is alleged to have reached out to the son of JDQ’s late founder Sheikh Jamil al-Rahman. The man is reported to have asked about how to obtain speeches by the man and said “he needed to discuss something with him.”

In March 2015, the man is alleged to have maintained a Facebook tribute page for the late JDQ founder Sheikh Jameel ur Rahman, an online space where he would post meeting information for the militant group — many of the meetings in Afghanistan. In May 2018, the man claims he went to Afghanistan to visit family. The FBI search warrant says photos from the trip show the man attended an event where JDQ’s leader spoke.

After returning to the U.S. three months later, the man filed a naturalization application and was asked if he had been a member of, or associated with, a terrorist organization. “[The man] answered “no” to the question,” according to the FBI search warrant. “[The man] also denied ever being a member of, helping, serving, or otherwise ever participating in an insurgent organization.”

The FBI alleges the man falsely denied ever claiming to be an American citizen, pointing to a Missouri voter registration application in which he allegedly identified himself as a citizen.

In 2019, the government executed three search warrants on the man’s Facebook pages: his personal page, the tribute page and a page where people would debate Islamic ideologies, according to the warrant’s probable cause statement.

In December 2020, the man returned to Afghanistan once more. Customs and Border Patrol agents found that he was traveling with a timer, cables, a power converter, a range finder, a pair of binoculars, and six cellphones. Still, he was allowed to travel. The government is unsure if he had that material when he returned because there was nothing reported out of the ordinary.

When asked about the warrant, the Afghan man told STLPR he wasn’t familiar with the allegations. When going through each of the government’s assertions, the man refused to speak about any involvement or communications with members of JDQ but said he is not a member or will ever be a member of a terror organization. He added that he never voted or intended to vote while not a U.S. citizen and underscored it is not illegal to travel with binoculars.

If the government found incriminating evidence, the man said, he should be afforded at trial before a judge and his peers.

“[The government] can prove it without a reasonable doubt in front of a jury and then go from there,” he said. “That’s the right way to do it.”

The arrest

ICE arrested the Afghan man on Aug. 25 as he began an early morning run, Estrada told STLPR last week. His wife disputes the date of the arrest, as an ICE statement says he entered federal custody on Aug. 26.

“He never came back,” she told STLPR last week, fearing at first that he had been injured. Then her phone rang. “My gut said answer it, and it was him stating that he had been arrested by ICE.”

He told STLPR on a call from the Ste. Genevieve Detention Center last week that he initially thought he was being robbed when a black vehicle with tinted windows rushed him. He said his entire life flashed in front of him as federal agents poured out of the vehicle, pointed guns at him and screamed they had a warrant for his arrest before taking him into custody.

"They put me on the ground and chained me up right there, and they were asking any questions and I remained silent," he said on Thursday. He said agents drove him to a police station parking lot where they took photos with him “as if they had arrested Osama bin Laden's accomplice.” "I kind of smiled at that point because there was a time when the U.S. forces relied upon what we said. We helped them,” he said. “How time changes.”

ICE detained and placed him in deportation proceedings with the help of the FBI, spokespeople from both agencies confirmed. The Afghan man told STLPR he believes his arrest may be tied to his attendance at a 2016 anti-Trump protest in downtown St. Louis. He said he attended after hearing the president repeatedly speak ill of people of color — including Muslims and Mexicans.

“I believed, and I still believe, [...] America stands against tyranny, against hate, and against religious bigotry,” he said. “I always believe in the American spirit and the freedom of speech and freedom of religion. I think that's the beautiful thing about the United States of America, and that's what makes the United States better and different.”

He said he didn’t know of any other reason he may be targeted, other than alluding to the Trump administration’s track record of policies around Muslim individuals.

“Today, it’s a permanent resident’s constitutionally guaranteed right taken away. Tomorrow, it’s yours,” he said. “If you’re a United States citizen, it’s coming to your doorstep. It’s scary and it’s not OK and shouldn’t be happening this way to anybody.”

St. Louis Public Radio’s Hiba Ahmad contributed to this report.

text:
A federal judge in New Jersey dismissed the Justice Department's challenge to Governor Mikie Sherrill's Executive Order No. 12 on 4 September 2026, rejecting the government's claims that the measure unlawfully interferes with federal civil immigration enforcement.

Sherrill signed the order on 11 February. It restricts federal immigration officers from entering, accessing or using nonpublic areas of property owned, operated, leased or controlled by covered New Jersey executive-branch agencies for civil immigration enforcement unless they have a judicial warrant.

The order also bars those agencies from allowing federal immigration officers to use state property as a staging area, processing location or operations base for civil immigration enforcement without a judicial warrant. It does not prevent federal authorities from entering areas open to the general public on the same terms as other members of the public.

The Justice Department filed its lawsuit against New Jersey and Sherrill on 23 February, arguing that Executive Order No. 12 violated the U.S. Constitution's Supremacy Clause. The complaint alleged that the order obstructed federal immigration enforcement and made some operations less safe. Those assertions were allegations advanced by the federal government, not findings by the court.

Judge Rejects Three DOJ Claims

U.S. District Judge Georgette Castner granted New Jersey and Sherrill's motion to dismiss on 4 September. Before addressing the merits, Castner found that the United States had Article III standing to pursue its claims, including because it had sufficiently alleged that the order could interfere with federal immigration operations.

The Justice Department advanced three principal theories. It argued that federal immigration law pre-empted the New Jersey order, that the measure directly regulated the federal government and that it unlawfully discriminated against federal officers.

Castner rejected the pre-emption claim. In her opinion, she found that the federal provisions cited by the government did not require New Jersey to provide state property or assistance for federal civil immigration enforcement. She wrote that Congress had contemplated state assistance with immigration enforcement on a voluntary basis.

The judge also said that interpreting federal law to compel New Jersey to provide such assistance would conflict with the anti-commandeering principle, which limits the federal government's ability to require states to administer or support federal programmes.

Castner separately rejected the Justice Department's direct-regulation theory. She found that New Jersey was acting as a proprietor by defining what activities could take place on its property rather than directly regulating how federal officers perform their duties.

The opinion also found that Executive Order No. 12 did not substantially interfere with federal operations. Castner noted that immigration enforcement could still occur near state courthouses, in public areas of state courthouses and in federal, county and municipal courthouses.

On the discrimination claim, Castner concluded that state and local law-enforcement officers were not similarly situated to federal immigration officers because civil immigration enforcement is a federal function. She therefore found that the government had not plausibly alleged unlawful discrimination under intergovernmental-immunity principles.

New Jersey Officials Welcome Dismissal

New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport welcomed the ruling in a statement issued on 4 September, saying the state had maintained from the outset that the executive order was 'plainly lawful.'

Davenport said the order reflected the Sherrill administration's commitment to protecting state workers and residents and said her office would continue working with the governor to protect immigrant communities.

Sherrill also issued a statement after the ruling, saying the decision supported her administration's position on restricting federal immigration officers' access to nonpublic state property.

The ruling leaves Executive Order No. 12 in effect after the Justice Department's federal challenge was dismissed at the district-court level. The order continues to apply to covered New Jersey executive-branch property while preserving access to public areas and other exceptions set out in its text, including compliance with valid judicial warrants and judicial orders.

US President Donald Trump has made combating illegal immigration a top priority of his second term, with authorities rounding up thousands of people and expanding detention centres.

A joint report by Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights in June said that the rate of people dying in ICE custody has reached its highest level in over a decade amid Trump’s crackdown.

The UN rights chief on Monday also called out a range of other US immigration enforcement practices, including forcing migrant returns to dangerous places and to countries they had no connection to.

“I urge the United States to halt the return of people to places where they could suffer irreparable harm, including Haiti, and to ensure due process for all removals to third countries,” he told the council.

The UN rights chief also voiced alarm at the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency’s reported plans to “equip immigration agents with electric shock gloves”, warning this would “increase the violence associated with their operations”.

The plan to purchase the shock gloves, which was first reported by The Associated Press, calls for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the ICE parent agency, to spend up to $20 million on what are described as “distraction and de-escalation” devices.

ICE has come in for criticism for a series of fatal shootings during enforcement operations, including those of two American citizens in Minnesota in January who were involved in anti-ICE protests.

Critics have focused on the forceful tactics used by ICE agents in rounding up migrants and on an alleged lowering of the standards of training for new recruits.

Turning to the West Bank and Gaza, Turk urged countries to end transfers of arms to Israel that risk being used to violate international law, and called on companies to stop business practices supporting illegal settlements.

He said Israel’s annexation of the occupied West Bank was “unfolding, unobstructed,” despite a clear ruling by the International Court of Justice.

“What more will it take for states to take action to prevent the entrenchment of occupation across land earmarked for Palestinians under the two-state solution?” he said.

“They (states) need to end the transfer to Israel of arms that risk being used to violate international law. Companies also need to end business practices that support illegal settlements,” he added.

The rights chief said words of condemnation “ring hollow in the face of deliberate violations and suffering,” calling for greater international efforts toward sustainable peace.

On Gaza, he said Israel has killed more than 1,300 Palestinians in daily strikes despite the ceasefire announced almost a year ago and continues to restrict humanitarian aid.

text:
ICE has deported the mother of David Garcia, a first‑year midshipman at the U.S. Naval Academy, after taking her into custody during her scheduled green card interview. The removal has intensified scrutiny of the administration’s immigration tactics, particularly toward military families.

The decision leaves Garcia — who began his service commitment this summer — separated from his mother as advocates warn more families could face similar disruptions.

The strongest confirmation came from Texas Democratic Representative Joaquin Castro, who said he informed Garcia and his relatives after learning that Maria Rocha‑Martinez had been deported Wednesday night.

Read More on News

“She was doing everything the right way,” Castro wrote, adding that the administration’s mass‑deportation push is “destroying families for profit.”

DHS later labeled her a “criminal illegal alien,” claiming she had previously been removed and reentered the country unlawfully — a felony under federal law.

Castro disputed the framing, arguing she had been following the legal process and should never have been detained in the first place.

Newsweek has reached out to Castro's office and ICE for comment.

A Family Torn Apart During a Routine Immigration Appointment

Maria Rocha‑Martinez arrived at her green card interview expecting to complete a long‑awaited step toward legal residency. Instead, ICE officers detained her on the spot and transferred her to the Dilley Immigration Processing Center, a facility Castro has repeatedly described as abusive and unfit for housing families.

“ICE took her when she showed up for her green card interview,” he said, noting she had been granted parole in place — a protection often extended to military families.

Under federal immigration law, parole in place is a discretionary protection sometimes granted to spouses, parents and children of U.S. service members, allowing them to remain in the country and adjust status despite lacking lawful admission.

The protection has limits, however, as a prior deportation can legally complicate or even bar eligibility, because unlawful reentry after removal is a felony that triggers reinstatement of the old deportation order.

In practice, that means DHS can treat the person as ineligible for parole in place even if they have been living in the U.S. for years and are attempting to regularize their status.

Rocha‑Martinez remained jailed for days as Castro attempted to visit her, but ICE denied access, citing a requirement that congressional requests be submitted 48 hours in advance.

Growing Alarm Over Targeting of Military Families

Castro has warned for months that the administration is increasingly targeting families connected to U.S. service members. In interviews and public posts, he has cited multiple cases, such as the father of a Navy sailor detained in Florida, the deportation of an Army sergeant’s wife to Honduras, and the detention of other spouses and parents of active‑duty personnel.

“The Trump Administration is targeting military families and leaving a dark stain on our nation,” he wrote in August, calling for Rocha‑Martinez’s immediate release.

The congressman’s criticism aligns with broader concerns raised by advocates who say ICE has escalated enforcement against individuals who traditionally received humanitarian discretion.

Castro argues that these actions undermine military readiness and morale, especially for young service members like Garcia, who began his training at the Naval Academy this summer.

“She raised a bright young man with good character who is serving our nation,” he said. “Maria should be home, not torn apart from her family and life.”

Inside Dilley: A Facility Under Intensifying Scrutiny

Rocha‑Martinez’s detention at Dilley placed her inside a facility already under national criticism. Castro has conducted nine inspections this year, describing Dilley as a “trailer prison” where children and families are held far beyond the 20‑day limit established under the Flores settlement.

“You have kids as young as 2 months old who have been in prison there,” he said, adding that some children have been held for months at a time.

ICE has repeatedly denied Castro access to specific detainees, including Rocha‑Martinez and other families he has attempted to meet.

DHS insists the restrictions are procedural, but Castro argues they are part of a pattern of obstruction meant to shield abusive practices from oversight.

“This is an agency that has become very abusive, that has absolutely gone rogue,” he said during a recent interview.

What Comes Next for the Garcia Family

With Rocha‑Martinez now in Mexico, Garcia faces the start of his Naval Academy career without his mother’s presence or support.

Castro says his office “worked day and night” to prevent the deportation but ultimately could not stop ICE from removing her.

The congressman has promised to continue pressing for reforms to protect military families and to shut down the Dilley facility entirely.

text:
Today the Immigration Health Surcharge increases from £624 per year to £1,035 per year. It’s more than a fivefold increase since 2015, when the surcharge was introduced at £200 per year.

For us in GMIAU’s Action Group, on the 10-year route to settlement, this will mean that applying for 2.5 years of Limited Leave to Remain will cost over £3600. Over the 10 years of the route we’ll spend nearly £20,000 in fees, not including legal fees and other associated costs, just to keep our legal status – which is based on our human rights. If we have a partner or child on the route the fees snowball even further.

The 10-year route is already unaffordable. We’ve spoken out about it before, bringing our concerns to Parliament, to local authorities and to the streets. We’ve explained, and research has shown, that visa fee levels lead to people struggling to pay for basic items and living in fear of losing status.

But our pleas haven’t been heard and once again the rug has been pulled from under us. We’re feeling disappointed and demoralised. None of us are living comfortably; we’re just trying to get by. We’re working hard to make ends meet to survive in this cost of living crisis and yet try to save enough money to pay for the visas to be renewed every 30 months. We’re scared – by the time our next renewal comes around, will things have changed again? We have to think twice about putting the heating on – can we save that money for our visa fees? Being at the mercy of the Home Office for ten years feels like a prison sentence.

The Immigration Health Surcharge is presented as our contribution to the NHS – which we are already paying for through our taxes, just like everyone else. The cost of living crisis and burden of fees means we don’t even always access the healthcare we need, like paying for prescriptions – the healthcare we’re paying twice for. It’s possible to get a fee waiver, but not all of us can access it. You have to prove you are on the verge of destitution; it can feel dehumanising.

We want to call out this policy for what it is: racist and hostile. We feel like the Home Office is not listening to us and people’s wellbeing is not being taken into account. We feel like they pick on migrants because no one is going to stand up and speak out about it. But we’re not going to sit back and keep quiet. In our group and others, we’re educating each other and the public, and people are calling out injustices and holding people in power to account.

See our campaign page below to find out more about our action group.

title: Found, But Not Rescued - In These Times
description:
One of the migrant boats, carrying 128 people, was eventually rescued by the Italian Coast Guard after a civilian alarm system raised an alert.
It’s common for children to be among the migrants saved from boats shipwrecked while crossing the Mediterranean: over half of the 53 people the Ocean Viking rescued from Daniel’s boat in May 2025 were children.
The Italian Coast Guard rescued one boat but did not return for Daniel’s.
The merchant vessel, the MV Bobic, registered in the Marshall Islands, turned south to Libya to return the rescued migrants.
They were among 276 people who were rescued over the course of a single day after being shipwrecked off the coast of Tunisia during a storm.
text:
In the middle of the ocean, a man was drowning. He could not hold fast to the ropes dangling from the bow and stern of the bulk carrier that stopped to help. Below, a small, blue wooden boat crammed with people was tossed by a raging storm. As high winds sloshed water over the deck, the passengers — who had sailed for a day and a night without drinking water — rushed toward the swaying ropes. But the lines slipped through their hands.

The children lacked the strength to climb. Even for the strong, a single slip could mean being crushed beneath the swaying hull of the massive ship.

“We were all very scared in the moment and drove away from [the] big ship,” Daniel, a survivor from Eritrea, reportedly told rescuers, describing how the migrant boat he was on powered away from the larger vessel in fear of being capsized. (Daniel is a pseudonym because survivors of deadly rescues at sea often face criminalization.)

“We tried to help, to throw [life rings],” to the man in the water, Daniel continued, ​“but he didn’t take it. We saw him go far away and we knew he [was] dying.”

When people drown, they don’t scream or wave; they fall silently. Their mouths gasp at the surface, and their arms and legs move like they’re climbing a ladder underwater — until they simply disappear. As the night’s darkness enveloped the 81 migrants remaining on the wooden boat, the man in the water slipped out of sight.

With no means of navigation, those left on board could only follow the flare of oil platforms as raw markers of north — or look to the stars to guide them.

A weekly digest of our best coverage

The migrants’ voyage, which had begun four nights earlier, on May 20, 2025, was described to me in great detail by rescue crewmembers who gathered Daniel’s testimony, along with that of others aboard the blue wooden boat, in the hours after the rescue. The voyage had begun in Libya’s coastal town of Sabratha, where two wooden boats set sail for Italy carrying 245 migrants, according to the rescuers. One of the migrant boats, carrying 128 people, was eventually rescued by the Italian Coast Guard after a civilian alarm system raised an alert.

But Daniel’s boat, carrying 117 people, was less fortunate, hitting bad weather near the Sabratha oil platform more than 60 miles off the Libyan coast.

What unfolded next — including unfinished rescue attempts by passing merchant vessels, three deaths and the return of 35 migrants to a Libyan detention center known for systemic torture — is the subject of intense legal and moral debate, drawing in multiple governments, international agencies, coast guards, NGOs and commercial shipping companies. At its heart lie serious potential violations of international human rights and refugee law.

But the deeper story is structural, rooted in decades of northbound wealth transfer, policies that facilitate unsafe migration routes and systems that drive vulnerable people into the hands of traffickers and abusers.

The 2015 launch of Operation Sophia, a European Union military operation designed to ​“disrupt human smuggling and trafficking networks,” increased surveillance on the Mediterranean Sea. But deaths at sea never stopped. Regular drones and planes from the European border agency Frontex hum over the waves, but the surveillance is geared at security, not protection. (Frontex disputes this.)

Today, Frontex does not perform rescues; instead, it uses a fleet of planes and drones to spot boats in distress. The agency’s crews radio the rescue coordination centers responsible for that stretch of sea, giving them the boats’ position, course and speed and copying neighboring centers on the same call, according to Frontex spokesman Chris Borowski.

In situations like Daniel’s, the Libyans may intercept the vessels — if they are in the Libyan search and rescue area — using boats donated by Italy. The migrants are then taken, or returned, to detention centers where survivors report widespread abuses.

In August 2025, the Ocean Viking, the rescue boat pictured above, came under heavy machine gun fire, reportedly from Libyan forces sailing a vessel gifted to them by Italy. The attack grounded the ship, stopping all rescues for months. Photo by Ali Arkady

In 2025, nearly 8,000 people died or went missing on dangerous migration routes, including those spanning the Mediterranean Sea between Africa and Europe, the Atlantic Ocean from West Africa toward the Canary Islands, and the Horn of Africa toward Saudi Arabia, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). IOM also found that in the same year, ​“270 human remains washed ashore on Mediterranean coasts,” pointing to untraced shipwrecks.

So far in 2026, at least 990 people have died trying to cross the Mediterranean — far more than the same period last year — including 53 migrants lost at sea in early February, their bodies seemingly washing up on Italy’s beaches following a violent winter storm. Days before that disaster, at least 15 migrants died in Greek waters, reportedly after their boat ​“collided” with a Greek Coast Guard vessel.

The man Daniel watched drown last May might never be included in NGO tallies of the dead. But his death still poses a vital question: Why was he — and later two others from the same boat, another man and a child, according to rescuers — allowed to die while trying to reach one of the wealthiest continents on earth? These are not just tragic accidents; they are potential crimes against humanity that could be prosecuted up official chains of command.

Now, human rights lawyers are asking the International Criminal Court to investigate European leaders, alongside Libyan suspects, following the death of 25,000 asylum seekers and the abuses of 150,000 survivors detained in Libya.

Of the 117 migrants who set off from Libya on the boat with Daniel, only 79 made it to Italy — feverish, fuel-burned and in shock. But all of them — the survivors, the dead and those returned to Libya — were equally victims, not just of the sea, but of hostile migration policies.

These people ​“are the ones that we know, who have relatives back in Africa, in the Middle East, who could put the dots together,” said Fellipe Lopes, a bearded Brazilian man then working on board the Ocean Viking, a rescue ship operated by European NGO SOS Mediterranee. With emotion in his voice, Lopes recalled, ​“You see a lot of activity [on that sea] — it is such a busy route with vessels, tankers, container vessels, plus military assets in the air and sea, and yet, people continue to drop constantly.”

“There are thousands of people we don’t know about,” Lopes said, ​“because they are just missing.”

The Ocean Viking was part of a group of around a dozen ships sponsored by civil society groups that work to bring migrants stranded in the Central Mediterranean ashore to Europe, filling the void left by the end of Italian rescue operation ​“Mare Nostrum,” or ​“Our Sea” — a massive search-and-rescue effort that saved thousands of lives until it was ended, thanks to political and financial pressure, in 2014.

At first, NGO rescue boats hoping to replace the Italian mission worked in concert with European authorities, but their movements later became increasingly restricted after Italy introduced new hard-line, anti-immigration legislation framed as anti-smuggling. (The Italian Coast Guard still performs rescues between Tunisia and the Italian island of Lampedusa, but it does not usually operate farther south towards Libya.)

Today, the NGO rescue boats attract a band of mostly European sailors with a punk aesthetic who reject the continent’s far-right, anti-migration turn and want to practice the dying art of humanitarianism.

The Ocean Viking is a large, red-and-white offshore tugboat, equipped with radar, a small hospital and living quarters for the crew. I joined the boat to document the crew’s rescue work in May 2025. We set sail from Syracuse, Sicily, and from there, veered south through a large storm towards Libya, pausing off the coast of Tunisia by the port city of Sfax to rescue 276 shipwrecked migrants. The morning of that rescue, an alert sounded at 3:53 a.m. on the ship’s radios. Seafarers pulled on their life vests, boots and waterproof trousers in the storeroom; out on deck, the lifeboats were being lowered down and hit the water by 4 a.m.

"Of the 117 migrants who set off from Libya on the boat with Daniel, only 79 made it to Italy—feverish, fuel-burned and in shock. But all of them—the survivors, the dead and those returned to Libya—were equally victims, not just of the sea, but of hostile migration policies."

In the dark, fear of the unknown often freezes migrants, one sailor told me, and rescuers rely on this alarm at the sight of an unknown ship to help keep migrant boats at a safe distance. This is the moment when most rescues go wrong, since migrants are often so relieved that they start to celebrate — sometimes jumping up and down, inadvertently causing their ship to capsize. But fear of the unknown can also keep survivors still while translators on the rescue ship explain that they’re sending out smaller boats to meet them.

Out on the deck of the Ocean Viking after the rescues, the Mediterranean air was warm and the sea calm. It was black night but there was light from the moon. Below me was the dark sea, swirling like milky blue tea and churning frothy whirlpools against the lifeboats now launching on the port side.

Amid the hum of the generators, sloshing of seawater and clomping of rubber boots, there was an atmosphere of sad diligence and worn-down optimism, broken occasionally by levity and games. The drama and intensity of the rescues was punctuated by long hours watching the waves; groups of migrant men passed the time sleeping or smoking. The sailors washed the deck and organized food handouts, tea and hot chocolate stations, and lines for the migrants to wash and charge their phones. One morning, I watched a sailor bent down, absorbed in the task of trying to dry a soaking wet passport with a hair dryer.

In the early 1990s, Spain and Italy introduced visa requirements for North African migrants, closing a period of some fluid movement. Before the Westernled wars in Iraq, Libya and Afghanistan, migration across the Mediterranean was mostly viewed in economic and not criminal terms. This shifted after the 2011 Libyan war, which ​“opened the door of Africa to Europe,” said Felippo Aquilino, another rescuer on board the Ocean Viking.

Aquilino, a Sicilian with salt-and-pepper hair, had known about the migrant route since a fishing boat full of strangers crashed outside his family’s cabin on the south coast of Lampedusa when he was five years old. He sat talking to me on the deck of the boat under bright sunshine and a strong wind. As an outpost that represents one of the nearest parts of Europe to Africa, Lampedusa has become such a symbol of the deadly Mediterranean crossing that Pope Francis famously made it the destination of his first official trip outside Rome in 2013, celebrating mass on an altar fashioned from the wood of shipwrecked migrant boats.

It’s common for children to be among the migrants saved from boats shipwrecked while crossing the Mediterranean: over half of the 53 people the Ocean Viking rescued from Daniel’s boat in May 2025 were children. (Photos by Ali Arkady)

During the second rescue on the morning of May 17, day broke in full color over the deck as the survivors appeared, clambering up from the lifeboats one by one into the morning and the noise and heat of the engines. And then there on the horizon was another blue wooden boat, listing violently and full of people frozen with fear. The rescuers pulled them into their lifeboats, water moving below their feet as they worked. It’s a strange environment for land people to work in, one of the sailors told me later.

The survivors had been sailing for days. They told me stories of trying to reach Europe on crowded boats, only to be captured at sea and sent back by Libyan forces, presumably the EU-equipped Libyan Coast Guard.

He tried to cross the sea to reach Europe five times between 2019 and 2025, but each time, he was returned by Libyan patrol boats. Sometimes, he was sent back and freed along with his fellow travellers.

The day after he was rescued, Ahmed — a Marxist from Sudan who said he fled Darfur in 2019, when his political activism made him an enemy of both the government and the rebels — told me that, for him, ​“There’s no way back, because I refuse two systems, not one.” He tried to cross the sea to reach Europe five times between 2019 and 2025, but each time, he was returned by Libyan patrol boats. Sometimes, he was sent back and freed along with his fellow travellers. But on other occasions, he said, he was sent to jails where he was tortured. Once, he was forced to pay the equivalent of $310 for his freedom. After his release, militias in Misrata forced him to work as a cleaner and guard — sometimes for pay, sometimes not, in a mix of indentured servitude and slavery.

Sitting on the deck of the Ocean Viking and looking out at the sea, a metal cross round his neck, another migrant named Josef described leaving Ethiopia’s city of Gondar because he couldn’t find work or money. In Libya, he’d been captured and sent to jail four times: twice for trying to cross the sea and twice just for being on the street. In jail, he said, he’d been kicked ​“like an animal” by guards until he could gather the bribe money to escape.

Sitting with the women and children outside their sleeping quarters, Helen, a young woman with a mournful air, said she was traveling with her husband. She was tired and withdrawn and didn’t join in when the other women sang and danced on deck with relief. The couple traveled from Ethiopia to Sudan and then Libya, where her husband took menial work. ​“Sometimes,” Helen recalled, the militia men ​“took him away, kidnapped him, and asked for money to release him.” The first time she tried to cross the sea, Libyans shot at their plastic boat and forced them off. ​“The men jumped in the water and the women cried, ​‘Our brothers, please help get them.’” The men were rescued and then beaten by the guards.

The second time, she was at sea for 12 hours before being captured and taken back to a prison in Libya, where she was held for nine months. She didn’t have words to describe how bad the treatment was there; when I asked about it, her eyes filled with tears and she began to rock back and forth.

But on other occasions, he said, he was sent to jails where he was tortured.

From Sfax, we headed to northern Italy, more than 600 miles away, to disembark the survivors under orders from Italian maritime authorities. After four days sailing together, I watched as the migrants stepped down from the boat, many without shoes or socks, to meet a delegation of local officials, the Italian Red Cross and the police. From here, they would start the next part of their journeys. A month later, Ahmed met the photographer I was traveling with, Ali, in Paris. Ahmed had walked all the way to France, crossing the Alps, with the help of kind strangers who treated his worn-out feet and bad stomach.

Often, migrants are so relieved to see an NGO rescue boat like the Ocean Viking that they start to celebrate—sometimes jumping up and down, inadvertently causing their small, overcrowded ships to capsize. (Photos by Ali Arkady)

In 2013, after the Arab Spring pro-democracy revolutions and foreign interventions curdled into war, crisis and displacement, Italy responded to the surge in migrant crossings and deaths at sea by launching ​“Mare Nostrum.” However, responsibility was later shifted to Frontex, which emphasized border security over rescue, creating a deadly gap in the Central Mediterranean.

In a 2025 press release, Frontex boasted of a 20% drop in ​“irregular border crossings” into Europe in the first five months of the year, attributing the decline to thousands of their officers working with national authorities to ​“safeguard borders and save lives at sea.”

Frontex’s budget surged to 1.1 billion euros in 2026, with an emphasis on funding high-tech surveillance. The agency relies on the Heron 1 drones manufactured by Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) and contracts with Airbus to provide surveillance drones over the Mediterranean. The agency frames this as a tool for safety, but the nearly 1 billion euros committed to long-term aerial surveillance since 2024 has done little to stop the death toll. Instead, it has facilitated a policy of remote detection and Libyan interception.

Frontex spokesman Chris Borowski said in response to inquiries from In These Times: ​“Detection is what starts the rescue. In 2025, Frontex assets contributed to saving 33,000 lives, and we’re past 7,000 already this year. … On the interception chain and non-refoulment: we comply with non-refoulment in everything we do, full stop.”

(Non-refoulement is a core principle under international human rights law prohibiting states from returning a person to a territory where they face real risks of persecution or irreparable harm.)

Borowski added: ​“When one of our aircraft finds a boat that’s about to sink, the job in that moment is to stop people from drowning. Saving those lives has to come first, because the alternative is watching people drown while everyone works out the politics. What a government does after an interception, Italy, Libya, or anyone else, is a separate and serious question, but it doesn’t change the fact that reporting a boat in distress is what keeps the people on it alive long enough for that question to even come up.”

“I don’t dispute that the reports of torture and extortion in Libyan detention are real and well documented. But the fix for that isn’t asking Frontex to stop reporting boats in distress, a duty every vessel at sea carries,” Borowski said. ​“It’s a decision on the political level. That call isn’t ours to make, and we won’t speak as though it is.”

A medic on board the Sumud Flotilla that sailed towards Gaza in September 2025 recalled watching Frontex drones with his fellow crewmembers. While the drones only monitor migrant traffic, the sheer number of them was disconcerting, said the medic, speaking on the condition of anonymity. The constant air surveillance ​“felt intimidating and dystopian,” he added.

Far-right politicians began to denigrate NGO operators as "sea taxis" or accomplices to smugglers, said the Ocean Viking’s Aquilino. This criminalization is a key vector in Europe’s broader hostility to migrants from countries destabilized by corruption, repression, and Western-backed wars and economic policies.

In 2017, the Italian government began introducing rules limiting the operations of NGO ships, followed by new laws carrying penalties in 2019, and further restrictions during the pandemic. Under mounting pressure from the far Right, Italy enacted the ​“Piantedosi Decree” in 2023. Named after Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi, the law imposed strict new limitations on NGO rescue operations, requiring vessels to head immediately to the port designated by authorities after every rescue and making ​“multi-rescue” missions much harder. That has the effect of reducing the time rescuers can spend at sea answering distress calls, driving up costs and increasing the likelihood of criminalization if paperwork is not filed correctly. Ships are now regularly detained for conducting additional rescues after being assigned a port of disembarkation.

Far-right politicians began to denigrate NGO operators as ​“sea taxis” or accomplices to smugglers, said the Ocean Viking’s Aquilino. This criminalization is a key vector in Europe’s broader hostility to migrants from countries destabilized by corruption, repression and Western-backed wars and economic policies.

The impact on operations has been huge. Before the war against NGO ships began, Aquilino said, the Ocean Viking spent roughly 300 days a year patrolling for distressed boats; under the Piantedosi Decree, that has dropped to 180 days. It was a sad irony that a year after the EU received the 2012 Nobel Peace Prize for decades of contributions to peace, democracy and human rights worldwide, ​“they started closing the borders and stopping the rescues,” he added.

After the EU signed a deal with Turkey in 2016 to reduce migration, Ocean Viking crewmember Lopes said there was a sudden increase in the number of Frontex personnel, boats, airplanes, drones and bases around Lesbos, the Greek island off Turkey that had become the epicenter of migrant arrivals to Europe. In 2015, when Kurdish-Syrian toddler Aylan Kurdi washed up drowned on a Turkish beach, global attention turned to Lesbos and the NGO presence on the island soared. Frontex personnel filled restaurants, along with members of the Greek Coast Guard and army. States began arresting humanitarian activists. The crackdown in Greek-Turkish waters, said Lopes, made the far more dangerous Central Mediterranean route, one of the deadliest in the world, much more popular.

The EU, the Italian foreign ministry, the Maltese maritime authorities, the Italian Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre and the Libyan Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre did not respond to requests for comment from In These Times, nor did Israeli Aerospace Industry or Airbus.

The Ocean Viking, pictured above, is equipped with radar, a small hospital and living quarters for its crew of rescuers. The movements of NGO rescue boats like this have become increasingly restricted after Italy introduced new hard-line, anti-immigration legislation. Photo by Ali Arkady

As his rescuers recount it, Daniel arrived alone at the rocky shore in Sabratha, Libya, last spring, ready to cross the Mediterranean to Europe, as merchants and sailors had done for thousands of years. He had already travelled more than 1,200 miles from his home in the closed dictatorship of Eritrea. On May 20, 2025, there was a storm brewing out beyond the oil rigs, as 245 passengers clambered aboard two 23-foot wooden boats, one painted bright blue.

Daniel was last to board the boat with a tall, jutting prow, a weak engine and not enough fuel. As the passengers reached the high seas that night, waves crashed against the skiff, upsetting fuel cans. Passenger vomit mixed with urine, kerosene and seawater, creating a noxious slurry below deck in the tightly packed hold. The next morning, the storm worsened, and a passenger sent out a phone alert. The Italian Coast Guard rescued one boat but did not return for Daniel’s. The Libyan Coast Guard sent a boat from Zawiyah, 30 miles west of Tripoli, to intercept the migrants and return them to Libya, but they hit bad weather, Ocean Viking crewmembers later told me, forcing the group to turn back.

The Ocean Viking was on its way, but was still returning from dropping off migrants shipwrecked near Tunisia—including Ahmed, Josef and Helen, whom I’d met—in northern Italy.

As Daniel’s boat drifted away from the drowning man, the crew of a large merchant ship trying to rescue them sent an urgent mayday signal about possible people in the water, requesting assistance and guidance on what to do with the 35 people they had managed to rescue before the migrant boat pulled away.

The merchant vessel, the MV Bobic, registered in the Marshall Islands, turned south to Libya to return the rescued migrants. The NGO Alarm Phone, which relays messages to rescue boats and authorities from shipwrecked migrants, informed the merchant ship that it was illegal to return migrants to Libya, where there is a credible risk of torture and abuse. A deputy commissioner of maritime affairs for the Republic of the Marshall Islands suggested the merchant vessel go to Tunisia, then asked Libya to take responsibility for the decision, according to emails published by Alarm Phone.

Merchant ships operate on strict margins and any rescue will cost crucial days sailing time for the captain and ship’s company. That evening, a relative of one of the rescued migrants told Alarm Phone that the 35 people who made it onboard the Bobic had been taken to Libya’s al-Nasr detention center in Zawiyah, notorious for torture.

The Ocean Viking was on its way, but was still returning from dropping off migrants shipwrecked near Tunisia — including Ahmed, Josef and Helen, whom I’d met — in northern Italy. If it hadn’t been compelled to drop them off first, as the new regulations dictated, it could have been closer to Daniel’s boat and more people may have survived.

On May 25, 2025, the evening after the MV Bobic rescue, another merchant ship, the MV Eco One, approached the 81 migrants, including Daniel, still adrift. The Eco One was roughly six times the size of their boat, but the survivors were so exhausted and scared of the bruising storm that they apparently lost fear of other threats and bravely tried to approach the ship’s colossal, metal hull.

The crew of the Eco One threw down a small rope with a ring at the end. The migrants rushed to climb aboard, and in the scrum, four people fell into the water, Daniel told the Ocean Viking’s crew. The Eco’s crew threw life rings down into the swell to catch the fallen. Two survivors were pulled from the water and hauled back onto the wooden boat, but the other two — one man of around 25 and a child of 13 — were too far away, according to Daniel’s account.

“We [sailed] away from the second ship as we saw too many people falling down. We were scared because of what happened with the rope. Everyone went for themselves,” Daniel told the Ocean Viking crew.

During the rescue attempt, the crew of the Eco One managed to recover 26 people from the boat before aborting the rescue due to the storm. The Italian maritime authorities then told the Eco One to take the survivors to Lampedusa and rescue the remaining shipwrecked people once weather conditions allowed. The Ocean Viking, then about an hour away, also received the order.

Neither the deputy commissioner of maritime affairs for the Republic of the Marshall Islands nor the management companies of the MV Bobic and Eco One responded to requests for comment.

If it hadn’t been compelled to drop them off first, as the new regulations dictated, it could have been closer to Daniel’s boat and more people may have survived.

At this point, Daniel and his fellow migrants still caught in the storm saw what could be another ship in the distance — possibly an oil rig resupply vessel, its deck lit up like a Christmas tree, so bright that ​“it blinded us,” according to Daniel. They called out to the ship, asking anyone on board to help them, but ​“no one listened,” he recalled. He went down below deck into the cramped hold and tried not to think about the storm, or the juddering prow threatening to break, or the lack of fuel, or the sick passengers.

When the Ocean Viking approached Daniel’s boat, it was midnight and the sea was black. A video of the rescue shows a headlamp jutting over bouncing, black waves, until the lights of the oil tanker that had passed by appeared in the distance. In the foreground is the tiny migrant boat, spinning on the swell.

The Ocean Viking rescuers couldn’t see anyone out on deck, but as they drew closer, a man shouted out, ​“there are more of us down below.”

As the Ocean Viking’s lifeboats finally reached the skiff, Aquilino noticed a strong smell of diesel. Many of the passengers were in various states of shock, he said, and most of them were sheltering below deck in the space filled with water. The women below deck ​“were not okay,” said Lopes.

The next day, he recalled seeing one woman whose eyes were rolling back in her head. ​“She was not there,” Lopes said. Aquilino described a woman who had fallen in the water as appearing to have just come ​“back from the dead.” In the aftermath of the rescue, she cried out for her brother, who may have been one of the men who drowned, according to Aquilino. The survivors were so traumatized that it was difficult for the rescuers to understand exactly what happened.

A group of migrants sleep aboard the Ocean Viking in May 2025. They were among 276 people who were rescued over the course of a single day after being shipwrecked off the coast of Tunisia during a storm. Photo by Ali Arkady

As European rights groups, humanitarian organizations, and lawyers push for accountability, the violent reality continues at sea. In early 2017, Italy signed an anti-migration deal with Libya, including significant support in the form of training and resources for the Libyan Coast Guard. Later that year, the Italian government invited Abd al-Rahman Milad—a notorious human trafficker as well as a chief of the Libyan Coast Guard — to Sicily to discuss anti-migrant coordination, even though a UN report determined Milad and his unit were responsible for shootings at sea.

This model of cutting deals in exchange for a reduction in migration flows is defined by a lack of a unified EU strategy that will ​“at best sustain the status quo,” said Mark Micallef, a director at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime. ​“This is more or less the model that Gaddafi himself had established, an extortion-type model where ​‘you give me money or I will send more migrants,’” Micallef continued. ​“What we see now is the proliferation of that model across Libya.”

But not only have these deals failed to prevent migrant flows, they are also driving instability, according to experts. In Libya, human smuggling and trafficking industries are ​“putting money in the hands of militias that are then in a much better position to undermine the political process and the peace process,” according to Micallef. A better approach, he said, should include a greater emphasis on law enforcement, actually going after high-level criminals, alongside a visa scheme and refugee track, as well as ​“red lines” for partnership countries. ​“You need to be able to say actually this is a line we won’t cross,” he said.

Allison West of the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights said pushbacks at sea to Libya mark the beginning of ​“the severe deprivation of liberty as a crime against humanity.”

“People are deprived of their liberty at sea and then taken straight into detention centers in a systematic manner,” West said. Referring to EU deals with Libya, she added that this process ​“establishes a pathway for individual criminal responsibility for high-ranking officials in charge of the policies that make this whole system possible.”

Following a similar attempt six years earlier, the submission names the European officials as co-perpetrators in the deaths of 25,000 asylum seekers, as well as abuses against some 150,000 survivors “abducted and forcibly transferred to Libya, where they were detained, tortured, raped, and enslaved.”

When Italian authorities control a rescue at sea, West said, this can be enough ​“to establish the co-perpetration” of crimes against humanity, provided migrants are subsequently pushed back to Libyan detention sites, where some become victims of enforced disappearances. Because these disappearances occur with the direct knowledge or acquiescence of state authorities, West added, ​“they also impose a number of positive obligations on states to search for, to investigate and to continue until the whereabouts of the person are actually found and known.”

In an October 2025 submission to the International Criminal Court, a group of lawyers accused 120 European leaders of committing crimes against humanity alongside Libyan suspects. Following a similar attempt six years earlier, the submission names the European officials as co-perpetrators in the deaths of 25,000 asylum seekers, as well as abuses against some 150,000 survivors ​“abducted and forcibly transferred to Libya, where they were detained, tortured, raped, and enslaved.”

Now, even the rescuers are coming under attack. Humanitarian vessels threaten the financial and logistical arrangements between the EU and Libya. For the militias running Libyan detention centers, these ships undermine the cyclical business model of extortion. West describes the violence directed at rescue boats as ​“a maritime front of this broader containment policy.”

In August 2025, the Ocean Viking came under heavy machine gun fire, reportedly from Libyan forces sailing a vessel gifted by Italy. The attack destroyed the Viking’s antennas, broke four windows and damaged three rescue boats and rescue equipment, grounding the ship and stopping all rescues for about four months. Aquilino, on board at the time, said the gunfire was intense. He heard the metallic clink of bullets hitting the roof, windows and doors of the bridge.

“We were all falling down on the floor,” he said, hiding and ​“waiting for it to finish.”

By early morning on May 26, all 53 survivors remaining in Daniel’s boat after the Eco One rescue made it on board the Ocean Viking. The Italians instructed the ship to drop them off in Livorno, Tuscany, approximately 560 miles away. Five survivors were medically evacuated, including a teenager whose skin had been burned by exposure to fuel in the hold of the boat, as well as her baby. Along with her went a man with a broken arm who fell while attempting to climb the rope during the first rescue and a woman who Aquilino said inhaled too much seawater, likely developing a lung infection.

Next, the Ocean Viking dropped off the dozens of lone children, along with the handful still with family members, in Sicily, following an appeal from the NGO to the island’s public prosecutor. But the Italian authorities did not allow the remaining 13 survivors to disembark there. Instead, the Ocean Viking traveled north to Livorno.

On May 29, the Ocean Viking dropped off the remaining passengers. The original group of 117 migrants had been split among three ports and one Libyan detention center. Three had drowned. According to the rescuers, on arrival in Italy, security officials were there to question the survivors.

Angelo Selim, the Ocean Viking’s search and rescue coordinator, who later spoke to me on the phone, detailed the harrowing journey of the survivors: the separation across distant ports, untreated injuries and the inhospitable welcome they received in Europe. He described the companions they had watched drown along the way.

“We don’t consider these people as humans,” he said. ​“The only reason this can happen is because we dehumanize these people. Until the last day, they suffer from our lack of empathy.”
