title: Eleventh Circuit's Zafirov Decision Leaves Key Constitutional Questions Open Regarding ...
authors: Ilene   Albala, Ilene Albala, Jordan Bock, Gregory Demske, Allan Medina, Kirk Ogrosky, Jordan L. Moran, Jenna Welsh
text:
In a panel opinion filed on September 1, 2026, the Eleventh Circuit vacated the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida’s decision in United States ex rel. Zafirov v. Florida Medical Associates, which had held that the qui tam provisions violate the Appointments Clause of Article II. But the decision left key constitutional questions open for courts, including potentially the Supreme Court, to consider in the future.

Background

As covered in prior Goodwin alerts here and here, the Zafirov case involves Clarissa Zafirov’s False Claims Act (FCA) lawsuit against various medical providers for allegedly misrepresenting patients’ medical conditions to Medicare. The government declined to intervene, but she continued to pursue the litigation on behalf of the United States as a relator. After defendants jointly moved for judgment on the pleadings or to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, the Middle District of Florida issued a groundbreaking decision finding that relators are “officers” under the Appointments Clause and holding that the qui tam provisions are thus unconstitutional.1

The district court explained that in assessing whether a qui tam relator is an “officer” under the Appointments Clause, it must consider, first, whether relators exercise significant authority under the laws of the United States, and second, whether relators occupy a continuing position established by law.2 It answered “yes” to both questions.

In an opinion that narrowly addressed only the second question, the Eleventh Circuit vacated and remanded. The court held that the “position” of a relator is “occasional and temporary because it lasts the length of one case” and a relator “does not have a permanent tenure.”3 The Eleventh Circuit further reasoned that relators also lack the “critical characteristic of an officer: that he receives a ‘continuing emolument.’”4 Relators’ compensation, the court noted, is limited to a one-time award that is contingent on the success of the case.5 Finally, the Eleventh Circuit concluded that the role of a relator is personal and not one that can be assumed by someone else.6

Implications & What’s Next

Though the parties had briefed and argued other constitutional issues, the Eleventh Circuit declined to address them. The court’s narrow decision therefore left key constitutional questions open, including whether the qui tam provisions violate the “Take Care Clause because the President lacks sufficient supervision and control over relators who wield executive power” and violate the “Vesting Clause because relators have the executive power to bring civil enforcement actions on behalf of the United States while the Constitution vests that power in the President alone.”7 The Eleventh Circuit directed the district court to consider these issues on remand, paving the way for another possible ruling that the qui tam provisions are unconstitutional on such alternative grounds.

The case could also potentially land before the Supreme Court, where defendants would need four votes to grant a cert petition. While the decision did not create a circuit split, at least three justices have expressed interest in considering the issue. On June 16, 2023, Justice Thomas authored a dissent in United States, ex rel. Polansky v. Executive Health Resources, Inc.8 His dissent expressed that “there are substantial arguments that the qui tam device is inconsistent with Article II and that private relators may not represent the interests of the United States in litigation.”9 In a concurring opinion authored by Justice Kavanaugh, joined by Justice Barrett, Justice Kavanaugh invited the Court to “consider the competing arguments on the Article II issue in an appropriate case.”10

A couple years later, Justice Kavanaugh wrote another concurring opinion, joined by Justice Thomas, in Wisconsin Bell, Inc. v. United States ex rel. Heath, again expressing that the “Court should consider the competing arguments on the Article II issue.”11

While there is potential Supreme Court appetite to consider the issue, it is also pending in two circuit courts. The Third Circuit heard oral argument months ago in United States ex rel. Penelow v. Janssen, No. 25-1818 (3d Cir.), where arguments raised on appeal include whether the qui tam provisions violate the Appointments, Vesting, and Take Care Clauses of Article II.

The Article II issue is also pending before the Fifth Circuit in United States ex rel. Taylor v. Healthcare Associates of Texas L.L.C., No. 25-10842 (5th Cir.), where two judges have expressed skepticism of the qui tam provisions’ constitutionality. Judge Duncan authored a concurrence in United States ex rel. Montcrief v. Peripheral Vascular Associates, P.A., describing the “constitutional flaws in the FCA’s qui tam device,” including that it violates both the Appointments Clause and Take Care Clause.12 Judge Ho likewise opined in a concurring opinion in another case that the Fifth Circuit “should revisit whether there are serious constitutional problems with the qui tam provisions of the” FCA.13

The Eleventh Circuit’s decision marks the first circuit court to speak on the topic since Justices Thomas, Kavanaugh, and Barrett have invited courts and litigants to consider Article II challenges to the qui tam provisions. But, as noted, its decision is a narrow one, and it leaves significant constitutional issues unresolved and several avenues for defendants facing qui tam litigation to continue to pursue.

text:
This story was originally published by WFYI Public Media.

By Caroline Beck and Zak Cassel

WFYI Public Media

September 6, 2026

Protesters gathered Saturday to make their presence known after increased activity from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement was witnessed across Indianapolis this past week. They met near the federal agency’s west side office.

The weekend protest followed two other demonstrations held at a hotel less than half a mile from the ICE office.

The increased ICE activity seen in Indianapolis coincides with a record-high number of arrests made by ICE in July, nearly 50,000 across the country, according to data gathered by the Deportation Data Project based at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA.

An unidentified spokesperson from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not answer questions sent by WFYI asking for the number of arrests made in Indiana this past week, or provide confirmation of increased enforcement operations in Indianapolis. They did reiterate their goal, at the directive of President Donald Trump, to deport criminals and anyone who entered the country illegally.

Saturday’s demonstration at the ICE office attracted over 100 protesters who oppose the influx of arrests and detainments witnessed through social media posts.

ICE agents and other law enforcement have been seen making arrests in residential neighborhoods, gas stations and other areas across the city.

Jesus Ramirez has been a community organizer and activist fighting for immigrants’ rights in Indiana for years. He said a few concerned individuals organized Saturday’s protest, not a single organization.

“It’s one of those things where as long as [ICE is] going to continue terrorizing our people, we’re going to continue to be in front of your building, being as loud as we possibly can to let you know that we’re not moving,” Ramirez told WFYI.

Ramirez said he knows some of the individuals recently arrested or detained by ICE. He believes the arrests have been racially motivated and that the agency is no longer focused on getting “the worst of the worst.”

“The collateral damage that we’re seeing is bigger than if they’re going for one person supposedly with a warrant, and there’s six other people around that have nothing to do with it,” Ramirez said. “They’re getting dragged along with no due process.”

Ramirez said he’s spoken with families who said they’re afraid to get groceries or send their kids to school.

An analysis done by the New York Times on ICE arrests found that a majority of immigrants arrested in July had not been charged with or convicted of a crime, but were accused of violating civil immigration laws.

Noise protests

On Thursday evening people arrived at a Hampton Inn, less than half a mile away from Indianapolis’ west side ICE office, where organizers believed ICE agents were staying as guests.

“It’s a noise rally, basically, to make sure that they feel very unwelcome, that they feel very uncomfortable, and that they don’t have a moment of peace while they’re here terrorizing Indianapolis residents,” organizer Stephen Lane, who is with the Indianapolis Party for Socialism and Liberation, told WFYI at the protest.

WFYI did not confirm whether ICE agents stayed at the hotel or not.

After the sun set, over 50 people were spread across the lawn in front of the hotel lobby. Organizers with megaphones led the demonstration in chants, including “ICE out now!” and “Chinga la migra!” Some had musical instruments — horns, a trombone and a saxophone — and played a beat on makeshift drums and bells.

Lane said he’s been checking on immigrant residents he knows in Indianapolis since arrest reports picked up.

“To see that they have to go through this, these raids in our communities, in our neighborhoods — it makes me sick seeing it happen all over the internet. I know that some people are hiding their immigrant neighbors in their house, like this is 1945 Germany,” Lane said. “It’s ridiculous.”

Some honked their cars while parked across the street. Others revved engines in the hotel parking lot. Semi-trucks and cars honked as they passed.

An officer with the Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department was dispatched to the hotel. Later, more IMPD officers arrived, Lane told WFYI. He said they told protesters the hotel wanted them to leave, and that they would violate a noise ordinance after 11 p.m. Lane said they decided to go home, then Friday morning around 6 a.m., a smaller crew set up across the street.

At the protest at the ICE office Saturday, Angelica Rabell said she felt like she needed to come because of the way she’s seen ICE officers treat immigrants, including legal citizens.

“Not only that, they had deported two people that I’ve known very close to me without any reason, and they also invaded the personal space of my own family members a few days ago,” Rabell said.

She said everything she’s seen in the past week has made her feel frustrated, and worried for those who don’t yet have full legal status. Rabell held a sign that read “no one deserves to die at the hands of ICE.”

Contact WFYI Government Reporter Caroline Beck at cbeck@wfyi.org

text:
INDIANAPOLIS (WISH) — Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have launched a series of raids across Indianapolis, sparking widespread fear and a sharp divide among the state’s political leaders. Multiple residents provided videos showing agents detaining individuals suspected of being in the country without legal authorization. One video shows a man in handcuffs pushed against a truck near the Carriage House Apartments on the city’s west side. Another shows an arrest at a Marathon gas station on East 38th Street.

Dallin Likens, an attorney with Banks and Brower, said the firm is seeing unusual confusion and fear among clients. He added that even those in the process of gaining citizenship now face uncertainty. Likens said federal policy changes have made it more difficult to secure releases from custody. Many individuals must now seek federal court orders, a process that is often cost-prohibitive.

“I would certainly say people are getting released from ICE custody, but it’s becoming much less likely and much more difficult.”

Mayor Joe Hogsett criticized the lack of communication from federal authorities, stating his office received no advance notice of the operations. Hogsett called the activity “cruelty” and noted that the raids are deterring residents from attending school, medical appointments, or grocery stores.

In contrast, U.S. Sen. Jim Banks supported the enforcement, stating on social media that ICE has a “constitutional responsibility” to deport those in the country illegally. Banks warned that he would not let Indianapolis become like Minneapolis.

U.S. Rep. Andre Carson launched a formal congressional inquiry into the scope and probable cause of the arrests. Carson, a former law enforcement officer, argued the arrests erode community trust and do not make the city safer. Carson said data indicate that 96% of ICE arrests in July involved individuals without prior criminal convictions. Carson expressed concern over racial profiling and government overreach. He also highlighted the danger of deporting Haitian immigrants to a country currently under a State Department travel advisory.

The political tension comes as Indiana focuses on its workforce needs. Otis Granberry of the Central Midwest Regional Council of Carpenters said the state needs more than 1,500 additional carpenters and millwrights by the end of the year to support major projects like the Eli Lilly expansions and the Lebanon data center. Granberry emphasized that union careers provide the wages and benefits families need to thrive. He also noted that unions are advocating for solutions to the state’s childcare shortage to help retain workers as older generations retire.

Democrat Laura Beck described a “culture of fear” that is harming the local economy. She argued that when people are afraid to go to work, they cannot pay rent or contribute to the community. Republican Matt Bell countered that the raids prioritize public safety and the rule of law.

Bell said that recent enforcement actions in Lawrence led to the apprehension of an individual with a felony drug warrant. While Beck warned of potential protests, Bell argued that local officials should cooperate with federal authorities to ensure community safety. He pointed to 287G agreements in nearby counties as a model for law enforcement cooperation.

text:
The far right, now on the cusp of power in France, could not have hoped for a better prelude to the 2027 presidential election campaign: a flood of teenagers crossing the border between Morocco and the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on July 30 and 31, making victory gestures. This was a perfect sequence to stoke fear of a so-called migratory "invasion," a narrative Marine Le Pen has long exploited.

European disarray, the lack of solidarity with Spain and calls from the right and far right to halt free movement with the country, even though none of the would-be emigrants from Ceuta managed to reach mainland Europe, all pointed to political leaders more eager to capitalize on a migration crisis than to unite in dealing with it.

Even a month later, it remains difficult to determine the origins of events that drove more than 70,000 people, mostly Moroccans, to cross the border illegally at the cost of around a hundred deaths. Although Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez dismissed, for lack of evidence, the idea of a Moroccan operation to pressure Madrid on Thursday, September 3, a Spanish police report highlighted the "permissiveness" of Moroccan security forces.

Sanchez also accused "social media networks linked to both Russia and Israel, as well as to a far-right international movement" of spreading false information about a possible route to Spain in order "to attack and divide Europe." These scenarios may have combined with the despair of Moroccan youth deprived of prospects by an economy built on privilege and cronyism. The new Ceuta crisis, in any case, illustrated the European Union's vulnerability to various forms of migratory pressure.

text:
Years ago, over curries at an embassy dinner, a charismatic Indian ambassador recounted some of his ripsnorting nicknames for fellow diplomats.

The Europeans, in particular the Scandinavians, he dubbed the “Axis of Good” because of smug human rights lectures delivered from high moral pedestals.

Those days might be numbered as European nations seek to borrow from Australia’s offshore immigration detention example and establish so-called return hubs in third countries for people with rejected asylum-seeker claims.

Rwanda and Uganda are in talks to host the centres. (A previous Denmark–Rwanda deal stalled.) Austrian media is reporting that Uganda could initially accommodate up to 10,000 migrants. (Opens in new window) Uzbekistan (Opens in new window) is another country reportedly in the mix.

On Friday, Denmark hosted immigration ministers from Germany, the Netherlands, Austria and Greece for talks, as a dozen demonstrators with megaphones and signs protested outside the Danish parliament.

“We expect to be ready to send the first foreigners to a partner country by the end of next year,” Danish immigration minister Morten Bødskov said, adding he hopes the first deal can be struck around New Year.

The facilities will not be a prison or detention camp, he said.

“It is an agreement with a partner country that gives people that have no legal grounds to be here an opportunity to have a new chance in the partner country,” he said.

The concept has echoes of Australia’s failed resettlement deals with Cambodia (Opens in new window) and Papua New Guinea (Opens in new window).

The five ministers will gather again in Munich later in September for further talks.

Fronting the media after the Copenhagen meeting, they had scant concrete details to share.

They insisted the return hubs “must have a measurable impact on reducing migration and perilous journeys to Europe” and that “Europe’s shared values and human rights must … be reflected in the way these arrangements are designed”.

As a former Canberra Press Gallery reporter who covered immigration at the height of Operation Sovereign Borders, I felt moments of déjà vu as these European ministers parroted lines Australian politicians have used for decades – “breaking the people smuggler’s business models” and “we will decide who comes to our country”.

It remains unclear exactly where duty of care or accountability on human rights violations would lie. The ministers said the International Organisation for Migration and United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees would be involved in monitoring the centres.

One hopes the ministers have done their homework and are taking lessons from Australia’s experience, which the United Nations (Opens in new window), Human Rights Watch (Opens in new window) and Amnesty International (Opens in new window) consider a human rights shitshow.

Denmark’s centre-left Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and her right-wing Italian counterpart Giorgia Meloni have pushed the European Union to take a harder line (Opens in new window) on border security and undocumented migrants and asylum seekers.

The continent is still reeling from the 2015 border security crisis that saw an influx of a million asylum seekers from Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq (Opens in new window).

In June this year, the European Parliament approved changes to migration policy (Opens in new window) to allow member states to set up deportation centres on foreign soil.

Chaotic scenes at Ceuta in August, in which tens of thousands of Moroccans surged into the little-known Spanish enclave in North Africa before being booted out, have also created urgency as far-right parties seek to capitalise on the saga (Opens in new window).

Rights groups are bracing for the worst. Amnesty International said there was a danger the centres “will become places where human rights do not seem to apply” (Opens in new window) and noted the dismal records of Rwanda and Uganda, including the persecution of LGBTQ people in the latter.

Its Netherlands branch described the moves as “a shameless attempt by the EU to shirk its responsibilities regarding migration and shift them onto countries in the South”.

“(European) governments across the political spectrum are now dancing to the same xenophobic and racist tune,” Amnesty NL said.

Other European attempts to send asylum seekers to non-European Union countries have struggled.

Italy has had legal woes (Opens in new window). It had hoped to send 3000 people to Albanian centres but so far only 500 (Opens in new window) have gone at a cost of €670 million (more than A$1 billion) – which is seven times more expensive than an equivalent Italian centre. (Opens in new window)

In 2023, Britain’s High Court ruled that Rwanda was not a safe country for the UK to deport asylum seekers (Opens in new window) arriving on British shores. Former British Labour prime minister Keir Starmer scrapped the deal with Kigali that was set up by conservative leader Boris Johnson’s government. Only four people ended up going to Rwanda and the exercise cost British taxpayers £290 million (A$545 million) (Opens in new window).

The European Union has long considered itself a bastion of human rights and says the bloc’s work “remained grounded in our commitment to protect human rights and democracy”.

“No amount of chaos or conflict will ever change the fact that human dignity, justice and accountability are the only path to peace and prosperity for all,” the EU’s top diplomat said in the foreword of its 2025 human rights annual report (Opens in new window).

But if European countries head down Australia’s asylum-seeker outsourcing path, suicides and self-harm (Opens in new window) are probably inevitable, not to mention the risk of riots and murders (Opens in new window), corruption scandals (Opens in new window) and dodgy contractors (Opens in new window).

Europe’s human rights halo might not be so shiny for much longer.

text:
During the early hours of a recent morning, legal advocates with the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition awakened to buzzing cell phones.

More than 120 men and women had been rounded up by immigration agents inside the Memphis nightclub, El Corralón. Their families and friends needed help.

"Parents didn't come home. Roommates and friends stopped answering the phone. Workers and business owners didn't show up on Monday morning, and cars were left in the parking lot of the nightclub," said Lisa Sherman Luna, the coalition's executive director.

The raid, executed through at least two search warrants obtained by the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation in Shelby County Criminal Court, and reviewed by the Tennessee Lookout, was among the largest immigrant roundups in recent Tennessee history.

The incident occurred amid an escalation in immigrant arrests nationwide that began at the start of summer, following a temporary decline in activity after the January shooting deaths by ICE agents of two Minneapolis residents.

Trump administration officials have touted the immigration crackdowns, in Memphis and elsewhere, as both part of a broader public safety push and a fulfillment of the president's campaign promises to stem illegal immigration.

"Thanks to President Trump's leadership, crime in the city of Memphis has plummeted," a statement from Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said recently.

"A big part of that success comes from arresting and deporting illegal aliens in the city," the statement said.

On Thursday, Sherman Luna joined national immigration advocates during a press conference to discuss the Memphis raid and other recent events in Tennessee that, they said, highlight the state's increasingly pivotal role in the Trump administration immigration enforcement and deportation agenda.

The Memphis nightclub raid is among a recent string of events in Tennessee tied to the Trump administration's immigration policies.

In May and June, four Black men were fatally shot in separate incidents by members of the Memphis Safe Task Force, a concentrated crime fighting effort that has brought multiple federal and state agencies, and the Tennessee National Guard, to Memphis. The task force includes Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Homeland Security Investigations, which both enforce immigration law. A Homeland Security Investigations officer fired her weapon during one of the four fatal encounters, according to the TBI. No charges have been brought against officers in any of the fatal shootings.

Late last month, the Lookout first reported the federal government's $63 million contract with the Alaska-based Koniag corporation to establish a 24-7 ICE call center in Tennessee to more closely coordinate with local law enforcement across the country to locate and detain immigrants, including children. (Contract documents initially placed the ICE coordination center in Adams, Tenn., before being updated to reflect Nashville is its planned location).

A spokesperson for Koniag last week did not respond to a request for more information. A spokesperson for ICE declined to discuss details of the planned coordination center.

The federal activities, paired with a slew of state-level legislation introducing immigration status verification into routine interactions with state and local government, "are turning Tennessee into a national hub for the mass deportation machine," Sherman Luna said.

Hadi Sedigh, senior strategist with the National Immigration Law Center, called Tennessee a "testing ground" for the Trump administration as it puts into place similar task force collaborations between federal and local law enforcement elsewhere. Sedigh also highlighted a key priority of the Trump administration to expand so-called 287(g) agreements that delegate immigration arrest powers to local police and sheriffs.

The administration's goal has been codified into law in Tennessee, with legislation enacted this year requiring all sheriffs and police departments to enter the agreements by 2027. Tennessee was among the first states to implement the requirement as part of a package of legislation targeting immigrants that grew out of meetings between Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton, R-Crossville, and White House advisor Stephen Miller.

"The mechanisms that helped make the midnight raid in Memphis possible, namely the 287(g) agreements and the joint federal task force model are, in effect, rapidly increasing in a number of jurisdictions throughout the country," Sedigh said.

text:
PHOENIX — Federal officials have apparently chosen a company with no experience conducting environmental reviews to perform one for a proposed Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility in Surprise.

In a Friday court filing, the Department of Homeland Security said it has retained a contractor to assist in the review, part of a deal with the state Attorney General’s Office to forestall a lawsuit. That deal prevents ICE from detaining people in the warehouse until DHS can prove it can house up to 1,500 people.

That filing does not list who will be conducting the review. But the city of Surprise, in a web post, said its staffers met with a GardaWorld representative who is seeking information for the assessment.

GardaWord has already signed a $313.4 million contract with DHS to renovate andoperate the facility. The agreement even provides for a possible extension through early 2029, making it worth more than $700 million.

GardaWorld, mostly known for things like providing security guards and operating a fleet of armored cars, referred all questions to Homeland Security.

That agency provided only a prepared statement about its focus on removing “the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens from the United States and is always evaluation the best methods to do so.”

As to the status of the Surprise facility, the statement effectively acknowledges that a federal court agreement with Attorney General Kris Mayes prevents anyone from being housed there until the agreed-to assessment is complete.

“DHS is moving swiftly to utilize EXISTING detention space with our state and county partners,” the statement reads. There was no answer to the question of GardaWorld’s experience — or even confirmation that company is doing the assessment.

Mayes filed suit in April after ICE purchased the facility. That federal ownership stripped city officials of any power to use their own zoning and other laws to restrict its operation.

But the attorney general is instead using the National Environmental Policy Act to require an assessment — if not a full-blown environmental impact statement. And Mayes has made it clear she believes that such an assessment will conclude that the site is inappropriate for such a facility.

That environmental impact is not just about the impact of the facility, like how its operation would affect the city’s sewage. The warehouse itself also sits across the street from a hazardous materials storage warehouse where chemical leaks or explosions are possible.

It is true, Mayes conceded in April, that there already are nearby homes where residents also would be affected by such an occurrence.

“But the major distinction is the sheer number of people who will be housed in this facility and can’t get out,” the attorney general said. “If this thing blows up, they will be locked in that facility with no way of getting out.”

That, she said, will create additional pressures on local fire departments and emergency responders.

And Mayes said the warehouse, if allowed to be used to house ICE detainees, will use so much water that it could leave firefighters without what they need to battle an explosion or blaze at the chemical facility.

The lawsuit initially drew derision from a representative from ICE.

“Let’s be hones about what is happening,” the statement read.

“This isn’t about the environment,” it said. “It’s about trying to stop President Trump from making America safe.”

And the representative dismissed the need for formal environmental studies.

“Prior to purchasing this site, ICE carefully evaluated the use of existing facilities to help minimize environmental impacts,” the statement said.

But facing a possible federal court order delaying — or even halting — the project, Homeland Security said it would provide the assessment. It also agreed not to open the facility until the assessment was completed. And the agency promised to provide regular updates to the court.

That latest update, filed Friday, is where Homeland Security said it had retained a contractor “and has begun working with the contractor.”

“The environmental review remains ongoing,” Julian Kurtz, an attorney with the U.S. Department of Justice, told Judge Susan Brnovich.

text:
A supervisor overseeing background checks warned last year that Immigration and Customs Enforcement was hiring many new officers who had not undergone basic vetting, violating federal rules and putting the agency at risk of misconduct, a newly released whistleblower complaint shows.

The official was a unit chief in ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility, where background checks were backlogged as ICE added thousands of new officers to carry out President Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign.

ICE's human resources division was making final job offers before preliminary vetting steps had been completed, including fingerprints, identity verification and credit checks, the official's complaint warned.

"This unprecedented lowering of standards sacrifices proper risk mitigation for expediency, placing DHS at risk of infiltration and insider compromise," the official wrote in a memo to the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General dated August 2025.

"This unprecedented lowering of standards sacrifices proper risk mitigation for expediency, placing DHS at risk of infiltration and insider compromise." – Former unit chief, in ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility

The New York Times first reported on the whistleblower complaint Sept. 3. The Associated Press obtained the complaint and a related memo from the now-retired ICE official's lawyer, Kevin Owen. The official's identity was redacted from the complaint. The Times said the official was a 17-year-agency employee and longtime Republican who had voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024.

ICE announced in January that it had hired 12,000 new officers in less than one year, a spree financed by a $75 billion infusion from Congress to increase the agency's arrests and deportations.

The rapid pace of the hiring, fueled by a $50,000 signing bonus, raised concerns about the quality of the new employees. An investigation by The Associated Press found that some of the new hires had serious financial problems in their backgrounds, had been accused of misconduct in prior jobs, and had checkered employment histories.

In July, Tom Homan, the White House border czar, said ICE would investigate apparent shortcomings in the vetting of an officer who shot and killed a 25-year-old motorist in Maine.

The whistleblower complaint said that "systemic breakdowns in vetting" violated several federal rules and standards designed to ensure candidates are suitable for sensitive law enforcement and national security positions.

The complaint said the lack of vetting created "increased vulnerability to insider threats, infiltration and foreign influence," undermined ICE's law enforcement operations and eroded public confidence in the agency.

It asked the inspector general to investigate the personnel vetting failures and for the agency to immediately suspend the improper practices, hold accountable those responsible for the violations and to review all recent hires to identify potential "insider threats."

The Office of Inspector General has previously announced that it is investigating ICE's hiring and training process, as well as security clearances granted to contractors and political appointees.

In a statement, ICE said Sept. 3 the whistleblower was no longer with the agency.

"The ICE Office of Professional Responsibility diligently applies the proper personnel vetting regulations, including guidelines for national security, and evaluates all available information for every applicant based on these factors," the statement said.

As the AP previously reported, ICE acknowledged that some applicants received "tentative selection letters" after their initial applications and interviews. Some were allowed to begin training before their background investigations were completed.

The whistleblower is the second insider to call out ICE's rush to put more officers on the streets as reckless.

A former agency lawyer and instructor at the ICE academy, Ryan Schwank, said the agency cut training on the use of force, firearms safety, and the rights of protesters last year. The Department of Homeland Security has since increased the amount of training for new officers.

___

text:
A surge in immigration arrests is sweeping up immigrants with no criminal record whatsoever, including many who were already known by the government, as officers push to meet quotas set by the Trump administration.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers broke records for the second Trump administration with back-to-back months of arrests topping 50,000 in July and August.

But the data undercut a long-running claim by the Trump administration that it is targeting the “worst of the worst” by removing those with criminal records.

In fact, more than half of those arrested — 55 percent — had no interaction with law enforcement whatsoever, while another 24 percent have faced charges but were never convicted, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project.

These statistics have raised reservations among some Republicans in Congress.

“I’ve been telling the administration that do not conflate the gangster with the gardener, the nanny with the narco,” said Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.), who represents a district where more than half the population is foreign born.

It’s a figure that reflects a growing dynamic in immigration enforcement under the Trump administration — going after those with pending asylum claims or are otherwise seeking to adjust their status who are already known to authorities.

“What this shows is that the Trump administration is expanding its mass deportation operations away from people who are public safety threats or who have had some interaction with the criminal justice system and towards everybody else in an effort to hit the quotas put on them by the White House,” Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow with the American Immigration Council, told The Hill.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has offered mixed messaging on the extent it is still prioritizing criminals for removal.

On social platform X, the department maintains that 70 percent of those arrested by ICE have criminal records — a statement that is demonstrably false based on its own data.

“I mean the 70 percent figure has not been true since May of 2025,” Reichlin-Melnick said.

“DHS has been giving the 70 percent figure for at least a year now. It’s not true. It hasn’t been true. The agency has released extensive data confirming that it’s not true.”

But in media appearances, leaders have also distanced themselves from stressing the importance of arresting criminals, even as media releases from the agency continue to tout deportations of “the worst of the worst.”

“These individuals that we’re going after — I don’t care if you have a criminal background or don’t have a criminal background, you chose to break the law when you came across our border illegally. It’s our position and our job to hunt you down and send you back to where you came from,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said this past week during an appearance on “The Ingraham Angle.”

Border czar Tom Homan also contradicted the DHS’s claims during an appearance on the same show in July.

“Just over half of everybody we’re arresting is a criminal. So about half are noncriminals,” he said.

“But bottom line is, everybody’s on the table. The numbers show it’s about half and half now. … And with the additional resources we got from the reconciliation bill, you wait to see what the numbers are this year.”

There have been several factors behind the uptick in arrests, from a stealthier approach to enforcement under Mullin that departed from the widely publicized raids used previously to more recent tactics like arrests of immigrants at airports.

“This is from all the different tactics coming together really for the first time. The street arrests happening at the same time you have all the check-ins for people, immigration court interactions. All that stuff’s coming together — the airport arrests,” said David Bier, director of immigration studies at the libertarian Cato Institute.

Bier noted that Mullin got to the department as “all these resources [were] coming online at the same time.”

“They’re paying people a huge amount of overtime. They have no worries about money, so you know that’s a big part of it too is they just have people working like crazy to get these through,” he said.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (Wash.), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary subcommittee on immigration, said the less overt operations carried out by Mullin are in part due to the backlash to the much publicized raids carried out under former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

“They are continuing this strategy quietly now because it was unpopular when it was loud. But they’re going to find out in November that it’s unpopular when it’s quiet as well,” she told The Hill.

“They’re just arresting anyone. It’s just all about their ultimate number.”

Reichlin-Melnick noted that many of those being arrested, beyond having no criminal record, are also people who are already in immigration processing.

“We’re seeing this expanded to people at airports, people who overstayed their visa solely because the U.S. government didn’t get around to adjudicating their case in time, and these are people who really have done nothing wrong. They took the path that the Trump administration itself used to say was the right way,” he said.

“More and more of those people are now being swept into the mass deportation machine, despite the fact that they have pending applications with the U.S. government and have been complying with every obligation put on them. So why is the administration going after them? Because in some ways they are the easiest targets. They tell the government who they are or where they live. … And so when the U.S. government needs to ramp up arrest numbers, it can just go after those people rather than having to find people that it doesn’t know about already.”

Bier noted the increase in the number of those arrested without a final order of removal — an order given by an immigration judge after determining someone should be deported — leaving them waiting in detention as they continue to fight their case.

“Pretty soon, it’s going to be a majority of their deportations are not going to be based on a final order of removal, which will be just a real threshold for proving the success of the strategy, which is arrest and detain people without removal orders, and then just hope they give up,” he said.

The surge in arrests has led to some backlash, even in solidly red Florida, where immigrant communities include naturalized citizens as well as those who do not have status.

“Look, I’ve always supported TPS for Venezuelans, for Haitians,” said Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart (R-Fla.), referencing the temporary protected status program that protects people who are otherwise deportable from being sent back to countries that are considered dangerous.

“Securing the border had to happen. It’s worked. It’s good. It’s good for our security. But some of the enforcement, I think, has been a bit of an overreach, to say the least — to say the least. I’ve expressed that.”

“You can enforce the border, but I think you also have to hopefully look at all the circumstances when you have some specific cases,” he added.

Salazar, who has sponsored the Dignity Act as a way to help those without legal status gain a pathway to remain in the country, said the administration has failed to account for the economic contribution made by those without criminal records who have been working in the U.S. for years.

“The people who’ve been here for decades in construction, hospitality, agricultural, healthcare, manufacturing [industries] — those people are needed, and we need it for the economy. It’s just that there is a disconnect. … The White House is not understanding that those people are needed for the economy,” she said.

“And that those are our values as Americans.”

text:
Protesters gathered Saturday to make their presence known after increased activity from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement was witnessed across Indianapolis this past week. They met near the federal agency's west side office.

The weekend protest followed two other demonstrations held at a hotel less than half a mile from the ICE office.

The increased ICE activity seen in Indianapolis coincides with a record-high number of arrests made by ICE in July, nearly 50,000 across the country, according to data gathered by the Deportation Data Project based at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA.

An unidentified spokesperson from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not answer questions sent by WFYI asking for the number of arrests made in Indiana this past week, or provide confirmation of increased enforcement operations in Indianapolis. They did reiterate their goal, at the directive of President Donald Trump, to deport criminals and anyone who entered the country illegally.

Saturday's demonstration at the ICE office attracted over 100 protesters who oppose the influx of arrests and detainments witnessed through social media posts.

ICE agents and other law enforcement have been seen making arrests in residential neighborhoods, gas stations and other areas across the city.

Jesus Ramirez has been a community organizer and activist fighting for immigrants' rights in Indiana for years. He said a few concerned individuals organized Saturday's protest, not a single organization.

"It's one of those things where as long as [ICE is] going to continue terrorizing our people, we're going to continue to be in front of your building, being as loud as we possibly can to let you know that we're not moving," Ramirez told WFYI.

Ramirez said he knows some of the individuals recently arrested or detained by ICE. He believes the arrests have been racially motivated and that the agency is no longer focused on getting "the worst of the worst."

"The collateral damage that we're seeing is bigger than if they're going for one person supposedly with a warrant, and there's six other people around that have nothing to do with it," Ramirez said. "They're getting dragged along with no due process."

Ramirez said he's spoken with families who said they're afraid to get groceries or send their kids to school.

An analysis done by the New York Times on ICE arrests found that a majority of immigrants arrested in July had not been charged with or convicted of a crime, but were accused of violating civil immigration laws.

Noise protests

On Thursday evening people arrived at a Hampton Inn, less than half a mile away from Indianapolis' west side ICE office, where organizers believed ICE agents were staying as guests.

"It's a noise rally, basically, to make sure that they feel very unwelcome, that they feel very uncomfortable, and that they don't have a moment of peace while they're here terrorizing Indianapolis residents," organizer Stephen Lane, who is with the Indianapolis Party for Socialism and Liberation, told WFYI at the protest.

WFYI did not confirm whether ICE agents stayed at the hotel or not.

After the sun set, over 50 people were spread across the lawn in front of the hotel lobby. Organizers with megaphones led the demonstration in chants, including "ICE out now!" and "Chinga la migra!" Some had musical instruments — horns, a trombone and a saxophone — and played a beat on makeshift drums and bells.

Lane said he's been checking on immigrant residents he knows in Indianapolis since arrest reports picked up.

"To see that they have to go through this, these raids in our communities, in our neighborhoods — it makes me sick seeing it happen all over the internet. I know that some people are hiding their immigrant neighbors in their house, like this is 1945 Germany," Lane said. "It's ridiculous."

Some honked their cars while parked across the street. Others revved engines in the hotel parking lot. Semi-trucks and cars honked as they passed.

An officer with the Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department was dispatched to the hotel. Later, more IMPD officers arrived, Lane told WFYI. He said they told protesters the hotel wanted them to leave, and that they would violate a noise ordinance after 11 p.m. Lane said they decided to go home, then Friday morning around 6 a.m., a smaller crew set up across the street.

At the protest at the ICE office Saturday, Angelica Rabell said she felt like she needed to come because of the way she's seen ICE officers treat immigrants, including legal citizens.

"Not only that, they had deported two people that I've known very close to me without any reason, and they also invaded the personal space of my own family members a few days ago," Rabell said.

She said everything she's seen in the past week has made her feel frustrated, and worried for those who don't yet have full legal status. Rabell held a sign that read "no one deserves to die at the hands of ICE."

Contact WFYI Government Reporter Caroline Beck at cbeck@wfyi.org

text:
By Jongwon Lee, American Community Media

SAVANNAH, Ga. — Kim vividly remembers the Sept. 4, 2025 ICE raid on the Hyundai-LG battery plant in Georgia. Working in an office near the facility, she learned from a coworker that the plant was surrounded by helicopters and military-style armored vehicles.

She turned on the television and saw news coverage of workers being handcuffed and shackled. By the end of the day, several of her coworkers had not returned to the Savannah-area joint-company plant, which was still under construction at the time.

When Kim — who asked to be identified only by her last name — drove to the plant after the raid, she found the parking lot filled with hundreds of empty vehicles.

“It was like the aftermath of a war zone,” she recalled.

Working as a human resources manager for an LG contractor which mobilized staff to help detainees, Kim spent hours every morning over the week following the raid outside the Folkston ICE Processing Center seeking visitation with detained colleagues.

“Some days, visitation was denied, or abruptly canceled after an hour or two without explanation or notice,” she said.

Her duties also included retrieving abandoned vehicles, contacting detainees’ families in South Korea and packing personal belongings — tasks she described as painful.

Ultimately, more than 300 South Korean nationals were released and returned to South Korea after eight days in detention.

When construction of the battery plant was completed in early 2026, Kim sold her home in Georgia and moved to Texas to work at another technology facility.

She said she had little optimism left for her future in Georgia, noting that Texas had not taken similar enforcement actions against invited foreign investors.

She noted that the experience left a lasting impact, leading her to refrain from international business travel to Mexico despite holding legal U.S. immigrant status for years.

Aftermath of the ICE raid

One year after the enforcement action, construction on the Hyundai-LG battery plant is finished. The Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America (HMGMA) appears fully operational, following executive announcements targeting increased production in Georgia.

However, a few blocks behind the facility, an Asian grocery store that once sold kimchi and ramen to workers has closed. Local resident Morgan Foreman noted that the store shut down months after the raid.

Local Korean restaurant owner Moon — who asked to be identified by his last name — noted that abandoned and returned items, including boxes of Korean ramen, accumulated at customer service centers in local grocery stores after Korean workers suddenly departed following the raid.

The raid also heavily impacted non-Korean workers.

According to Jenny Miron of local non-profit Migrant Equity Southeast (MESE), at least 175 Latino workers — primarily from Venezuela — were detained.

Following the release and departure of the South Korean workers, only nine Latino workers are known to have been released through legal support from organizations like MESE. The remaining workers were deported, removed, granted voluntary departure or opted for self-deportation.

“Many Latino workers still remain in legal limbo and face pressure to leave the country,” Miron said.

She added that heightened ICE activity and police presence have contributed to financial hardship and legal uncertainty among affected families: “Community organizations have had to step in with direct support, including gift cards, food boxes, transportation and pro bono legal assistance to help families stay afloat.”

A continued atmosphere of fear

A year after the raid, ongoing enforcement activities continue to cause concern among workers in coastal Georgian communities like Savannah.

Miron noted that heavy police presence and ICE activity have created an atmosphere of fear, leaving some community members hesitant to go to work, shop for groceries or drop their children off at school.

Similar concerns have been raised in metro Atlanta.

Eulen Jang, policy advocacy manager at the Asian American Advocacy Fund (AAAF), addressed the DeKalb County Board of Education on Aug. 10, urging officials to protect students from ICE activities within the district.

“This isn’t a political issue; it’s a student safety issue and an immigrant rights issue,” Jang testified.

She added: “There are many instances of ICE agents showing up at homes, worksites, and other locations without presenting a warrant, or using documentation that is legally insufficient. It can be intimidating to staff members if ICE shows up to a school while personnel are unclear about district procedures or how to verify legal authenticity.”

On Aug. 7, three days before Jang’s testimony, ICE announced the arrest of 1,226 individuals across Georgia as part of an enforcement initiative designated “Operation Safe Community — Atlanta.”

According to ICE statements, 720 of those arrested had prior criminal charges or convictions in the United States, while the remaining 506 had no criminal records but were cited for immigration violations.

The recent ICE operations in metro Atlanta have drawn public scrutiny.

On Aug. 11, WSB-TV reported that ICE agents mistakenly handcuffed a U.S. citizen, John Phillips, on a jet bridge at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport.

ICE later confirmed that agents were searching for a British national with the same name and date of birth.

Local law enforcement agencies have noted a lack of direct coordination with federal officers.

During an Aug. 12 “Coffee with a Cop” event with members of the Korean community, representatives from the Duluth Police Department stated that they had not been contacted nor consulted by ICE regarding recent arrests in metro Atlanta.

In both coastal Georgia and metro Atlanta, community members state that systemic issues remain unresolved a year after the ICE raid in Georgia.

Corey Foreman, a Savannah-area businessman and Democratic candidate for the state Senate, characterized the 2025 raid as more of a “media stunt” than a targeted immigration operation, noting that “many workers were on valid visas for technical setup rather than permanent immigration.”

He added that public updates and media coverage ceased shortly after the raid, leaving residents with little information regarding subsequent developments.

Miron expressed concern over the persistent “status quo” one year later, emphasizing the role of community support, social media campaigns and donations in providing essential food, transportation and legal assistance.

“Solidarity gives our immigrant communities hope,” Miron said. “Even as the political landscape changes daily, knowing there are people willing to offer support encourages individuals to speak out and help one another.”
